**Surat al-Anbiya' (The Prophets)**
112 verses, Meccan

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿The reckoning of mankind has drawn near, yet they are heedless and turn away.﴾ ﴿No new reminder comes to them from their Lord but they listen to it while playing,﴾ ﴿their hearts distracted. And the wrongdoers confide in secret, saying: "Is this not but a human being like you? Will you then go to sorcery with your eyes open?"﴾

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿The reckoning of mankind has drawn near, yet they are heedless and turn away.﴾ ﴿No new reminder comes to them from their Lord but they listen to it while playing,﴾ ﴿their hearts distracted. And the wrongdoers confide in secret, saying: "Is this not but a human being like you? Will you then go to sorcery with your eyes open?"﴾.

Know that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The reckoning of mankind has drawn near﴾ contains several issues (masa'il, sing. mas'alah, a point of discussion):

**The first issue:** Nearness is only conceivable in place or in time. Nearness of place is impossible here, so nearness of time is what is meant. The meaning is: the time of their reckoning has drawn near for mankind.

**The second issue:** Someone may ask how the reckoning can be described as having "drawn near" when more than six hundred years have passed since this statement. The answer has three aspects:

First: it is near in the sight of God, exalted is He. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿They ask you to hasten the punishment, but God will not fail His promise. Indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count.﴾ (Al-Hajj 22:47).

Second: every coming thing is near, however long the wait for it may be, and it is only what has passed that is distant. The poet said:

*"May what you desire never cease to be nearer than tomorrow,
and may what you fear never cease to be further than yesterday."*

Third: when a transaction is deferred to a year and a month of it has passed, one does not say the term has drawn near. But when more of it has passed than remains, one says the term has drawn near. On this aspect, the scholars said: this indicates the nearness of the Resurrection. For this aspect, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I was sent and the Hour are like these two," and it has been said that he, peace be upon him, concluded prophethood with this. All of this is because the remaining portion of the period of accountability is less than what has passed.

**The third issue:** God mentioned this nearness because of the benefit it holds for those who are accountable, so that it is closer to making them avoid sins and guard against them out of fear of it. And God knows best.

**The fourth issue:** He did not specify the time because keeping it hidden is better, just as keeping the time of death hidden is better.

**The fifth issue:** The benefit in naming the Day of Resurrection the Day of Reckoning is that reckoning is what reveals a person's state, so fear of mentioning it is greater.

**The sixth issue:** The intended meaning of "mankind" must be those who are subject to reckoning, namely the accountable, and not those who have no part in it. Then Ibn 'Abbas said: the intended meaning of "mankind" is the polytheists. This is the use of a generic term for a part of its referents, based on the evident indication, which is what follows of the attributes of the polytheists.

As for His saying: ﴿yet they are heedless and turn away﴾, know that He described them with two matters: heedlessness and turning away. As for heedlessness, the meaning is that they are oblivious of their reckoning and inattentive, not reflecting on their end, even though their intellects require that there must be a recompense for the doer of good and the doer of evil. Then, when they awaken from the slumber of heedlessness and the sleep of ignorance, by means of the verses and warnings recited to them, they turn away and stop their ears.

As for His saying: ﴿No new reminder comes to them from their Lord﴾, there are issues concerning it:

**The first issue:** Ibn Abi 'Abla read *muhdathun* ("new") in the nominative case, as an attribute of the noun (*mahall*) (i.e., of the word "reminder" in its position).

**The second issue:** God mentioned this to show that they are turning away. This is because God renews the reminder for them from time to time, and shows them a verse after a verse and a sura after a sura, so as to repeat the admonition and exhortation in their ears, perhaps they would be warned. Yet this only increases them in play and mockery.

**The third issue:** The Mu'tazilah (a theological school that held the Qur'an was created in time) argued for the createdness of the Qur'an from this verse. They said: The Qur'an is a *dhikr* (reminder), and the *dhikr* is created, so the Qur'an is created. The proof that the Qur'an is a *dhikr* is God's saying describing the Qur'an: ﴿It is only a reminder to the worlds﴾ (Sad 38:87), and His saying: ﴿It is indeed a reminder for you and your people﴾ (Al-Zukhruf 43:44), and His saying: ﴿Sad. By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾ (Sad 38:1), and His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Reminder﴾ (Al-Hijr 15:9), and His saying: ﴿It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an﴾ (Ya-Sin 36:69), and His saying: ﴿And this is a blessed reminder which We have sent down﴾ (Al-Anbiya' 21:50). The proof that the reminder is created is His saying in this place: ﴿No new reminder comes to them from their Lord﴾, and His saying in Surat al-Shu'ara': ﴿No new reminder comes to them from the Most Merciful﴾ (Al-Shu'ara' 26:5). Then they said: the combination of these two explicit premises becomes like an explicit statement that the Qur'an is created.

The answer has two aspects:

The first: His saying ﴿It is only a reminder to the worlds﴾ (Sad 38:87) and His saying ﴿And this is a blessed reminder﴾ (Al-Anbiya' 21:50) refer to what is composed of letters and sounds. If we add to it His saying ﴿No new reminder comes to them from their Lord﴾, it follows that what is composed of letters and sounds is created. That is not disputed; rather its createdness is known by necessity. The dispute is only about the eternity of God's speech in another sense.

The second: His saying ﴿No new reminder comes to them from their Lord﴾ does not indicate the createdness of everything that is a reminder, but only of a reminder that is new. This is like the statement of someone: "No virtuous man enters this town but they hate him." This does not indicate that every man must be virtuous, but rather that among men there is one who is virtuous. If that is so, the verse indicates only that some of the reminder is new, and the statement of the argument becomes thus: The Qur'an is a reminder, and some of the reminder is new. This produces nothing, just as the statement of someone: "Man is an animal, and some animals are horses" produces nothing. Thus it becomes clear that what they took to be decisive does not even yield a weak supposition, let alone certainty.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 21, verses 2–3:

As for His saying, ﴿except that they listen to it while they play﴾, ﴿their hearts distracted﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: This is a rebuke of the disbelievers and a warning to others against doing the same, because benefit from what is heard can only come through what reaches the heart of reflection and contemplation. When they listen to it while playing, they attain only mere hearing, in which even an animal may share with a human. Then God, exalted is He, emphasized their blame with His saying, ﴿their hearts distracted﴾. The word "lāhiyah" (distracted) derives from "lahā 'anhu," meaning he became heedless and neglectful. He mentioned "play" (la'ib) before "distraction" (lahw) as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The life of this world is only play and distraction﴾ [Muhammad: 36], as an indication that their occupation with play, which means mockery and ridicule, is caused by distraction, which means inattentiveness and heedlessness. They engaged in play because of their distraction and their being oblivious to the truth. And God knows best what is correct.

The second issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: ﴿while they play﴾ and ﴿their hearts distracted﴾ are two successive circumstantial clauses (ḥālān), either coordinated or interlinked. And whoever reads "lāhiyatun" with a nominative ending (ar-raf') makes it a single circumstance, because "their hearts distracted" is a second predicate following the predicate of "they" (hum) in His saying.

As for His saying, ﴿And they secretly conferred, those who did wrong﴾, there are two questions:

The first question: "al-najwā" is a noun from "al-tanājī" (private conversation) and can only be done in secret, so what is the meaning of His saying, ﴿they secretly conferred﴾? The answer: its meaning is that they went to great lengths to conceal it, making it such that no one would notice their private consultation.

The second question: Why did He say, ﴿And they secretly conferred, those who did wrong﴾? The answer: "those who did wrong" is a substitute for the subject of "they secretly conferred," to indicate that they are the ones characterized by gross wrongdoing in what they concealed. Or it follows the dialect of one who said: "The fleas bit me" (akalūnī al-barāghīth). Or it is in the accusative case by way of censure. Or it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is "they secretly conferred," placed before it, and the meaning is "and these people secretly conferred," so the explicit noun is placed in the position of the pronoun to record their act as wrongdoing.

As for His saying, ﴿Is this anything but a human being like you? Will you then approach magic while you see?﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said that this entire statement is in the accusative case as a substitute for "al-najwā," meaning "and they secretly conferred this discourse." It is also possible that the estimate is "and they secretly conferred and said this statement."

The second issue: They concealed this discourse for two reasons. The first: that this was a semblance of consultation among themselves and mutual discussion in seeking a way to demolish his affair, and it is the custom of those consulting to strive to keep their secrets from their enemies. The second: it is possible that they concealed their private conversation about this and then said to the Messenger of God and the believers: "If what you call to is true, then tell us what we have concealed."

The third issue: They attacked his prophethood on two grounds. The first: that he is a human being like them. The second: that what he brought is magic. Both attacks are invalid. As for the first: prophethood's validity rests on miracles and proofs, not on outward forms. For if God sent an angel to them, it would not be known that he was a prophet by his form; rather it would be known only by knowledge. When this is manifested through one who is a human, it is obligatory that he be a prophet. Indeed, it is more fitting that the one sent to humans be a human, because a person is closer to accepting from those of his own kind and more at ease with them. As for the second, which is that what the Messenger, peace be upon him, brought is magic and that they see it as magic, this is also ignorance, because everything the Messenger brought, both the Qur'an and other things, is manifest in its condition, with no deception or confusion in it. He, peace be upon him, challenged them with the Qur'an repeatedly over a period of time while they were masters of eloquence and rhetoric, and they were in the utmost eagerness to nullify his affair. The strongest means of nullifying his affair would be to counter the Qur'an. Had they been able to counter it, it would have been impossible for them not to do so, because an act, when the motives are abundant and the obstacle is removed, is bound to occur. Since they did not produce it, this indicates that it is in itself a miracle and that they recognized its true state. How then could it be said that it is magic, when the situation is as we have described? All of this shows that they were knowledgeable of his truthfulness, except that they were disguising matters to their weak followers with such statements, though they were obstinate in denying it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 21, verses 4–6:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said: "My Lord knows every word in the heaven and the earth, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing."﴾ ﴿Nay, they say: "Confused dreams! Nay, he has invented it! Nay, he is a poet! Let him bring us a sign, as the earlier messengers were sent."﴾ ﴿No town that We destroyed before them believed. Will they then believe?﴾

As for His saying: ﴿He said: "My Lord knows every word in the heaven and the earth, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing."﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: It has been recited as "Qāla rabbī" (He said: "My Lord"), as a quotation of the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This is the reading of Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs from ʿAsim. The rest read "Qul" (Say), with a damma on the qaf, the alif omitted, and the lam sukun.

The second issue: When Exalted Allah placed this statement right after what He related about them, it must serve as a response to what they had said. It is as if He said: Even though you conceal your speech and your slander, indeed My Lord knows of it, and He is behind His punishment. So threaten them with this, so that they do not return to the like of it.

The third issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: If you say, why was it not said, "He knows the secret," in accordance with His saying: ﴿And they conceal their private counsel﴾? I say: "Speech" is general, encompassing both the secret and the open, so knowing it implies knowing the secret plus more. Thus it is more emphatic in showing His awareness of their private counsel than saying: ﴿He knows the secret﴾ [Ta-Ha: 7]. Just as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He knows the secret﴾ is more emphatic than saying "He knows their secret." If you say: Why did He leave the more emphatic form in surah al-Furqan in His saying: ﴿Say: "He who knows the secret in the heavens and the earth has sent it down."﴾ [al-Furqan: 6]? I say: It is not obligatory to use the more emphatic form in every passage; rather, He uses emphasis once and the more emphatic form at another time. Moreover, the difference is that here He first mentioned that they conceal their private counsel, so it is as if He intended to say: "Indeed My Lord knows what they conceal," so He placed "speech" in the place of that for intensification. There, He intended to describe His essence by saying: ﴿who has sent it down, He who knows the secret in the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Furqan: 6]. This is like His saying: ﴿Knower of the unseen﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 109], and ﴿the Knower of the unseen, from whom not an atom's weight escapes﴾ [Saba': 3].

The fourth issue: He placed the All-Hearing before the All-Knowing because hearing the speech must come first, and then acquiring knowledge of its meaning. As for His saying: ﴿Nay, they say: "Confused dreams! Nay, he has invented it! Nay, he is a poet! Let him bring us a sign, as the earlier messengers were sent."﴾, know that He, exalted is He, returned to relating their saying connected to His saying: ﴿Is this not but a human like you? Will you then approach magic while you see?﴾ Then He said: ﴿Nay, they say: "Confused dreams! Nay, he has invented it! Nay, he is a poet!"﴾. So He related these five statements from them there. The arrangement of their speech is as if they said: "We claim that his being a human prevents him from being a messenger of Allah, the Exalted. Suppose we grant that it does not prevent it; but we do not grant that this Qur'an is a miracle. Then either we support that the eloquence of the Qur'an is beyond human capacity, and we say: why could it not be magic? And even if we do not support that, if we claim it is in the utmost incoherence, we say: it is confused dreams; if we claim it is intermediate between incoherence and eloquence, we say: it is invention; and if we claim it is eloquent speech, we say: it is of the same kind of eloquence as all other poets. In all these estimations, it does not established that it is a miracle." When they had finished enumerating these possibilities, they said: ﴿Let him bring us a sign, as the earlier messengers were sent.﴾ The meaning is that they demanded a clear sign that none of these possibilities could touch, such as the signs related from Musa and ʿIsa, peace be upon them both. Then Allah, exalted is He, began the answer to this last demand with His saying: ﴿No town that We destroyed before them believed. Will they then believe?﴾ The meaning is that they are more stubborn than those who proposed signs to their prophets and promised that they would believe upon them; but when those came to them, they broke their promise and opposed, so Allah destroyed them. Therefore, had We given them what they propose, they would have been even more prone to breaking their word. Al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him, said: They were not answered because the ruling of Allah, exalted is He, is that whoever denies after being granted what he proposed of signs, a punishment of annihilation must surely descend upon him; and His ruling had already passed regarding the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) specifically, in contrast to this; therefore He did not answer them.

This is like His saying: ﴿Knower of the unseen﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 109], and ﴿the Knower of the unseen, from whom not an atom's weight escapes﴾ [Saba': 3].

The fourth issue: He placed the All-Hearing before the All-Knowing because hearing the speech must come first, and then acquiring knowledge of its meaning. As for His saying: ﴿Nay, they say: "Confused dreams! Nay, he has invented it! Nay, he is a poet! Let him bring us a sign, as the earlier messengers were sent."﴾, know that He, exalted is He, returned to relating their saying connected to His saying: ﴿Is this not but a human like you? Will you then approach magic while you see?﴾ Then He said: ﴿Nay, they say: "Confused dreams! Nay, he has invented it! Nay, he is a poet!"﴾. So He related these five statements from them there. The arrangement of their speech is as if they said: "We claim that his being a human prevents him from being a messenger of Allah, the Exalted. Suppose we grant that it does not prevent it; but we do not grant that this Qur'an is a miracle. Then either we support that the eloquence of the Qur'an is beyond human capacity, and we say: why could it not be magic? And even if we do not support that, if we claim it is in the utmost incoherence, we say: it is confused dreams; if we claim it is intermediate between incoherence and eloquence, we say: it is invention; and if we claim it is eloquent speech, we say: it is of the same kind of eloquence as all other poets. In all these estimations, it does not established that it is a miracle." When they had finished enumerating these possibilities, they said: ﴿Let him bring us a sign, as the earlier messengers were sent.﴾ The meaning is that they demanded a clear sign that none of these possibilities could touch, such as the signs related from Musa and ʿIsa, peace be upon them both. Then Allah, exalted is He, began the answer to this last demand with His saying: ﴿No town that We destroyed before them believed. Will they then believe?﴾ The meaning is that they are more stubborn than those who proposed signs to their prophets and promised that they would believe upon them; but when those came to them, they broke their promise and opposed, so Allah destroyed them. Therefore, had We given them what they propose, they would have been even more prone to breaking their word. Al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him, said: They were not answered because the ruling of Allah, exalted is He, is that whoever denies after being granted what he proposed of signs, a punishment of annihilation must surely descend upon him; and His ruling had already passed regarding the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) specifically, in contrast to this; therefore He did not answer them.

﴿Surely We sent not before you any but men whom We inspired. So ask the People of the Reminder, if you do not know.﴾ ﴿And We did not make them bodies that do not eat food, nor were they immortal.﴾ ﴿Then We fulfilled Our promise to them, and We saved them and whom We willed, and We destroyed the transgressors.﴾ ﴿Indeed We have sent down to you a Book in which is your reminder. Will you not then understand?﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, answered their first objection, which was their saying: ﴿This is not but a human being like you﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 33], with His words: ﴿And We sent not before you any but men whom We inspired.﴾ He made clear that this has been God's practice regarding the messengers before Muhammad (ﷺ), and that being human did not prevent them from being messengers, despite the signs that appeared through them. If this holds for them, then signs like theirs have appeared through Muhammad (ﷺ), so there is no basis for objection to his being a human being. As for His words: ﴿So ask the People of the Reminder﴾, the meaning is that He commanded them to ask the People of the Reminder (ahl al-dhikr), who are the People of the Book, so that they would inform them that God's messengers, to whom revelation was sent, were human beings and not angels. He referred them to these people only because they were following the polytheists in their hostility toward the Messenger of God (ﷺ). He, exalted is He, said: ﴿You will surely hear from those who were given the Book before you and from those who associate partners [with God] much harm﴾ [Al 'Imran: 186].

If it is said: if the Jews and Christians are not trusted, how is it permissible for Him to command them to ask these people about the messengers? We say: when their report is widely transmitted (mutawatir) and reaches the level of necessary knowledge, that is permissible, just as the report of disbelievers may be acted upon when it is widely transmitted, in the same way that the report of believers is acted upon. Some people said: the intended meaning of the People of the Reminder is the People of the Qur'an. This is far-fetched, because they were disparaging the Qur'an and the Messenger (ﷺ). As for the reliance of many jurists on this verse for the claim that the layman may refer to the legal opinions of scholars, and that a mujtahid may follow the view of another mujtahid, this is far-fetched, because this verse is a direct address (khitab mushafah) and relates to a specific event and is specifically connected to the Jews and Christians.

Then He, exalted is He, made clear that He did not make the messengers before Him bodies that do not eat food. There are several discussions regarding this:

The first discussion: His words ﴿that do not eat food﴾ are an attribute of "bodies," and the meaning is: We did not make the prophets beings with bodies that were not eating.

The second discussion: He used the singular "body" to denote the category, as if He said: beings of a kind of bodies.

The third discussion: they used to say: ﴿What is this messenger who eats food and walks in the markets? Why has not an angel been sent down to him so that he might be a warner with him?﴾ [al-Furqan: 7]. God answered: ﴿And We did not make them bodies that do not eat food﴾. Thus He made clear that this has been God's practice regarding the messengers before, and that He did not make them bodies that do not eat, but bodies that eat food and do not live forever in this world, rather they die like others. By this He alerted that what made them messengers is something other than that, namely the appearance of miracles at their hands and their freedom from attributes that would detract from conveying the message.

As for His words: ﴿Then We fulfilled Our promise to them﴾, the author of al-Kashshaf (Kashshaf) said: this is like His words: ﴿And Musa chose from his people seventy men﴾ [al-A'raf: 155]. The original is "from his people," and "fulfilled their promise to them" is similar. The meaning of ﴿and whom We willed﴾ is the believers. The exegetes said: what is meant is that His promise, exalted is His majesty, had preceded that He would destroy by the punishment of annihilation only those who denied the messengers, not the messengers themselves nor those who believed in them. He made the fulfilling of what He promised to be "truth" insofar as it reveals the truth. The meaning of ﴿and We destroyed the transgressors﴾ is that They were destroyed by the punishment of annihilation, and the intended meaning is not the punishment of the Hereafter, because this is a report of what has passed and preceded.

Then He, exalted is He, made clear by His words: ﴿Indeed We have sent down to you a Book in which is your reminder﴾ the magnitude of His blessing upon them through the Qur'an, in religion and in this world. Therefore He said: ﴿in which is your reminder﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations. The first: "your reminder" means your honor and your renown, as He said: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 44]. The second: the intended meaning is that it is a reminder for you, so that you may beware of what is not lawful and desire what is obligatory, and the intended meaning of the "reminder" is the promise and the threat, as He said: ﴿And remind, for indeed the reminder benefits the believers﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 55]. The third: the intended meaning is the mention of your religion, what is obligatory and what is not, so that you may succeed in Paradise if you hold fast to it. All of these are possible.

His words ﴿Will you not then understand?﴾ are like an urging to reflect on the Qur'an, because they were heedless, since engaging in vain discourse (khawd) is a consequence of heedlessness, and reflection repels that vain discourse. Averting harm from oneself is a consequence of the act. So whoever does not reflect, it is as if he has departed from reason.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 21, verses 11–16:

Page 126

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿How many a town have We broken, which was wrongdoing, and raised after it another people.﴾ ﴿So when they perceived Our might, behold, they were fleeing from it.﴾ ﴿Do not flee, but return to that in which you were given luxury, and to your dwellings, that you may be questioned.﴾ ﴿They said, "Woe to us! Indeed we have been wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿And that remained their cry until We made them as a harvest, extinguished.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, related from them those objections, and those objections were evidently baseless, since the conditions of miraculousness were complete in the Qur'an, it became clear to every intelligent person that it is miraculous. At that point it became clear that their preoccupation with raising those objections was for the sake of love of the world and love of leadership within it. So He, glorified be He, pressed hard in rebuking them for that, and said: ﴿How many a town have We broken﴾. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: al-qasm (breaking) is the most grievous kind of breaking, namely the breaking that separates the parts of a thing from one another, unlike al-kasr (simple breaking). He mentioned "the town" and that it was wrongdoing, and he meant its people, by way of figurative extension (tawassu'), since reason indicates that a town cannot be a wrongdoer or a bearer of obligation. The indication is also in His saying: ﴿and raised after it another people﴾. So the meaning is: We destroyed a people and raised up another people. He said: ﴿So when they perceived Our might﴾, up to His saying: ﴿They said, "Woe to us! Indeed we have been wrongdoers."﴾ All of this befits only its people, who were charged with affirming the messengers, but they denied them. Were it not for these indications, it would not be permissible for Him, glorified be He, to mention the metaphor, because that would give the impression of falsehood.

They differed regarding this destruction. Ibn ʿAbbas said: what is meant by it is killing by the sword, and what is meant by "the town" is Haḍūr, and Saḥūl, two towns in Yemen to which garments are attributed. In a hadith: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was shrouded in two Saḥūlī garments," and it is also narrated as "Ḥaḍūrī." It is narrated: "God sent to them a prophet, and they killed him, so God empowered Bukhtnasar over them, just as He empowered him over the people of Bayt al-Maqdis, and he uprooted them." It is also narrated: "When the swords seized them, a caller called out from heaven: 'O avengers of the prophets!' Then they regretted and acknowledged their error." Al-Hasan said: what is meant is the punishment of uprooting (ʿadhab al-istiʾṣal). Know that this is closer, because attributing that to God, exalted is He, is closer than attributing it to the killer. Then, even supposing that it is taken to mean the punishment of killing, what is the evidence for the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas? Perhaps Ibn ʿAbbas mentioned Haḍūr because it is one of the towns that God intended by this verse.

As for His saying: ﴿So when they perceived Our might, behold, they were fleeing from it﴾, the meaning is: when they knew the severity of Our punishment and Our seizing with sensory knowledge and direct witnessing, they ran in their homes. Al-rakḍ is striking the animal with the foot, and from it is His saying: ﴿Strike with your foot﴾ [Ṣad: 42]. It is permissible that they mounted their beasts, spurring them, fleeing and routed from their town when the vanguard of the punishment overtook them. It is also permissible that they were likened, in the swiftness of their running on foot, to riders spurring their mounts.

As for His saying: ﴿Do not flee﴾, the author of al-Kashshaf said: the saying is omitted. If you ask: who is the speaker? Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 21, verses 11–16:

Page 126

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿How many a town have We broken, which was wrongdoing, and raised after it another people.﴾ ﴿So when they perceived Our might, behold, they were fleeing from it.﴾ ﴿Do not flee, but return to that in which you were given luxury, and to your dwellings, that you may be questioned.﴾ ﴿They said, "Woe to us! Indeed we have been wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿And that remained their cry until We made them as a harvest, extinguished.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, related from them those objections, and those objections were evidently baseless, since the conditions of miraculousness were complete in the Qur'an, it became clear to every intelligent person that it is miraculous. At that point it became clear that their preoccupation with raising those objections was for the sake of love of the world and love of leadership within it. So He, glorified be He, pressed hard in rebuking them for that, and said: ﴿How many a town have We broken﴾. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: al-qasm (breaking) is the most grievous kind of breaking, namely the breaking that separates the parts of a thing from one another, unlike al-kasr (simple breaking). He mentioned "the town" and that it was wrongdoing, and he meant its people, by way of figurative extension (tawassu'), since reason indicates that a town cannot be a wrongdoer or a bearer of obligation. The indication is also in His saying: ﴿and raised after it another people﴾. So the meaning is: We destroyed a people and raised up another people. He said: ﴿So when they perceived Our might﴾, up to His saying: ﴿They said, "Woe to us! Indeed we have been wrongdoers."﴾ All of this befits only its people, who were charged with affirming the messengers, but they denied them. Were it not for these indications, it would not be permissible for Him, glorified be He, to mention the metaphor, because that would give the impression of falsehood.

They differed regarding this destruction. Ibn ʿAbbas said: what is meant by it is killing by the sword, and what is meant by "the town" is Haḍūr, and Saḥūl, two towns in Yemen to which garments are attributed. In a hadith: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was shrouded in two Saḥūlī garments," and it is also narrated as "Ḥaḍūrī." It is narrated: "God sent to them a prophet, and they killed him, so God empowered Bukhtnasar over them, just as He empowered him over the people of Bayt al-Maqdis, and he uprooted them." It is also narrated: "When the swords seized them, a caller called out from heaven: 'O avengers of the prophets!' Then they regretted and acknowledged their error." Al-Hasan said: what is meant is the punishment of uprooting (ʿadhab al-istiʾṣal). Know that this is closer, because attributing that to God, exalted is He, is closer than attributing it to the killer. Then, even supposing that it is taken to mean the punishment of killing, what is the evidence for the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas? Perhaps Ibn ʿAbbas mentioned Haḍūr because it is one of the towns that God intended by this verse.

As for His saying: ﴿So when they perceived Our might, behold, they were fleeing from it﴾, the meaning is: when they knew the severity of Our punishment and Our seizing with sensory knowledge and direct witnessing, they ran in their homes. Al-rakḍ is striking the animal with the foot, and from it is His saying: ﴿Strike with your foot﴾ [Ṣad: 42]. It is permissible that they mounted their beasts, spurring them, fleeing and routed from their town when the vanguard of the punishment overtook them. It is also permissible that they were likened, in the swiftness of their running on foot, to riders spurring their mounts.

As for His saying: ﴿Do not flee﴾, the author of al-Kashshaf said: the saying is omitted. If you ask: who is the speaker? We say: it may be some of the angels, or some of the believers, or they may be addressed with that even if it was not said, or the Lord of Might may say it and make His angels hear it so that it benefits them in their religion, or He may inspire them with that so that they speak it to themselves.

As for His saying: ﴿and return to that in which you were given luxury, and to your dwellings﴾, that is, of the living and the comfort and the pleasant condition. Itrāf is the wantonness of blessing, which is affluence (tarrufh).

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿that you may be questioned﴾, it is mockery and rebuke directed at them. Then in it there are several aspects:

First: that is, return to your blessings and your dwellings, that you may be questioned tomorrow about what befell you and what descended upon your wealth and your dwellings, so that you answer the questioner from knowledge and direct witnessing.

Second: return as you were in your assemblies, until your servants ask you, and whoever is subject to your command and prohibition, and says to you: "What do you order, and what do you decree?" as is the custom of masters.

Third: people will ask you in your gatherings, to help them in the calamities that befall them, and they will consult you on important matters, and seek help from your opinions.

Fourth: those who come to you as guests and those who seek your favor will ask you, either because they were generous, spending their wealth to be seen by people and seeking praise, or because they were miserly, and so it was said to them as mockery upon mockery and rebuke upon rebuke.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So that remained their cry﴾, the author of al-Kashshaf said: "that" refers to ﴿Woe to us!﴾, because it is a cry, as if it were said: "So that cry remained their cry."

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 21, verses 17–18:**

﴿We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in play.﴾ ﴿Had We wished to take a pastime, We would have taken it from Our presence, if We were ever to do (so).﴾ ﴿Rather, We hurl the truth against falsehood, and it crushes it, and behold, it vanishes. And woe to you for what you describe.﴾ Know that in this there are several issues (masʼalah):

**The first issue:** Regarding the connection of this verse with what precedes it, there are two views. The first: when God, exalted is He, explained the destruction of the people of the town because of their denial, He followed it with what indicates that He did this out of justice and as a requital for what they did. So He said: ﴿We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in play.﴾ That is, We did not make this raised canopy and this spread bed, and what is between them of wonders and marvels, as tyrants make their ceilings and carpets for amusement and play. We made them for religious and worldly benefits. As for the religious benefits, let those who reflect reflect upon them, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and they reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 191]. As for the worldly benefits, they are due to the countless benefits connected with them. This is like His saying: ﴿and We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain﴾ [Sad: 27], and His saying: ﴿We did not create them except with truth﴾ [al-Dukhan: 39].

The second view: the purpose of this passage is to establish the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and to refute those who deny it, because He manifested the miracle (muʻjizah) through him. If Muhammad were a liar, then the manifestation of the miracle through him would be a matter of play, and that is negated of Him. If he were truthful, then this is what is sought, and at that point all the criticisms they mentioned become void.

**The second issue:** Al-Qadi Abd al-Jabbar said: the verse indicates that play does not come from God, for if it did, He would be a player (laʻib), since the word "lāʻib" in the language is the name for the doer of play, and negating the name established for the act requires negating the act. The answer: this is refuted by the question of the motive (dāʻi), as has passed more than once.

As for His saying: ﴿Had We wished to take a pastime, We would have taken it from Our presence, if We were ever to do (so).﴾ Know that His saying ﴿We would have taken it from Our presence﴾ means: from the side of Our power. It has also been said: "lahw" means "child" in the dialect of Yemen; it has also been said: "woman." It has also been said: "from Our presence" means from the angels, not from humans, refuting those who claimed the birth of the Messiah and Uzayr.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, We hurl the truth against falsehood﴾, know that His saying ﴿Rather (bal)﴾ is a turning away from taking pastime and play, and a declaration of His transcendence above it in Himself, as if He said: "Glory be to Us! That We should take pastime and play! Rather, it is part of Our custom and the requirement of Our wisdom that We overcome play with seriousness and refute falsehood with truth." For this He used the metaphors of "hurling" (qadhf) and "crushing" (damgh) to depict its annulment. He made it as if it were a solid body, like a rock, hurled at a soft body and crushing it. As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And woe to you for what you describe﴾, it means: those who hold fast to denying the Messenger (ﷺ), attributing the Qur'an to being magic, "confused dreams," and other falsehoods. This is what He intended by His saying: ﴿for what you describe﴾.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 21, verses 19–20:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth. And those near Him are not too proud to worship Him, nor do they tire.﴾ ﴿They exalt [Him] night and day; they do not slacken.﴾ And in this are several issues:

The first issue: Regarding the connection of this verse to what precedes it, there are two views. The first: when He, exalted is He, negated play from Himself, and the negation of play is not valid except by negating need, and the negation of need is not valid except by complete power, He therefore followed that verse with His saying: ﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth,﴾ to indicate by that the perfection of dominion and power. The second, and it is the closer: when He, exalted is He, related the speech of those who attack the prophethoods, answered it, and clarified that their purpose in those attacks is rebellion and refusal to submit, He clarified in this verse that He, exalted is He, is far above their obedience, because He is the owner of all created and originated beings; and because the angels, despite their greatness, obey Him and fear Him, humans, despite their extreme weakness, are more deserving of obeying Him.

The second issue: His saying, ﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth,﴾ means that all the accountable beings in the heavens and the earth are His servants, and He is the Creator of them and the Bestower upon them of all kinds of blessings; so it is obligatory upon all to obey Him and submit to His judgment.

The third issue: the indication of His saying, ﴿And those near Him are not too proud to worship Him,﴾ that the angel is more excellent than the human, is from three aspects, which have already been explained in Surat al-Baqarah.

The fourth issue: His saying, ﴿And those near Him,﴾ is by the consensus of the community (ijma') referring to the angels, and because He described them as: ﴿They exalt [Him] night and day; they do not slacken,﴾ and this does not befit humans. This nearness is the nearness of honor and rank, not the nearness of place and direction. So it is as if He, exalted is He, said: the angels, with their complete honor and utmost greatness, do not disdain His worship; how then is it fitting for weak humans to rebel against His obedience?

The fifth issue: al-Zajjaj said: ﴿Nor do they tire﴾ means they do not grow weary or exhausted. The author of al-Kashshaf said: If you say, "istihsar" is an intensification of "husur" (weariness), so the more eloquent way to describe them would be to negate even the slightest weariness from them, I say: in "istihsar" there is a clarification that what they are engaged in necessitates the utmost and extreme weariness, and that they are deserving of those arduous acts of worship to the point of becoming weary in what they do. As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They exalt [Him] night and day; they do not slacken,﴾ the meaning is that their glorification is continuous and constant at all their times, not interrupted by a pause for leisure or for other occupation. It is related from Abd Allah ibn al-Harith ibn Nawfal, who said: I said to Ka'b: "What do you think of the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿They exalt [Him] night and day; they do not slacken,﴾ then He said: ﴿Who made the angels messengers﴾ [Fatir: 1]. Would that messengership not prevent them from this glorification?" And also He said: ﴿Upon them is the curse of Allah, and of the angels and of mankind, all together﴾ [al-Baqarah: 161]. How then do they occupy themselves with cursing while they are occupied with glorification?" Ka'b al-Ahbar answered and said: Glorification for them is like breathing for us; just as our being occupied with breathing does not prevent us from speaking, so their being occupied with glorification does not prevent them from all other deeds. If it is said: this analogy is not valid, because being occupied with breathing did not prevent speech only because the instrument of breathing is not the instrument of speech, whereas glorification and cursing are both of the same kind as speech, so their combination is impossible. The answer: what is the improbability in God, exalted is He, creating for them many tongues, with some of which they glorify God and with others they curse the enemies of God? Or it may be said that the meaning of His saying, ﴿they do not slacken,﴾ is that they do not slacken in the resolve to perform it at its fitting times, just as one says: "So-and-so is steadfast in the congregational prayers; he does not slacken from them," which does not mean that he is always occupied with them, but rather that he is steadfast in the resolve to perform them at their times.

"Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 21, verse 21:"

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or have they taken gods from the earth who raise the dead?﴾ ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined. So glory be to Allah, Lord of the Throne, above what they describe.﴾ ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned.﴾ ﴿Or have they taken gods besides Him? Say: "Bring your proof. This is the reminder of those with me and the reminder of those before me." But most of them do not know the truth, so they turn away.﴾ ﴿We did not send before you any messenger except that We revealed to him that there is no god but Me, so worship Me.﴾

Know that the discourse from the beginning of the surah up to this point concerned prophethood and what is connected with it, in question and answer. As for these verses, they explain tawhid (the oneness of God) and the negation of rivals and equals.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or have they taken gods from the earth who raise the dead?﴾, there are several issues in it:

The first issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Am (أم) here is the disjunctive one, which means bal (بل, "rather"), and the hamzah has permitted a turning away from what precedes it and a denial of what follows it. The denounced matter is their taking gods from the earth who raise the dead. By my life, among the greatest of denounced things is that the dead be raised by a portion of the dead." If you say: How did He denounce upon them taking gods who raise the dead, when they did not claim this for their gods, but were at the furthest extreme from this claim? For they, together with their acknowledgment of Allah and that He is the Creator of the heavens and the earth, denied resurrection, and they say: ﴿Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?﴾ So how would they claim it for something inanimate that is not described with power at all? I say: Because when they occupied themselves with worshipping them, and worship must have a benefit which is reward, their undertaking to worship them necessitates their acknowledgment that they are capable of gathering, raising, rewarding and punishing. So He mentioned that by way of mocking them and ascribing ignorance to them, meaning: if they are not capable of giving life, causing death, harming or benefiting, then what intellect permits their taking them as gods?

The second issue: His saying ﴿from the earth﴾ is like your saying: "So-and-so is from Mecca or from Medina," meaning a Meccan or a Medinan. The meaning of attributing them to the earth is an indication that they are the idols that are worshipped on the earth, because gods are of two kinds: earthly and heavenly. It is also permissible that what is meant is gods of the substance of the earth, since they are either carved from some stones or made from some of the earth's substances.

The third issue: The point in ﴿they raise﴾ is the sense of exclusivity, as if it were said: "Or have they taken gods from the earth, none of whom can raise except they alone?"

The fourth issue: Al-Hasan read (yanshurun), and both are dialectal forms: anshara Allah al-mawta and nashara-ha (Allah raised the dead, and they raised them).

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 21, verses 22–23 (part 1 of 3):

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined﴾, there are two issues concerning it.

The first issue: The grammarians said that "illa" (except) here carries the meaning of "ghayr" (other than). That is, had there been in them something other than the One who is their Creator administering their affairs and managing them, both would have been ruined. It is not permissible for it to carry the meaning of exception (istithna'), because if we interpreted it as exception, the meaning would be: "Had there been in them gods with whom Allah was not present, they would have been ruined." This would imply, by way of inference (mafhum), that if there were gods in them with Allah present alongside them, ruin would not occur. That is false, because if there were gods in them, whether Allah was with them or not, ruin would be necessary. Since its interpretation as exception has been ruled out, it is established that the intended meaning is what we have mentioned.

The second issue: The theologians (mutakallimun) said: The assertion that there exist two gods leads to an impossibility, so the assertion that there exist two gods must be impossible. We say that it leads to an impossibility because if we suppose the existence of two gods, each of them must be capable of all possible things (maqdurat). If that is so, each of them would be capable of moving Zayd and of making him still. So if we suppose that one of them wills to move him and the other wills to make him still, then either both wills take effect, which is impossible because the joining of two opposites is impossible; or neither takes effect, which is also impossible, because the obstacle to the existence of the willed outcome of each is the willed outcome of the other, so the willed outcome of one is prevented only when the willed outcome of the other exists, and vice versa. Then if both were prevented together, they would both exist together, which is impossible; or the willed outcome of one of them takes effect without the other's, which is also impossible, for two reasons:

The first of them: If each of them were capable of what has no limit, it would be impossible for one of them to be more capable than the other. Rather, they must be equal in capability. And when they are equal in capability, it is impossible for the willed outcome of one to become more deserving of occurrence than the willed outcome of the other; otherwise it would entail preferring a possible thing without a preponderant cause.

The second of them: If the willed outcome of one occurs without that of the other, then the one whose will occurred is capable, and the one whose will did not occur is incapable, and incapacity is a deficiency, which is impossible with respect to Allah.

If it is said: Ruin only arises when they differ in will, and you do not claim that their differing in will is necessary; rather the most you claim is that their differing in will is possible. So if ruin is based upon difference in will, and this difference is possible, and what is based upon the possible is possible, then ruin is possible and not actual. How then does Allah, exalted is He, affirm with certainty that ruin occurs?

We say: The answer is in two respects. The first: Perhaps He, glorified is He, treated the possible as if it were actual, on the basis of what is apparent, inasmuch as subjects are ruined by the management of two kings because of the rivalry that arises between them. The second, and it is the stronger: that we demonstrate the necessity of ruin not from the aspect we have mentioned, but from another aspect. We say: If we suppose two gods, each of them would be capable of all possible things, so that there would result the occurrence of one possible thing from two independent agents in one respect, and this is impossible, because the attribution of an act to its agent is due to its possibility. So when each of them is independent in bringing it into being, the act, given this, is necessarily existent, and therefore its attribution to this one is impossible, since it has come about from both of them together, so that it would follow that it is independent of both together and needs both together, and that is impossible. This is a complete argument in the matter of tawhid (divine unity). We say: The assertion that two gods exist leads to the impossibility of the occurrence of what is willed by either of them; and when that is so, it must be that nothing ever occurs, and then ruin certainly occurs. Or we say: If we assume two gods, either they agree or they differ. If they agree upon one thing, then that one thing is capable for both of them and willed by both of them, so its occurrence would be by both of them, and that is impossible. If they differ, then either both willed outcomes occur, or neither occurs, or one occurs without the other; and all of these are impossible. Thus it is established that ruin is necessary under every assumption.

If you say: Why is it not permissible that they agree upon one thing without ruin following, because ruin only follows if each of them wished to bring it into being himself, and that is difference? But if each of them wished that its bringer be one of them specifically, then in that case there is no necessity of a created thing occurring between two creators.

We say: Its being brought into being by one of them is either the very capability and will, or the very effect, or a third matter. If it is the first, then it entails sharing in capability and will and sharing in the bringer. If it is the second, then the occurrence of that effect by the capability and will of one of them is no more preferable than its occurrence by the capability of the other; for each of them has an independent will with regard to influence. If it is the third, namely that the bringer of it is a third matter, then that third matter, if it is eternal, it is impossible for it to be the object of will; and if it is originated, then it is the very effect itself, and this category becomes the second category that we mentioned.

Know that when you have grasped the reality of this proof, you will recognize that everything in this upper and lower world of originated and created things is a proof of the oneness of Allah, exalted is He; indeed, the existence of each of the substances and accidents is a complete proof of tawhid from the aspect we have explained. This proof has been mentioned by Allah, exalted is He, in various places of His Book. Know also that there are other proofs for the oneness of Allah, exalted is He.

The first of them, and it is the strongest: It may be said: If we suppose two necessarily existent beings (wajib al-wujud li-dhatihima), then they must share in existence, and each of them must be distinguished from the other by its own essence, and what makes them share is other than what makes them distinct. Thus each of them is composed of that by which it shares with the other and that by which it is distinguished from it. Every composite is dependent upon its part, and its part is other than it; so every composite is dependent upon something other than itself. And everything dependent upon something other than itself is possible in its essence (mumkin li-dhatihi). So the necessarily existent in its essence is possible in its essence. This is a contradiction. Therefore, the necessarily existent is none but the One, and everything else is possible and dependent upon Him; and everything dependent for its existence upon another is originated. So everything other than Allah, exalted is He, is originated. This proof can also be made an explanation of this verse; for we have only argued that it follows from assuming two necessarily existent beings that none of them is necessary; and when the necessary is not found, none of these possible things is found; and then ruin follows. Thus it is established that from the existence of two gods there follows the ruin of the entire world.

The second: If we suppose two gods, each of them would necessarily share with the other in divinity, and each must be distinguished from the other by something; for otherwise plurality would not be realized. So that by which they are distinguished is either an attribute of perfection or not. If it is an attribute of perfection, then whoever lacks it would lack perfection, and so would be deficient, and the deficient cannot be a god. If it is not an attribute of perfection, then whoever is described by it would be described by what is not an attribute of perfection, and so would be deficient. It may also be said: If that by which they are distinguished is required for the realization of divinity, then whoever lacks it is not a god; and if it is not required for divinity, then attribution of it is not necessary, and so it requires a specifier, and whoever is described by it is dependent and in need.

The third: It may be said: If we suppose two gods, they must be such that others can distinguish between them; but distinction in our minds is achieved only by difference in place, or in time, or in necessity and possibility; and all of these are impossible with respect to God; so the achievement of distinction is impossible.

The fourth: Either one of the two gods is sufficient for managing the world or he is not. If he is sufficient, then the second is superfluous and not needed, and that is a deficiency, and the deficient is not

يَكُونُ إلَهًا. وخامِسُها: أنَّ العَقْلَ يَقْتَضِي احْتِياجَ المُحْدَثِ إلى الفاعِلِ ولا امْتِناعَ في كَوْنِ الفاعِلِ الواحِدِ مُدَبِّرًا لِكُلِّ العالَمِ، فَأمّا ما وراءَ ذَلِكَ فَلَيْسَ عَدَدٌ أوْلى مِن عَدَدٍ فَيُفْضِي ذَلِكَ إلى وُجُودِ أعْدادٍ لا نِهايَةَ لَها وذَلِكَ مُحالٌ فالقَوْلُ بِوُجُودِ الآلِهَةِ مُحالٌ. وسادِسُها: أنَّ أحَدَ الإلَهَيْنِ إمّا أنْ يَقْدِرَ عَلى أنْ يَخُصَّ نَفْسَهُ بِدَلِيلٍ يَدُلُّ عَلَيْهِ ولا يَدُلُّ عَلى غَيْرِهِ أوْ لا يَقْدِرَ عَلَيْهِ، والأوَّلُ مُحالٌ لِأنَّ دَلِيلَ الصّانِعِ لَيْسَ إلّا بِالمُحْدَثاتِ ولَيْسَ في حُدُوثِ المُحْدَثاتِ ما يَدُلُّ عَلى تَعْيِينِ أحَدِهِما دُونَ الثّانِي، والتّالِي مُحالٌ لِأنَّهُ يُفْضِي إلى كَوْنِهِ عاجِزًا عَنْ تَعْرِيفِ نَفْسِهِ عَلى التَّعْيِينِ، والعاجِزُ لا يَكُونُ إلَهًا. وسابِعُها: أنَّ أحَدَ الإلَهَيْنِ إمّا أنْ يَقْدِرَ عَلى أنْ يَسْتُرَ شَيْئًا مِن أفْعالِهِ عَنِ الآخَرِ أوْ لا يَقْدِرَ، فَإنْ قَدَرَ لَزِمَ أنْ يَكُونَ المَسْتُورُ عَنْهُ جاهِلًا، وإنْ لَمْ يَقْدِرْ لَزِمَ كَوْنُهُ عاجِزًا. وثامِنُها: لَوْ قَدَّرْنا إلَهَيْنِ لَكانَ مَجْمُوعُ قُدْرَتَيْهِما بَيْنَهُما أقْوى مِن قُدْرَةِ كُلِّ واحِدٍ مِنهُما وحْدَهُ، فَيَكُونُ كُلُّ واحِدٍ مِنَ القُدْرَتَيْنِ مُتَناهِيًا والمَجْمُوعُ ضِعْفُ المُتَناهِي فَيَكُونُ الكُلُّ مُتَناهِيًا. وتاسِعُها: العَدَدُ ناقِصٌ لِاحْتِياجِهِ إلى الواحِدِ، والواحِدُ الَّذِي يُوجَدُ مِن جِنْسِهِ عَدَدٌ ناقِصٌ ناقِصٌ، لِأنَّ العَدَدَ أزْيَدُ مِنهُ، والنّاقِصُ لا يَكُونُ إلَهًا فالإلَهُ واحِدٌ لا مَحالَةَ. وعاشِرُها: أنّا لَوْ فَرَضْنا مَعْدُومًا مُمْكِنَ الوُجُودِ ثُمَّ قَدَّرْنا إلَهَيْنِ فَإنْ لَمْ يَقْدِرْ واحِدٌ مِنهُما عَلى إيجادِهِ كانَ كُلُّ واحِدٍ مِنهُما عاجِزًا والعاجِزُ لا يَكُونُ إلَهًا، وإنْ قَدَرَ أحَدُهُما دُونَ الآخَرِ فَهَذا الآخَرُ يَكُونُ إلَهًا، وإنْ قَدِرا جَمِيعًا فَإمّا أنْ يُوجِداهُ بِالتَّعاوُنِ فَيَكُونُ كُلُّ واحِدٍ مِنهُما مُحْتاجًا إلى إعانَةِ الآخَرِ، وإنْ قَدَرَ كُلُّ واحِدٍ عَلى إيجادِهِ بِالِاسْتِقْلالِ فَإذا أوْجَدَهُ أحَدُهُما فَإمّا أنْ يَبْقى الثّانِي قادِرًا عَلَيْهِ وهو مُحالٌ لِأنَّ إيجادَ المَوْجُودِ مُحالٌ، وإنْ لَمْ يَبْقَ فَحِينَئِذٍ يَكُونُ الأوَّلُ قَدْ أزالَ قُدْرَةَ الثّانِي وعَجْزَهُ فَيَكُونُ مَقْهُورًا تَحْتَ تَصَرُّفِهِ فَلا يَكُونُ إلَهًا. فَإنْ قِيلَ الواجِدُ إذا أوْجَدَ مَقْدُورَهُ فَقَدْ زالَتْ قُدْرَتُهُ عَنْهُ فَيَلْزَمُكُمُ العَجْزُ، قُلْنا: الواحِدُ إذا أوْجَدَهُ فَقَدْ نَفَذَتْ قُدْرَتُهُ فَنَفاذُ القُدْرَةِ لا يَكُونُ عَجْزًا، أمّا الشَّرِيكُ فَإنَّهُ لَمّا نَفَذَتْ قُدْرَتُهُ لَمْ يَبْقَ لِشَرِيكِهِ قُدْرَةٌ البَتَّةَ بَلْ زالَتْ قُدْرَتُهُ بِسَبَبِ قُدْرَةِ الأوَّلِ فَيَكُونُ تَعْجِيزًا. الحادِيَ عَشَرَ: أنَّ نُقَرِّرَ هَذِهِ الدَّلالَةَ عَلى وجْهٍ آخَرَ وهو أنْ نُعَيِّنَ جِسْمًا ونَقُولَ هَلْ يَقْدِرُ كُلُّ واحِدٍ مِنهُما عَلى خَلْقِ الحَرَكَةِ فِيهِ بَدَلًا عَنِ السُّكُونِ وبِالعَكْسِ، فَإنْ لَمْ يَقْدِرْ كانَ عاجِزًا وإنْ قَدَرَ فَنَسُوقُ الدَّلالَةَ إلى أنْ نَقُولَ: إذا خَلَقَ أحَدُهُما فِيهِ حَرَكَةً امْتَنَعَ عَلى الثّانِي خَلْقُ السُّكُونِ، فالأوَّلُ أزالَ قُدْرَةَ الثّانِي وعَجَّزَهُ فَلا يَكُونُ إلَهًا، وهَذانَ الوَجْهانِ يُفِيدانِ العَجْزَ نَظَرًا إلى قُدْرَتَيْهِما، والدَّلالَةُ الأُولى إنَّما تُفِيدُ العَجْزَ بِالنَّظَرِ إلى إرادَتَيْهِما. وثانِي عَشَرَها: أنَّهُما لَمّا كانا عالِمَيْنِ بِجَمِيعِ المَعْلُوماتِ كانَ عِلْمُ كُلِّ واحِدٍ مِنهُما مُتَعَلِّقًا بِعَيْنِ مَعْلُومِ الآخَرِ فَوَجَبَ تَماثُلُ عِلْمَيْهِما، والذّاتُ القابِلَةُ لِأحَدِ المِثْلَيْنِ قابِلَةٌ لِلْمِثْلِ الآخَرِ، فاخْتِصاصُ كُلِّ واحِدٍ مِنهُما بِتِلْكَ الصِّفَةِ مَعَ جَوازِ اتِّصافِهِ بِصِفَةِ الآخَرِ عَلى البَدَلِ يَسْتَدْعِي مُخَصِّصًا يُخَصِّصُ كُلَّ واحِدٍ مِنهُما بِعِلْمِهِ وقُدْرَتِهِ فَيَكُونُ كُلُّ واحِدٍ مِنهُما عَبْدًا فَقِيرًا ناقِصًا. وثالِثَ عَشَرَها: أنَّ الشَّرِكَةَ عَيْبٌ ونَقْصٌ في الشّاهِدِ، والفَرْدانِيَّةُ والتَّوَحُّدُ صِفَةُ كَمالٍ، ونَرى المُلُوكَ يَكْرَهُونَ الشَّرِكَةَ في المُلْكِ الحَقِيرِ المُخْتَصَرِ أشَدَّ الكَراهِيَةِ، ونَرى أنَّهُ كُلَّما كانَ المُلْكُ أعْظَمَ كانَتِ النَّفْرَةُ عَنِ الشَّرِكَةِ أشَدَّ، فَما ظَنُّكَ بِمُلْكِ اللَّهِ عَزَّ وجَلَّ ومَلَكُوتِهِ، فَلَوْ أرادَ أحَدُهُما اسْتِخْلاصَ المُلْكِ لِنَفْسِهِ فَإنْ قَدَرَ عَلَيْهِ كانَ المَغْلُوبُ فَقِيرًا عاجِزًا فَلا يَكُونُ إلَهًا، وإنْ لَمْ يَقْدِرْ عَلَيْهِ كانَ في أشَدِّ الغَمِّ والكَراهِيَةِ فَلا يَكُونُ إلَهًا. ورابِعَ عَشَرَها: أنّا لَوْ قَدَّرْنا إلَهَيْنِ لَكانَ إمّا أنْ يَحْتاجَ كُلُّ واحِدٍ مِنهُما إلى الآخَرِ أوْ يَسْتَغْنِيَ كُلُّ واحِدٍ مِنهُما عَنِ الآخَرِ أوْ يَحْتاجَ أحَدُهُما إلى الآخَرِ والآخَرُ يَسْتَغْنِي عَنْهُ، فَإنْ كانَ الأوَّلَ كانَ كُلُّ واحِدٍ مِنهُما ناقِصًا لِأنَّ المُحْتاجَ ناقِصٌ، وإنْ كانَ الثّانِيَ كانَ كُلُّ واحِدٍ مِنهُما مُسْتَغْنِيًا عَنْهُ، والمُسْتَغْنى عَنْهُ ناقِصٌ، ألا تَرى أنَّ البَلَدَ إذا كانَ لَهُ رَئِيسٌ والنّاسُ يُحَصِّلُونَ مَصالِحَ البَلَدِ

مِن غَيْرِ رُجُوعٍ مِنهم إلَيْهِ ومِن غَيْرِ التِفاتٍ مِنهم إلَيْهِ عُدَّ ذَلِكَ الرَّئِيسُ ناقِصًا، فالإلَهُ هو الَّذِي يُسْتَغْنى بِهِ ولا يُسْتَغْنى عَنْهُ، وإنِ احْتاجَ أحَدُهُما إلى الآخَرِ مِن غَيْرِ عَكْسٍ كانَ المُحْتاجُ ناقِصًا والمُحْتاجُ إلَيْهِ هو الإلَهُ. واعْلَمْ أنَّ هَذِهِ الوُجُوهَ ظَنِّيَّةٌ إقْناعِيَّةٌ والِاعْتِمادَ عَلى الوُجُوهِ المُتَقَدِّمَةِ، أمّا الدَّلائِلُ السَّمْعِيَّةُ فَمِن وُجُوهٍ:
أحَدُها: قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿هُوَ الأوَّلُ والآخِرُ والظّاهِرُ والباطِنُ﴾ [الحَدِيدِ: ٣] فالأوَّلُ هو الفَرْدُ السّابِقُ، ولِذَلِكَ لَوْ قالَ: أوَّلُ عَبْدٍ اشْتَرَيْتُهُ فَهو حُرٌّ فَلَوِ اشْتَرى أوَّلًا عَبْدَيْنِ لَمْ يَحْنَثْ لِأنَّ شَرْطَ الأوَّلِ أنْ يَكُونَ فَرْدًا وهَذا لَيْسَ بِفَرْدٍ، فَلَوِ اشْتَرى بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ واحِدًا لَمْ يَحْنَثْ أيْضًا لِأنَّ شَرْطَ الفَرْدِ أنْ يَكُونَ سابِقًا وهَذا لَيْسَ بِسابِقٍ، فَلَمّا وصَفَ اللَّهُ تَعالى نَفْسَهُ بِكَوْنِهِ أوَّلًا وجَبَ أنْ يَكُونَ فَرْدًا سابِقًا فَوَجَبَ أنْ لا يَكُونَ لَهُ شَرِيكٌ. وثانِيها: قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وعِنْدَهُ مَفاتِحُ الغَيْبِ لا يَعْلَمُها إلّا هُوَ﴾ [الأنْعامِ: ٥٩] فالنَّصُّ يَقْتَضِي أنْ لا يَكُونَ أحَدٌ سِواهُ عالِمًا بِالغَيْبِ ولَوْ كانَ لَهُ شَرِيكٌ لَكانَ عالِمًا بِالغَيْبِ وهو خِلافُ النَّصِّ. وثالِثُها: أنَّ اللَّهَ تَعالى صَرَّحَ بِكَلِمَةِ ﴿لا إلَهَ إلّا هُوَ﴾ [البَقَرَةِ: ٢٥٥] في سَبْعَةٍ وثَلاثِينَ مَوْضِعًا مِن كِتابِهِ، وصَرَّحَ بِالوَحْدانِيَّةِ في مَواضِعَ نَحْوَ قَوْلِهِ: ﴿وإلَهُكم إلَهٌ واحِدٌ﴾ [البَقَرَةِ: ١٦٣] وقَوْلِهِ: ﴿قُلْ هو اللَّهُ أحَدٌ﴾ [الإخْلاصِ: ١] وكُلُّ ذَلِكَ صَرِيحٌ في البابِ. ورابِعُها: قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿كُلُّ شَيْءٍ هالِكٌ إلّا وجْهَهُ﴾ حُكْمٌ بِهَلاكِ كُلِّ ما سِواهُ، ومَن عُدِمَ بَعْدَ وجُودِهِ لا يَكُونُ قَدِيمًا، ومَن لا يَكُونُ قَدِيمًا لا يَكُونُ إلَهًا. وخامِسُها: قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿لَوْ كانَ فِيهِما آلِهَةٌ إلّا اللَّهُ لَفَسَدَتا﴾ وهو كَقَوْلِهِ: ﴿ولَعَلا بَعْضُهم عَلى بَعْضٍ﴾ [المُؤْمِنُونَ: ٩١] وقَوْلِهِ: ﴿إذًا لابْتَغَوْا إلى ذِي العَرْشِ سَبِيلًا﴾ [الإسْراءِ: ٤٢] . وسادِسُها: قَوْلُهُ: ﴿وإنْ يَمْسَسْكَ اللَّهُ بِضُرٍّ فَلا كاشِفَ لَهُ إلّا هو وإنْ يُرِدْكَ بِخَيْرٍ فَلا رادَّ لِفَضْلِهِ﴾ [يُونُسَ: ١٠٧] وقالَ في آيَةٍ أُخْرى: ﴿قُلْ أفَرَأيْتُمْ ما تَدْعُونَ مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ إنْ أرادَنِيَ اللَّهُ بِضُرٍّ هَلْ هُنَّ كاشِفاتُ ضُرِّهِ أوْ أرادَنِي بِرَحْمَةٍ هَلْ هُنَّ مُمْسِكاتُ رَحْمَتِهِ﴾ [الزُّمَرِ: ٣٨] . وسابِعُها: قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿قُلْ أرَأيْتُمْ إنْ أخَذَ اللَّهُ سَمْعَكم وأبْصارَكم وخَتَمَ عَلى قُلُوبِكم مَن إلَهٌ غَيْرُ اللَّهِ يَأْتِيكم بِهِ﴾ [الأنْعامِ: ٤٦] وهَذا الحَصْرُ يَدُلُّ عَلى نَفْيِ الشَّرِيكِ. وثامِنُها: قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿اللَّهُ خالِقُ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ﴾ [الزُّمَرِ: ٦٢] فَلَوْ وُجِدَ الشَّرِيكُ لَمْ يَكُنْ خالِقًا فَلَمْ يَكُنْ فِيهِ فائِدَةٌ. واعْلَمْ أنَّ كُلَّ مَسْألَةٍ لا تَتَوَقَّفُ مَعْرِفَةُ صِدْقِ الرُّسُلِ عَلَيْها فَإنَّهُ يُمْكِنُ إثْباتُها بِالسَّمْعِ، والوَحْدانِيَّةُ لا تَتَوَقَّفُ مَعْرِفَةُ صِدْقِ الرُّسُلِ عَلَيْها، فَلا جَرَمَ يُمْكِنُ إثْباتُها بِالدَّلائِلِ السَّمْعِيَّةِ، واعْلَمْ أنَّ مَن طَعَنَ في دَلالَةِ التَّمانُعِ فَسَرَّ الآيَةَ بِأنَّ المُرادَ لَوْ كانَ في السَّماءِ والأرْضِ آلِهَةٌ تَقُولُ بِإلَهِيَّتِها عَبَدَةُ الأوْثانِ لَزِمَ فَسادُ العالَمِ لِأنَّها جَماداتٌ لا تَقْدِرُ عَلى تَدْبِيرِ العالَمِ فَيَلْزَمُ فَسادُ العالَمِ، قالُوا وهَذا أوْلى لِأنَّهُ تَعالى حَكى عَنْهم قَوْلَهُ: ﴿أمِ اتَّخَذُوا آلِهَةً مِنَ الأرْضِ هم يُنْشِرُونَ﴾ ثُمَّ ذَكَرَ الدَّلالَةَ عَلى فَسادِ هَذا فَوَجَبَ أنْ يَخْتَصَّ الدَّلِيلُ بِهِ وبِاللَّهِ التَّوْفِيقُ.
أمّا قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿فَسُبْحانَ اللَّهِ رَبِّ العَرْشِ عَمّا يَصِفُونَ﴾ فَفِيهِ مَسْألَتانِ:
المَسْألَةُ الأُولى: أنَّهُ سُبْحانَهُ لَمّا أقامَ الدَّلالَةَ القاطِعَةَ عَلى التَّوْحِيدِ قالَ بَعْدَهُ: ﴿فَسُبْحانَ اللَّهِ رَبِّ العَرْشِ عَمّا يَصِفُونَ﴾ أيْ هو مُنَزَّهٌ لِأجْلِ هَذِهِ الأدِلَّةِ عَنْ وصْفِهِمْ بِأنَّ مَعَهُ إلَهًا، وهَذا تَنْبِيهٌ عَلى أنَّ الِاشْتِغالَ بِالتَّسْبِيحِ إنَّما يَنْفَعُ بَعْدَ إقامَةِ الدَّلالَةِ عَلى كَوْنِهِ تَعالى مُنَزَّهًا وعَلى أنَّ طَرِيقَةَ التَّقْلِيدِ طَرِيقَةٌ مَهْجُورَةٌ.
المَسْألَةُ الثّانِيَةُ: لِقائِلٍ أنْ يَقُولَ: أيُّ فائِدَةٍ لِقَوْلِهِ: ﴿فَسُبْحانَ اللَّهِ رَبِّ العَرْشِ عَمّا يَصِفُونَ﴾ ولِمَ لَمْ يَكْتَفِ بِقَوْلِهِ: ﴿سُبْحانَ اللَّهِ عَمّا يَصِفُونَ﴾ [المؤمنون: ٩١] ؟ وجَوابُهُ أنَّ هَذِهِ المُناظَرَةَ إنَّما وقَعَتْ مَعَ عَبْدَةِ الأصْنامِ، إلّا أنَّ الدَّلِيلَ الَّذِي ذَكَرَهُ اللَّهُ تَعالى يَعُمُّ جَمِيعَ المُخالِفِينَ، ثُمَّ إنَّهُ تَعالى بَعْدَ ذِكْرِ الدَّلِيلِ العامِّ نَبَّهَ
