عَلى نُكْتَةٍ خاصَّةٍ بِعَبَدَةِ الأصْنامِ، وهي أنَّهُ كَيْفَ يَجُوزُ لِلْعاقِلِ أنْ يَجْعَلَ الجَمادَ الَّذِي لا يَعْقِلُ ولا يُحِسُّ شَرِيكًا في الإلَهِيَّةِ لِخالِقِ العَرْشِ العَظِيمِ ومُوجِدِ السَّماواتِ والأرَضِينَ ومُدَبِّرِ الخَلائِقِ مِنَ النُّورِ والظُّلْمَةِ واللَّوْحِ والقَلَمِ والذّاتِ والصِّفاتِ والجَمادِ والنَّباتِ وأنْواعِ الحَيَواناتِ أجْمَعِينَ.
* * *
أمّا قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿لا يُسْألُ عَمّا يَفْعَلُ وهم يُسْألُونَ﴾ فاعْلَمْ أنَّهُ مُشْتَمِلٌ عَلى بَحْثَيْنِ: أحَدُهُما: أنَّ اللَّهَ تَعالى لا يُسْألُ عَنْ شَيْءٍ مِن أفْعالِهِ ولا يُقالُ لَهُ لِمَ فَعَلْتَ. والثّانِي: أنَّ الخَلائِقَ مَسْؤُولُونَ عَنْ أفْعالِهِمْ. أمّا البَحْثُ الأوَّلُ فَفِيهِ مَسْألَتانِ:
المَسْألَةُ الأُولى: وجْهُ تَعَلُّقِ هَذِهِ الآيَةِ بِما قَبْلَها أنَّ عُمْدَةَ مَن أثْبَتَ لِلَّهِ شَرِيكًا لَيْسَتْ إلّا طَلَبَ اللَّمِّيَّةِ في أفْعالِ اللَّهِ تَعالى، وذَلِكَ لِأنَّ الثَّنَوِيَّةَ والمَجُوسَ وهُمُ الَّذِينَ أثْبَتُوا الشَّرِيكَ لِلَّهِ تَعالى قالُوا: رَأيْنا في العالَمِ خَيْرًا وشَرًّا ولَذَّةً وألَمًا وحَياةً ومَوْتًا وصِحَّةً وسَقَمًا وغِنًى وفَقْرًا، وفاعِلُ الخَيْرِ خَيِّرٌ وفاعِلٌ الشَّرِّ شِرِّيرٌ، ويَسْتَحِيلُ أنْ يَكُونَ الفاعِلُ الواحِدُ خَيِّرًا وشِرِّيرًا مَعًا، فَلا بُدَّ مِن فاعِلَيْنِ لِيَكُونَ أحَدُهُما فاعِلًا لِلْخَيْرِ والآخَرُ فاعِلًا لِلشَّرِّ. ويَرْجِعُ حاصِلُ هَذِهِ الشُّبْهَةِ إلى أنَّ مُدَبِّرَ العالَمِ لَوْ كانَ واحِدًا لَما خَصَّ هَذا بِالحَياةِ والصِّحَّةِ والغِنى، وخَصَّ ذَلِكَ بِالمَوْتِ والألَمِ والفَقْرِ، فَيَرْجِعُ حاصِلُهُ إلى طَلَبِ اللَّمِّيَّةِ في أفْعالِ اللَّهِ تَعالى، فَلَمّا كانَ مَدارُ أمْرِ القائِلِينَ بِالشَّرِيكِ عَلى طَلَبِ اللَّمِّيَّةِ لا جَرَمَ أنَّهُ سُبْحانَهُ وتَعالى بَعْدَ أنْ ذَكَرَ الدَّلِيلَ عَلى التَّوْحِيدِ ذَكَرَ ما هو النُّكْتَةُ الأصْلِيَّةُ في الجَوابِ عَنْ شُبْهَةِ القائِلِينَ بِالشَّرِيكِ؛ لِأنَّ التَّرْتِيبَ الجَيِّدَ في المُناظَرَةِ أنْ يَقَعَ الِابْتِداءُ بِذِكْرِ الدَّلِيلِ المُثْبِتِ لِلْمَطْلُوبِ ثُمَّ يَذْكُرَ بَعْدَهُ ما هو الجَوابُ عَنْ شُبْهَةِ الخَصْمِ.

**Second issue: on the proof that He, glorified is He, "cannot be questioned about what He does."** As for the People of the Sunnah, they argued for this with several arguments.

First: If everything were caused by a cause, the causality of that cause would itself be caused by another cause, and this would lead to an infinite regress (tasalsul). To stop the regress, one must arrive at something that is independent of a cause. The most fitting of things for this is the Essence of God, the Exalted, and His Attributes. Just as His Essence is exempt from needing an agent or a cause, His Attributes are free from needing one who originates them or one who specifies them. Likewise, His agency must be exalted above being attributed to a compelling or determining cause.

Second: If His agency were caused by some cause, that cause would either be necessary or contingent. If it were necessary, then its necessity would entail the necessity of His being an agent, and in that case He would be a necessary cause by essence, not an agent by choice. If it were contingent, then that cause would also be an act of God, the Exalted. His agency would then depend on that cause and require another cause, and this would lead to an infinite regress, which is impossible.

Third: If the cause of God's agency toward the world were eternal, then His agency toward the world would have to be eternal, and so the world would be eternal. If it were originated, it would need another cause, and this would lead to an infinite regress.

Fourth: Whoever performs an act for a purpose either is able to attain that purpose without this intermediary, or is not able to. If he is able, then the intermediary is pointless (ʿabath). If he is not able, then he is incapable (ʿājiz), and incapacity is impossible for God, the Exalted. Incapacity is not impossible for us, which is why our acts are caused by purposes. All of this is impossible with respect to God, the Exalted.

Fifth: If His act were caused by a purpose, that purpose would either return to God, the Exalted, or to His servants. The first is impossible, because He is exempt from benefit and harm. Since that is invalid, it is established that the purpose must return to the servants. But the servants have no purpose except the attainment of pleasures and the absence of pains, and God, the Exalted, is able to bring these about directly, without any intermediaries. Since this is the case, it is impossible that He should do anything for the sake of something else.

Sixth: If He did an act for a purpose, then the existence and non-existence of that purpose would be, with respect to Him, either equal or unequal. If they were equal, it would be impossible for it to be a purpose. If they were unequal, it would follow that He is deficient in His essence and complete through something else, and that is impossible. If you say: although the existence and non-existence of that purpose are equal with respect to Him, with respect to the servants, existence is better than non-existence. We reply: the attainment of that preference by the servant, and the non-attainment of it by him, are either equal with respect to him or not equal, and the first division returns.

Seventh: Existence is either He, glorified is He, or His dominion. His dominion, and one who disposes of his own property, is not asked, "Why did you do that?"

Eighth: Whoever says to another, "Why did you do that?", this question is only appropriate where it is possible that the one asking could prevent the one questioned from his act. This is impossible for the servant with respect to God, the Exalted. For if He did whatever act He wished, how could the servant prevent Him from it? Either by threatening Him with punishment and pain, which is impossible for God, the Exalted; or by threatening Him with deserving blame, departing from wisdom, and being characterized by foolishness, as the Mu'tazilah say, and this too is impossible. For His deserving praise and His being characterized by the attributes of wisdom and majesty are essential matters belonging to Him. And what is established for a thing by its essence cannot change because of a change in external accidental attributes.

Through these arguments it is established that it is not permissible to say to God, regarding His acts, "Why did You do this act?" For every thing is His creation, and there is no cause for His creating.

As for the Mu'tazilah, they conceded that it is not permissible to say to God, "Why did You do this act?", but they built this on another principle: that He, the Exalted, knows the ugliness of ugly things, and knows that He is independent of them. Whoever is like this would be impossible to do what is ugly. When we know this, we know in general that whatever God, the Exalted, does is wisdom and correctness. Since this is so, it is not permissible for the servant to say to God, "Why did You do this?"

* * *

As for the second discussion, which is His saying, exalted is He: **"and they will be questioned"** (21:23). This indicates that the responsible persons (mukallafun) are held accountable for their acts. On this there are two issues.

**The first issue:** The discussion of this questioning is either about its rational possibility or about its occurrence as established by revelation (sam'i). As for rational possibility, the disagreement here is with those who deny the obligations (al-takalif), and they argued for their position with several arguments.

First: They said: Obligation either applies to the servant in a state where his motive toward the act and its omission are equal, or in a state where one of them is preferred over the other. The first is impossible, because in a state of equality, preference is impossible; and in a state where preference is impossible, obligation to prefer is an obligation to the impossible. The second is impossible, because in a state of preference, the preferred option is necessary to occur and the non-preferred option is impossible to occur; and obligation to bring about what must occur is pointless, while obligation to bring about what is impossible to occur is an obligation to what cannot be borne.

Second: They said: Whatever God knows will occur is necessary to occur, so obligation to it is pointless; and whatever God knows will not occur is impossible to occur, so obligation to it is an obligation to what cannot be borne.

Third: They said: The servant's questioning is either for a benefit or not for a benefit. If it is for a benefit, that benefit either returns to God, the Exalted, in which case He would be in need, which is impossible; or it returns to the servant, which is also impossible, because his being questioned, since it is a cause for directing punishment at him, is not a benefit returning to him but a harm returning to him. If there is no benefit in the questioning, it is pointless, which is not permissible for the Wise; rather, it would be harm, which is not permissible for the Merciful.

The answer to these arguments is from two aspects.

The first: Your purpose in raising this doubt, which negates obligation, is to make us affirm the negation of obligation. So it is as if you are obligating us to negate obligation, which is self-contradictory.

The second: The basis of your speech in these doubts rests on a single point, namely that all obligations are obligations to what cannot be borne, so it is not permissible for the Wise to impose them on the servants. Thus the sum of these doubts returns to saying to Him, "Why did You obligate Your servants?" But we have already shown that He, glorified is He, "is not questioned about what He does, whereas they are questioned." It is thus clear from this that His saying "He is not questioned about what He does" is like the foundation and principle for His saying "and they are questioned." So reflect on these marvelous subtleties, so that you may grasp a part of the secrets of the science of the Qur'an.

As for the occurrence established by revelation, one may say: His saying "and they are questioned," although it is reinforced by His saying, "By your Lord, We will certainly question them all" (al-Hijr 15:92), and by His saying, "Stop them, for they are to be questioned" (al-Saffat 37:24), nevertheless seems to contradict His saying: "So on that Day, neither man nor jinn will be questioned about his sin" (al-Rahman 55:39). The answer is that the Day of Resurrection is a long day with many stations, so each of the negation and affirmation is applied to a different station, to remove the contradiction.

**The second issue:** The Mu'tazilah said regarding this several points.

First: If He, the Exalted, were the Creator of both good and evil, it would be necessary that He be questioned about what He does; indeed, He would be blamed for what deserves blame, just as He is praised for what deserves praise.

Second: It would be necessary that they not be questioned about matters when there is no agent other than Him.

Third: It would not be permissible for them to be questioned about their deeds, since they have no deeds.

Fourth: Their deeds are not something they can deviate from, in terms of Him having created and originated them in them.

Fifth: He, the Exalted, has explicitly stated in many places that He accepts the proof (ḥujjah) of the servants against Him, as in His saying: "Messengers as bearers of good news and warners, so that people will have no argument against God after the messengers" (al-Nisa' 4:165). This requires that they have an argument against Him before the sending of the messengers. And He said: "If We had destroyed them with a punishment before this, they would have said, 'Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger so that we might follow Your signs before we were humiliated and disgraced?'" (Taha 20:134). Similar verses are numerous, and all of them indicate that the servant's proof is directed against God, the Exalted.

Sixth: Thumamah said: When the servant stands on the Day of Resurrection, God, the Exalted, will say, "What drove you to disobey Me?" And he will say, according to the doctrine of Jabr (determinism): "My Lord, You created me a disbeliever, commanded me to do what I am not able to do, and placed a barrier between me and it." There is no doubt that according to the doctrine of Jabr he would be truthful. And God, the Exalted, said: "This is a day when the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness" (al-Ma'idah 5:119). So it must be that this speech benefits him. It was said to him: And who will leave him to say this speech or to argue? Thumamah said: Is it not that when God prevents him from speech and argument, He knows that He has prevented him from what, had He not prevented him, would have left him silenced? And this is the utmost of being silenced.

The answer to these points: They are countered by the question of the motive (masʼalat al-dāʻī) and the question of knowledge (masʼalat al-ʻilm), and then by the eight arguments we have explained, in which we showed that it is impossible to seek the "why" (lamiyyah) of God's acts and rulings.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 21, verses 22–23 (part 1 of 3):

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined﴾, there are two issues concerning it.

The first issue: The grammarians said that "illa" (except) here carries the meaning of "ghayr" (other than). That is, had there been in them something other than the One who is their Creator administering their affairs and managing them, both would have been ruined. It is not permissible for it to carry the meaning of exception (istithna'), because if we interpreted it as exception, the meaning would be: "Had there been in them gods with whom Allah was not present, they would have been ruined." This would imply, by way of inference (mafhum), that if there were gods in them with Allah present alongside them, ruin would not occur. That is false, because if there were gods in them, whether Allah was with them or not, ruin would be necessary. Since its interpretation as exception has been ruled out, it is established that the intended meaning is what we have mentioned.

The second issue: The theologians (mutakallimun) said: The assertion that there exist two gods leads to an impossibility, so the assertion that there exist two gods must be impossible. We say that it leads to an impossibility because if we suppose the existence of two gods, each of them must be capable of all possible things (maqdurat). If that is so, each of them would be capable of moving Zayd and of making him still. So if we suppose that one of them wills to move him and the other wills to make him still, then either both wills take effect, which is impossible because the joining of two opposites is impossible; or neither takes effect, which is also impossible, because the obstacle to the existence of the willed outcome of each is the willed outcome of the other, so the willed outcome of one is prevented only when the willed outcome of the other exists, and vice versa. Then if both were prevented together, they would both exist together, which is impossible; or the willed outcome of one of them takes effect without the other's, which is also impossible, for two reasons:

The first of them: If each of them were capable of what has no limit, it would be impossible for one of them to be more capable than the other. Rather, they must be equal in capability. And when they are equal in capability, it is impossible for the willed outcome of one to become more deserving of occurrence than the willed outcome of the other; otherwise it would entail preferring a possible thing without a preponderant cause.

The second of them: If the willed outcome of one occurs without that of the other, then the one whose will occurred is capable, and the one whose will did not occur is incapable, and incapacity is a deficiency, which is impossible with respect to Allah.

If it is said: Ruin only arises when they differ in will, and you do not claim that their differing in will is necessary; rather the most you claim is that their differing in will is possible. So if ruin is based upon difference in will, and this difference is possible, and what is based upon the possible is possible, then ruin is possible and not actual. How then does Allah, exalted is He, affirm with certainty that ruin occurs?

We say: The answer is in two respects. The first: Perhaps He, glorified is He, treated the possible as if it were actual, on the basis of what is apparent, inasmuch as subjects are ruined by the management of two kings because of the rivalry that arises between them. The second, and it is the stronger: that we demonstrate the necessity of ruin not from the aspect we have mentioned, but from another aspect. We say: If we suppose two gods, each of them would be capable of all possible things, so that there would result the occurrence of one possible thing from two independent agents in one respect, and this is impossible, because the attribution of an act to its agent is due to its possibility. So when each of them is independent in bringing it into being, the act, given this, is necessarily existent, and therefore its attribution to this one is impossible, since it has come about from both of them together, so that it would follow that it is independent of both together and needs both together, and that is impossible. This is a complete argument in the matter of tawhid (divine unity). We say: The assertion that two gods exist leads to the impossibility of the occurrence of what is willed by either of them; and when that is so, it must be that nothing ever occurs, and then ruin certainly occurs. Or we say: If we assume two gods, either they agree or they differ. If they agree upon one thing, then that one thing is capable for both of them and willed by both of them, so its occurrence would be by both of them, and that is impossible. If they differ, then either both willed outcomes occur, or neither occurs, or one occurs without the other; and all of these are impossible. Thus it is established that ruin is necessary under every assumption.

If you say: Why is it not permissible that they agree upon one thing without ruin following, because ruin only follows if each of them wished to bring it into being himself, and that is difference? But if each of them wished that its bringer be one of them specifically, then in that case there is no necessity of a created thing occurring between two creators.

We say: Its being brought into being by one of them is either the very capability and will, or the very effect, or a third matter. If it is the first, then it entails sharing in capability and will and sharing in the bringer. If it is the second, then the occurrence of that effect by the capability and will of one of them is no more preferable than its occurrence by the capability of the other; for each of them has an independent will with regard to influence. If it is the third, namely that the bringer of it is a third matter, then that third matter, if it is eternal, it is impossible for it to be the object of will; and if it is originated, then it is the very effect itself, and this category becomes the second category that we mentioned.

Know that when you have grasped the reality of this proof, you will recognize that everything in this upper and lower world of originated and created things is a proof of the oneness of Allah, exalted is He; indeed, the existence of each of the substances and accidents is a complete proof of tawhid from the aspect we have explained. This proof has been mentioned by Allah, exalted is He, in various places of His Book. Know also that there are other proofs for the oneness of Allah, exalted is He.

The first of them, and it is the strongest: It may be said: If we suppose two necessarily existent beings (wajib al-wujud li-dhatihima), then they must share in existence, and each of them must be distinguished from the other by its own essence, and what makes them share is other than what makes them distinct. Thus each of them is composed of that by which it shares with the other and that by which it is distinguished from it. Every composite is dependent upon its part, and its part is other than it; so every composite is dependent upon something other than itself. And everything dependent upon something other than itself is possible in its essence (mumkin li-dhatihi). So the necessarily existent in its essence is possible in its essence. This is a contradiction. Therefore, the necessarily existent is none but the One, and everything else is possible and dependent upon Him; and everything dependent for its existence upon another is originated. So everything other than Allah, exalted is He, is originated. This proof can also be made an explanation of this verse; for we have only argued that it follows from assuming two necessarily existent beings that none of them is necessary; and when the necessary is not found, none of these possible things is found; and then ruin follows. Thus it is established that from the existence of two gods there follows the ruin of the entire world.

The second: If we suppose two gods, each of them would necessarily share with the other in divinity, and each must be distinguished from the other by something; for otherwise plurality would not be realized. So that by which they are distinguished is either an attribute of perfection or not. If it is an attribute of perfection, then whoever lacks it would lack perfection, and so would be deficient, and the deficient cannot be a god. If it is not an attribute of perfection, then whoever is described by it would be described by what is not an attribute of perfection, and so would be deficient. It may also be said: If that by which they are distinguished is required for the realization of divinity, then whoever lacks it is not a god; and if it is not required for divinity, then attribution of it is not necessary, and so it requires a specifier, and whoever is described by it is dependent and in need.

The third: It may be said: If we suppose two gods, they must be such that others can distinguish between them; but distinction in our minds is achieved only by difference in place, or in time, or in necessity and possibility; and all of these are impossible with respect to God; so the achievement of distinction is impossible.

The fourth: Either one of the two gods is sufficient for managing the world or he is not. If he is sufficient, then the second is superfluous and not needed, and that is a deficiency, and the deficient is not

مِن عَدَدٍ فَيُفْضِي ذَلِكَ إلى وُجُودِ أعْدادٍ لا نِهايَةَ لَها وذَلِكَ مُحالٌ فالقَوْلُ بِوُجُودِ الآلِهَةِ مُحالٌ. وسادِسُها: أنَّ أحَدَ الإلَهَيْنِ إمّا أنْ يَقْدِرَ عَلى أنْ يَخُصَّ نَفْسَهُ بِدَلِيلٍ يَدُلُّ عَلَيْهِ ولا يَدُلُّ عَلى غَيْرِهِ أوْ لا يَقْدِرَ عَلَيْهِ، والأوَّلُ مُحالٌ لِأنَّ دَلِيلَ الصّانِعِ لَيْسَ إلّا بِالمُحْدَثاتِ ولَيْسَ في حُدُوثِ المُحْدَثاتِ ما يَدُلُّ عَلى تَعْيِينِ أحَدِهِما دُونَ الثّانِي، والتّالِي مُحالٌ لِأنَّهُ يُفْضِي إلى كَوْنِهِ عاجِزًا عَنْ تَعْرِيفِ نَفْسِهِ عَلى التَّعْيِينِ، والعاجِزُ لا يَكُونُ إلَهًا. وسابِعُها: أنَّ أحَدَ الإلَهَيْنِ إمّا أنْ يَقْدِرَ عَلى أنْ يَسْتُرَ شَيْئًا مِن أفْعالِهِ عَنِ الآخَرِ أوْ لا يَقْدِرَ، فَإنْ قَدَرَ لَزِمَ أنْ يَكُونَ المَسْتُورُ عَنْهُ جاهِلًا، وإنْ لَمْ يَقْدِرْ لَزِمَ كَوْنُهُ عاجِزًا. وثامِنُها: لَوْ قَدَّرْنا إلَهَيْنِ لَكانَ مَجْمُوعُ قُدْرَتَيْهِما بَيْنَهُما أقْوى مِن قُدْرَةِ كُلِّ واحِدٍ مِنهُما وحْدَهُ، فَيَكُونُ كُلُّ واحِدٍ مِنَ القُدْرَتَيْنِ مُتَناهِيًا والمَجْمُوعُ ضِعْفُ المُتَناهِي فَيَكُونُ الكُلُّ مُتَناهِيًا. وتاسِعُها: العَدَدُ ناقِصٌ لِاحْتِياجِهِ إلى الواحِدِ، والواحِدُ الَّذِي يُوجَدُ مِن جِنْسِهِ عَدَدٌ ناقِصٌ ناقِصٌ، لِأنَّ العَدَدَ أزْيَدُ مِنهُ، والنّاقِصُ لا يَكُونُ إلَهًا فالإلَهُ واحِدٌ لا مَحالَةَ. وعاشِرُها: أنّا لَوْ فَرَضْنا مَعْدُومًا مُمْكِنَ الوُجُودِ ثُمَّ قَدَّرْنا إلَهَيْنِ فَإنْ لَمْ يَقْدِرْ واحِدٌ مِنهُما عَلى إيجادِهِ كانَ كُلُّ واحِدٍ مِنهُما عاجِزًا والعاجِزُ لا يَكُونُ إلَهًا، وإنْ قَدَرَ أحَدُهُما دُونَ الآخَرِ فَهَذا الآخَرُ يَكُونُ إلَهًا، وإنْ قَدِرا جَمِيعًا فَإمّا أنْ يُوجِداهُ بِالتَّعاوُنِ فَيَكُونُ كُلُّ واحِدٍ مِنهُما مُحْتاجًا إلى إعانَةِ الآخَرِ، وإنْ قَدَرَ كُلُّ واحِدٍ عَلى إيجادِهِ بِالِاسْتِقْلالِ فَإذا أوْجَدَهُ أحَدُهُما فَإمّا أنْ يَبْقى الثّانِي قادِرًا عَلَيْهِ وهو مُحالٌ لِأنَّ إيجادَ المَوْجُودِ مُحالٌ، وإنْ لَمْ يَبْقَ فَحِينَئِذٍ يَكُونُ الأوَّلُ قَدْ أزالَ قُدْرَةَ الثّانِي وعَجْزَهُ فَيَكُونُ مَقْهُورًا تَحْتَ تَصَرُّفِهِ فَلا يَكُونُ إلَهًا. فَإنْ قِيلَ الواجِدُ إذا أوْجَدَ مَقْدُورَهُ فَقَدْ زالَتْ قُدْرَتُهُ عَنْهُ فَيَلْزَمُكُمُ العَجْزُ، قُلْنا: الواحِدُ إذا أوْجَدَهُ فَقَدْ نَفَذَتْ قُدْرَتُهُ فَنَفاذُ القُدْرَةِ لا يَكُونُ عَجْزًا، أمّا الشَّرِيكُ فَإنَّهُ لَمّا نَفَذَتْ قُدْرَتُهُ لَمْ يَبْقَ لِشَرِيكِهِ قُدْرَةٌ البَتَّةَ بَلْ زالَتْ قُدْرَتُهُ بِسَبَبِ قُدْرَةِ الأوَّلِ فَيَكُونُ تَعْجِيزًا. الحادِيَ عَشَرَ: أنَّ نُقَرِّرَ هَذِهِ الدَّلالَةَ عَلى وجْهٍ الدَّلالَةَ إلى أنْ نَقُولَ: إذا خَلَقَ أحَدُهُما فِيهِ حَرَكَةً امْتَنَعَ عَلى الثّانِي خَلْقُ السُّكُونِ، فالأوَّلُ أزالَ قُدْرَةَ الثّانِي وعَجَّزَهُ فَلا يَكُونُ إلَهًا، وهَذانَ الوَجْهانِ يُفِيدانِ العَجْزَ نَظَرًا إلى قُدْرَتَيْهِما، والدَّلالَةُ الأُولى إنَّما تُفِيدُ العَجْزَ بِالنَّظَرِ إلى إرادَتَيْهِما. وثانِي عَشَرَها: أنَّهُما لَمّا كانا عالِمَيْنِ بِجَمِيعِ المَعْلُوماتِ كانَ عِلْمُ كُلِّ واحِدٍ مِنهُما مُتَعَلِّقًا بِعَيْنِ مَعْلُومِ الآخَرِ فَوَجَبَ تَماثُلُ عِلْمَيْهِما، والذّاتُ القابِلَةُ لِأحَدِ المِثْلَيْنِ قابِلَةٌ لِلْمِثْلِ الآخَرِ، فاخْتِصاصُ كُلِّ واحِدٍ مِنهُما بِتِلْكَ الصِّفَةِ مَعَ جَوازِ اتِّصافِهِ بِصِفَةِ الآخَرِ عَلى البَدَلِ يَسْتَدْعِي مُخَصِّصًا يُخَصِّصُ كُلَّ واحِدٍ مِنهُما بِعِلْمِهِ وقُدْرَتِهِ فَيَكُونُ كُلُّ واحِدٍ مِنهُما عَبْدًا فَقِيرًا ناقِصًا. وثالِثَ عَشَرَها: أنَّ الشَّرِكَةَ عَيْبٌ ونَقْصٌ في الشّاهِدِ، والفَرْدانِيَّةُ والتَّوَحُّدُ صِفَةُ كَمالٍ، ونَرى المُلُوكَ يَكْرَهُونَ الشَّرِكَةَ في المُلْكِ الحَقِيرِ المُخْتَصَرِ أشَدَّ الكَراهِيَةِ، ونَرى أنَّهُ كُلَّما كانَ المُلْكُ أعْظَمَ كانَتِ النَّفْرَةُ عَنِ الشَّرِكَةِ أشَدَّ، فَما ظَنُّكَ بِمُلْكِ اللَّهِ عَزَّ وجَلَّ ومَلَكُوتِهِ، فَلَوْ أرادَ أحَدُهُما اسْتِخْلاصَ المُلْكِ لِنَفْسِهِ فَإنْ قَدَرَ عَلَيْهِ كانَ المَغْلُوبُ فَقِيرًا عاجِزًا فَلا يَكُونُ إلَهًا، وإنْ لَمْ يَقْدِرْ عَلَيْهِ كانَ في أشَدِّ الغَمِّ والكَراهِيَةِ فَلا يَكُونُ إلَهًا. أوَّلًا عَبْدَيْنِ لَمْ يَحْنَثْ لِأنَّ شَرْطَ الأوَّلِ أنْ يَكُونَ فَرْدًا وهَذا لَيْسَ بِفَرْدٍ، فَلَوِ اشْتَرى بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ واحِدًا لَمْ يَحْنَثْ أيْضًا لِأنَّ شَرْطَ الفَرْدِ أنْ يَكُونَ سابِقًا وهَذا لَيْسَ بِسابِقٍ، فَلَمّا وصَفَ اللَّهُ تَعالى نَفْسَهُ بِكَوْنِهِ أوَّلًا وجَبَ أنْ يَكُونَ فَرْدًا سابِقًا فَوَجَبَ أنْ لا يَكُونَ لَهُ شَرِيكٌ. وثانِيها: قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وعِنْدَهُ مَفاتِحُ الغَيْبِ لا يَعْلَمُها إلّا هُوَ﴾ [الأنْعامِ: ٥٩] فالنَّصُّ يَقْتَضِي أنْ لا يَكُونَ أحَدٌ سِواهُ عالِمًا بِالغَيْبِ ولَوْ كانَ لَهُ شَرِيكٌ لَكانَ عالِمًا بِالغَيْبِ وهو خِلافُ النَّصِّ. وثالِثُها: أنَّ اللَّهَ تَعالى صَرَّحَ بِكَلِمَةِ ﴿لا إلَهَ إلّا هُوَ﴾ [البَقَرَةِ: ٢٥٥] في سَبْعَةٍ وثَلاثِينَ مَوْضِعًا مِن كِتابِهِ، وصَرَّحَ بِالوَحْدانِيَّةِ في مَواضِعَ نَحْوَ قَوْلِهِ: ﴿وإلَهُكم إلَهٌ واحِدٌ﴾ [البَقَرَةِ: ١٦٣] وقَوْلِهِ: ﴿قُلْ هو اللَّهُ أحَدٌ﴾ [الإخْلاصِ: ١] وكُلُّ ذَلِكَ صَرِيحٌ في البابِ. ورابِعُها: قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿كُلُّ شَيْءٍ هالِكٌ إلّا وجْهَهُ﴾ حُكْمٌ بِهَلاكِ كُلِّ ما سِواهُ، ومَن عُدِمَ بَعْدَ وجُودِهِ لا يَكُونُ قَدِيمًا، ومَن لا يَكُونُ قَدِيمًا لا يَكُونُ إلَهًا. وخامِسُها: قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿لَوْ كانَ فِيهِما آلِهَةٌ إلّا اللَّهُ لَفَسَدَتا﴾ وهو كَقَوْلِهِ: ﴿ولَعَلا بَعْضُهم عَلى بَعْضٍ﴾ [المُؤْمِنُونَ: ٩١] وقَوْلِهِ: ﴿إذًا لابْتَغَوْا إلى ذِي العَرْشِ سَبِيلًا﴾ [الإسْراءِ: ٤٢] . وسادِسُها: قَوْلُهُ: ﴿وإنْ يَمْسَسْكَ اللَّهُ بِضُرٍّ فَلا كاشِفَ لَهُ إلّا هو وإنْ يُرِدْكَ بِخَيْرٍ فَلا رادَّ لِفَضْلِهِ﴾ [يُونُسَ: ١٠٧] وقالَ في آيَةٍ أُخْرى: ﴿قُلْ أفَرَأيْتُمْ ما تَدْعُونَ مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ إنْ أرادَنِيَ اللَّهُ بِضُرٍّ هَلْ هُنَّ كاشِفاتُ ضُرِّهِ أوْ أرادَنِي بِرَحْمَةٍ هَلْ هُنَّ مُمْسِكاتُ رَحْمَتِهِ﴾ [الزُّمَرِ: ٣٨] . وسابِعُها: قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿قُلْ أرَأيْتُمْ إنْ أخَذَ اللَّهُ سَمْعَكم وأبْصارَكم وخَتَمَ عَلى قُلُوبِكم مَن إلَهٌ غَيْرُ اللَّهِ يَأْتِيكم بِهِ﴾ [الأنْعامِ: ٤٦] وهَذا الحَصْرُ يَدُلُّ عَلى نَفْيِ الشَّرِيكِ. وثامِنُها: قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿اللَّهُ خالِقُ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ﴾ [الزُّمَرِ: ٦٢] فَلَوْ وُجِدَ الشَّرِيكُ لَمْ يَكُنْ خالِقًا فَلَمْ يَكُنْ فِيهِ فائِدَةٌ. واعْلَمْ أنَّ كُلَّ مَسْألَةٍ لا تَتَوَقَّفُ مَعْرِفَةُ صِدْقِ الرُّسُلِ عَلَيْها فَإنَّهُ يُمْكِنُ إثْباتُها بِالسَّمْعِ، والوَحْدانِيَّةُ لا تَتَوَقَّفُ مَعْرِفَةُ صِدْقِ الرُّسُلِ عَلَيْها، فَلا جَرَمَ يُمْكِنُ إثْباتُها بِالدَّلائِلِ السَّمْعِيَّةِ، واعْلَمْ أنَّ مَن طَعَنَ في دَلالَةِ التَّمانُعِ فَسَرَّ الآيَةَ بِأنَّ المُرادَ لَوْ كانَ في السَّماءِ والأرْضِ آلِهَةٌ تَقُولُ بِإلَهِيَّتِها عَبَدَةُ الأوْثانِ لَزِمَ فَسادُ العالَمِ لِأنَّها جَماداتٌ لا تَقْدِرُ عَلى تَدْبِيرِ العالَمِ فَيَلْزَمُ فَسادُ العالَمِ، قالُوا وهَذا أوْلى لِأنَّهُ تَعالى حَكى عَنْهم قَوْلَهُ: ﴿أمِ اتَّخَذُوا آلِهَةً مِنَ الأرْضِ هم يُنْشِرُونَ﴾ ثُمَّ ذَكَرَ الدَّلالَةَ عَلى فَسادِ هَذا فَوَجَبَ أنْ يَخْتَصَّ الدَّلِيلُ بِهِ وبِاللَّهِ التَّوْفِيقُ.
أمّا قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿فَسُبْحانَ اللَّهِ رَبِّ العَرْشِ عَمّا يَصِفُونَ﴾ فَفِيهِ مَسْألَتانِ:
المَسْألَةُ الأُولى: أنَّهُ سُبْحانَهُ لَمّا أقامَ الدَّلالَةَ القاطِعَةَ عَلى التَّوْحِيدِ قالَ بَعْدَهُ: ﴿فَسُبْحانَ اللَّهِ رَبِّ العَرْشِ عَمّا يَصِفُونَ﴾ أيْ هو مُنَزَّهٌ لِأجْلِ هَذِهِ الأدِلَّةِ عَنْ وصْفِهِمْ بِأنَّ مَعَهُ إلَهًا، وهَذا تَنْبِيهٌ عَلى أنَّ الِاشْتِغالَ بِالتَّسْبِيحِ إنَّما يَنْفَعُ بَعْدَ إقامَةِ الدَّلالَةِ عَلى كَوْنِهِ تَعالى مُنَزَّهًا وعَلى أنَّ طَرِيقَةَ التَّقْلِيدِ طَرِيقَةٌ مَهْجُورَةٌ.
المَسْألَةُ الثّانِيَةُ: لِقائِلٍ أنْ يَقُولَ: أيُّ فائِدَةٍ لِقَوْلِهِ: ﴿فَسُبْحانَ اللَّهِ رَبِّ العَرْشِ عَمّا يَصِفُونَ﴾ ولِمَ لَمْ يَكْتَفِ بِقَوْلِهِ: ﴿سُبْحانَ اللَّهِ عَمّا يَصِفُونَ﴾ [المؤمنون: ٩١] ؟ وجَوابُهُ أنَّ هَذِهِ المُناظَرَةَ إنَّما وقَعَتْ مَعَ عَبْدَةِ الأصْنامِ، إلّا أنَّ الدَّلِيلَ الَّذِي ذَكَرَهُ اللَّهُ تَعالى يَعُمُّ جَمِيعَ المُخالِفِينَ، ثُمَّ إنَّهُ تَعالى بَعْدَ ذِكْرِ الدَّلِيلِ العامِّ نَبَّهَ
[Page 134]
عَلى نُكْتَةٍ خاصَّةٍ بِعَبَدَةِ الأصْنامِ، وهي أنَّهُ كَيْفَ يَجُوزُ لِلْعاقِلِ أنْ يَجْعَلَ الجَمادَ الَّذِي لا يَعْقِلُ ولا يُحِسُّ شَرِيكًا في الإلَهِيَّةِ لِخالِقِ العَرْشِ العَظِيمِ ومُوجِدِ السَّماواتِ والأرَضِينَ ومُدَبِّرِ الخَلائِقِ مِنَ النُّورِ والظُّلْمَةِ واللَّوْحِ والقَلَمِ والذّاتِ والصِّفاتِ والجَمادِ والنَّباتِ وأنْواعِ الحَيَواناتِ أجْمَعِينَ.
* * *
أمّا قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿لا يُسْألُ عَمّا يَفْعَلُ وهم يُسْألُونَ﴾ فاعْلَمْ أنَّهُ مُشْتَمِلٌ عَلى بَحْثَيْنِ: أحَدُهُما: أنَّ اللَّهَ تَعالى لا يُسْألُ عَنْ شَيْءٍ مِن أفْعالِهِ ولا يُقالُ لَهُ لِمَ فَعَلْتَ. والثّانِي: أنَّ الخَلائِقَ مَسْؤُولُونَ عَنْ أفْعالِهِمْ. أمّا البَحْثُ الأوَّلُ فَفِيهِ مَسْألَتانِ:
المَسْألَةُ الأُولى: وجْهُ تَعَلُّقِ هَذِهِ الآيَةِ بِما قَبْلَها أنَّ عُمْدَةَ مَن أثْبَتَ لِلَّهِ شَرِيكًا لَيْسَتْ إلّا طَلَبَ اللَّمِّيَّةِ في أفْعالِ اللَّهِ تَعالى، وذَلِكَ لِأنَّ الثَّنَوِيَّةَ والمَجُوسَ وهُمُ الَّذِينَ أثْبَتُوا الشَّرِيكَ لِلَّهِ تَعالى قالُوا: رَأيْنا في العالَمِ خَيْرًا وشَرًّا ولَذَّةً وألَمًا وحَياةً ومَوْتًا وصِحَّةً وسَقَمًا وغِنًى وفَقْرًا، وفاعِلُ الخَيْرِ خَيِّرٌ وفاعِلٌ الشَّرِّ شِرِّيرٌ، ويَسْتَحِيلُ أنْ يَكُونَ الفاعِلُ الواحِدُ خَيِّرًا وشِرِّيرًا مَعًا، فَلا بُدَّ مِن فاعِلَيْنِ لِيَكُونَ أحَدُهُما فاعِلًا لِلْخَيْرِ والآخَرُ فاعِلًا لِلشَّرِّ. ويَرْجِعُ حاصِلُ هَذِهِ الشُّبْهَةِ إلى أنَّ مُدَبِّرَ العالَمِ لَوْ كانَ واحِدًا لَما خَصَّ هَذا بِالحَياةِ والصِّحَّةِ والغِنى، وخَصَّ ذَلِكَ بِالمَوْتِ والألَمِ والفَقْرِ، فَيَرْجِعُ حاصِلُهُ إلى طَلَبِ اللَّمِّيَّةِ في أفْعالِ اللَّهِ تَعالى، فَلَمّا كانَ مَدارُ أمْرِ القائِلِينَ بِالشَّرِيكِ عَلى طَلَبِ اللَّمِّيَّةِ لا جَرَمَ أنَّهُ سُبْحانَهُ وتَعالى بَعْدَ أنْ ذَكَرَ الدَّلِيلَ عَلى التَّوْحِيدِ ذَكَرَ ما هو النُّكْتَةُ الأصْلِيَّةُ في الجَوابِ عَنْ شُبْهَةِ القائِلِينَ بِالشَّرِيكِ؛ لِأنَّ التَّرْتِيبَ الجَيِّدَ في المُناظَرَةِ أنْ يَقَعَ الِابْتِداءُ بِذِكْرِ الدَّلِيلِ المُثْبِتِ لِلْمَطْلُوبِ ثُمَّ يَذْكُرَ بَعْدَهُ ما هو الجَوابُ عَنْ شُبْهَةِ الخَصْمِ.

**Second issue: on the proof that He, glorified is He, "cannot be questioned about what He does."** As for the People of the Sunnah, they argued for this with several arguments.

First: If everything were caused by a cause, the causality of that cause would itself be caused by another cause, and this would lead to an infinite regress (tasalsul). To stop the regress, one must arrive at something that is independent of a cause. The most fitting of things for this is the Essence of God, the Exalted, and His Attributes. Just as His Essence is exempt from needing an agent or a cause, His Attributes are free from needing one who originates them or one who specifies them. Likewise, His agency must be exalted above being attributed to a compelling or determining cause.

Second: If His agency were caused by some cause, that cause would either be necessary or contingent. If it were necessary, then its necessity would entail the necessity of His being an agent, and in that case He would be a necessary cause by essence, not an agent by choice. If it were contingent, then that cause would also be an act of God, the Exalted. His agency would then depend on that cause and require another cause, and this would lead to an infinite regress, which is impossible.

Third: If the cause of God's agency toward the world were eternal, then His agency toward the world would have to be eternal, and so the world would be eternal. If it were originated, it would need another cause, and this would lead to an infinite regress.

Fourth: Whoever performs an act for a purpose either is able to attain that purpose without this intermediary, or is not able to. If he is able, then the intermediary is pointless (ʿabath). If he is not able, then he is incapable (ʿājiz), and incapacity is impossible for God, the Exalted. Incapacity is not impossible for us, which is why our acts are caused by purposes. All of this is impossible with respect to God, the Exalted.

Fifth: If His act were caused by a purpose, that purpose would either return to God, the Exalted, or to His servants. The first is impossible, because He is exempt from benefit and harm. Since that is invalid, it is established that the purpose must return to the servants. But the servants have no purpose except the attainment of pleasures and the absence of pains, and God, the Exalted, is able to bring these about directly, without any intermediaries. Since this is the case, it is impossible that He should do anything for the sake of something else.

Sixth: If He did an act for a purpose, then the existence and non-existence of that purpose would be, with respect to Him, either equal or unequal. If they were equal, it would be impossible for it to be a purpose. If they were unequal, it would follow that He is deficient in His essence and complete through something else, and that is impossible. If you say: although the existence and non-existence of that purpose are equal with respect to Him, with respect to the servants, existence is better than non-existence. We reply: the attainment of that preference by the servant, and the non-attainment of it by him, are either equal with respect to him or not equal, and the first division returns.

Seventh: Existence is either He, glorified is He, or His dominion. His dominion, and one who disposes of his own property, is not asked, "Why did you do that?"

Eighth: Whoever says to another, "Why did you do that?", this question is only appropriate where it is possible that the one asking could prevent the one questioned from his act. This is impossible for the servant with respect to God, the Exalted. For if He did whatever act He wished, how could the servant prevent Him from it? Either by threatening Him with punishment and pain, which is impossible for God, the Exalted; or by threatening Him with deserving blame, departing from wisdom, and being characterized by foolishness, as the Mu'tazilah say, and this too is impossible. For His deserving praise and His being characterized by the attributes of wisdom and majesty are essential matters belonging to Him. And what is established for a thing by its essence cannot change because of a change in external accidental attributes.

Through these arguments it is established that it is not permissible to say to God, regarding His acts, "Why did You do this act?" For every thing is His creation, and there is no cause for His creating.

As for the Mu'tazilah, they conceded that it is not permissible to say to God, "Why did You do this act?", but they built this on another principle: that He, the Exalted, knows the ugliness of ugly things, and knows that He is independent of them. Whoever is like this would be impossible to do what is ugly. When we know this, we know in general that whatever God, the Exalted, does is wisdom and correctness. Since this is so, it is not permissible for the servant to say to God, "Why did You do this?"

* * *

As for the second discussion, which is His saying, exalted is He: **"and they will be questioned"** (21:23). This indicates that the responsible persons (mukallafun) are held accountable for their acts. On this there are two issues.

**The first issue:** The discussion of this questioning is either about its rational possibility or about its occurrence as established by revelation (sam'i). As for rational possibility, the disagreement here is with those who deny the obligations (al-takalif), and they argued for their position with several arguments.

First: They said: Obligation either applies to the servant in a state where his motive toward the act and its omission are equal, or in a state where one of them is preferred over the other. The first is impossible, because in a state of equality, preference is impossible; and in a state where preference is impossible, obligation to prefer is an obligation to the impossible. The second is impossible, because in a state of preference, the preferred option is necessary to occur and the non-preferred option is impossible to occur; and obligation to bring about what must occur is pointless, while obligation to bring about what is impossible to occur is an obligation to what cannot be borne.

Second: They said: Whatever God knows will occur is necessary to occur, so obligation to it is pointless; and whatever God knows will not occur is impossible to occur, so obligation to it is an obligation to what cannot be borne.

Third: They said: The servant's questioning is either for a benefit or not for a benefit. If it is for a benefit, that benefit either returns to God, the Exalted, in which case He would be in need, which is impossible; or it returns to the servant, which is also impossible, because his being questioned, since it is a cause for directing punishment at him, is not a benefit returning to him but a harm returning to him. If there is no benefit in the questioning, it is pointless, which is not permissible for the Wise; rather, it would be harm, which is not permissible for the Merciful.

The answer to these arguments is from two aspects.

The first: Your purpose in raising this doubt, which negates obligation, is to make us affirm the negation of obligation. So it is as if you are obligating us to negate obligation, which is self-contradictory.

The second: The basis of your speech in these doubts rests on a single point, namely that all obligations are obligations to what cannot be borne, so it is not permissible for the Wise to impose them on the servants. Thus the sum of these doubts returns to saying to Him, "Why did You obligate Your servants?" But we have already shown that He, glorified is He, "is not questioned about what He does, whereas they are questioned." It is thus clear from this that His saying "He is not questioned about what He does" is like the foundation and principle for His saying "and they are questioned." So reflect on these marvelous subtleties, so that you may grasp a part of the secrets of the science of the Qur'an.

As for the occurrence established by revelation, one may say: His saying "and they are questioned," although it is reinforced by His saying, "By your Lord, We will certainly question them all" (al-Hijr 15:92), and by His saying, "Stop them, for they are to be questioned" (al-Saffat 37:24), nevertheless seems to contradict His saying: "So on that Day, neither man nor jinn will be questioned about his sin" (al-Rahman 55:39). The answer is that the Day of Resurrection is a long day with many stations, so each of the negation and affirmation is applied to a different station, to remove the contradiction.

**The second issue:** The Mu'tazilah said regarding this several points.

First: If He, the Exalted, were the Creator of both good and evil, it would be necessary that He be questioned about what He does; indeed, He would be blamed for what deserves blame, just as He is praised for what deserves praise.

Second: It would be necessary that they not be questioned about matters when there is no agent other than Him.

Third: It would not be permissible for them to be questioned about their deeds, since they have no deeds.

Fourth: Their deeds are not something they can deviate from, in terms of Him having created and originated them in them.

Fifth: He, the Exalted, has explicitly stated in many places that He accepts the proof (ḥujjah) of the servants against Him, as in His saying: "Messengers as bearers of good news and warners, so that people will have no argument against God after the messengers" (al-Nisa' 4:165). This requires that they have an argument against Him before the sending of the messengers. And He said: "If We had destroyed them with a punishment before this, they would have said, 'Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger so that we might follow Your signs before we were humiliated and disgraced?'" And he will say, according to the doctrine of Jabr (determinism): "My Lord, You created me a disbeliever, commanded me to do what I am not able to do, and placed a barrier between me and it." There is no doubt that according to the doctrine of Jabr he would be truthful. And God, the Exalted, said: "This is a day when the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness" (al-Ma'idah 5:119). So it must be that this speech benefits him. It was said to him: And who will leave him to say this speech or to argue? Thumamah said: Is it not that when God prevents him from speech and argument, He knows that He has prevented him from what, had He not prevented him, would have left him silenced? And this is the utmost of being silenced.

The answer to these points: They are countered by the question of the motive (masʼalat al-dāʻī) and the question of knowledge (masʼalat al-ʻilm), and then by the eight arguments we have explained, in which we showed that it is impossible to seek the "why" (lamiyyah) of God's acts and rulings.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 21, verses 28–29:

God, exalted is He, says: ﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son." Glory be to Him! Rather, they are honored servants.﴾ ﴿They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command.﴾ ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they do not intercede except for those whom He approves, and they are fearful out of awe of Him.﴾ ﴿And whoever among them says, "Indeed, I am a god besides Him," We shall recompense him with Hell. Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers.﴾

Know that when God, glory be to Him and exalted, had shown by clear proofs that He is exempt from any partner, rival or equal, He followed this with His freedom from having a son. So He said: ﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son."﴾ This was revealed concerning Khuza'ah, when they said, "The angels are the daughters of God." They added to this that He had become related by marriage to the jinn, as God related about them, when He said: ﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 158]

Then God, glory be to Him and exalted, declared Himself free of this by His saying "Glory be to Him," because a son must necessarily resemble the father. If God had a son, he would resemble Him in some respects, and then he would necessarily differ from Him in another respect; what makes them share is other than what makes them distinct, so composition would occur in the essence of God, glory be to Him and exalted. Every composite thing is contingent (mumkin), so His taking a son would indicate that He is contingent and not necessary. That would remove Him from the level of divinity and place Him within the level of servitude. For this reason He declared Himself free of it.

As for His saying: ﴿Rather, they are honored servants,﴾ know that when God, glory be to Him, had declared Himself free of having a son, He informed that they are servants, and servitude is incompatible with being begotten, but they are honored and preferred over the rest of the servants. It was also read: (honored, they do not precede Him), from "sabaqtuhu" (I outran him), "fa-sabaqtuhu asbiquhu." The meaning is that they follow Him in His speech and do not say anything until He has said it, so their speech does not precede His speech. Just as their speech follows His speech, their action is likewise founded on His command; they do not perform any deed unless they have been commanded to do it.

Then God, glory be to Him, mentioned what functions as the cause of this obedience, saying: ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them.﴾ The meaning is that when they knew that He, glory be to Him, knows all that is known, they knew that He knows their outward and inward states, and this was a motive for them to the utmost humility and perfect servitude. The commentators gave several interpretations of this:
First: Ibn Abbas said: He knows what they have advanced and what they have delayed of their deeds.
Second: What is before them is the Hereafter, and what is behind them is this world; it has also been said the reverse.
Third: Muqatil said: He knows what was before He created them and what will be after their creation. The real meaning is that they move under His power in His dominion, and He encompasses them. If this is their state, how can they deserve worship, and how can they come forward before God, Exalted, and intercede for one whom God has not permitted Him to intercede for? Then He clarified this meaning by saying: ﴿And they do not intercede except for those whom He approves,﴾ that is, for one who is acceptable to God. ﴿And they are fearful out of awe of Him﴾ that is, out of their fear of Him. The verbal noun is here construed as an object of the verb (i.e., "their fear of Him" is read as "their awe of Him"). ﴿Fearful (mushfiqun)﴾ means fearing, not feeling secure from His plan.
It is related from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that: "He saw Gabriel, peace be upon him, on the night of the Ascension, prostrate like a felt mat out of fear of God, Exalted." A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿They will not speak except one whom the Most Merciful has permitted.﴾ [Al-Naba: 38]

As for His saying, Exalted: ﴿And whoever among them says, "Indeed, I am a god besides Him," We shall recompense him with Hell,﴾ the meaning is that whoever among the angels says that statement, We shall requite that speaker with this recompense. This does not indicate that they said that or that they actually said it; it is close to His saying: ﴿If you were to associate partners with God, your deeds would surely be nullified.﴾ [Al-Zumar: 65] Here there are issues:

The first issue: These attributes indicate servitude and are incompatible with being begotten, for several reasons. First: When they went to such lengths in obedience that they say no word and do no deed except by His command, these are attributes of servants, not attributes of sons. Second: Since He, glory be to Him, knows the secrets of the angels, while they do not know the secrets of God, Exalted, the god deserving worship must be He, not these angels. This proof is the very same as what Jesus, peace be upon him, stated in His saying: ﴿You know what is in my soul, and I do not know what is in Your soul.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 116] Third: They do not intercede except for one whom He approves, and one who is a god or a son of God would not be such. Fourth: They are in the utmost state of fear and apprehension, and that is nothing but the attribute of servants. Fifth: By His saying: ﴿And whoever among them says, "Indeed, I am a god besides Him," We shall recompense him with Hell,﴾ God alerted that their state is the state of all other accountable servants regarding promise and threat, so how could it be valid for them to be gods?

The second issue: The Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazilites, a rationalist theological school) argued with His saying: ﴿And they do not intercede except for those whom He approves﴾ that intercession in the Hereafter does not belong to the people of major sins, because one does not say of the people of major sins that God approves of them. The answer: Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, and al-Dahhak said: ﴿Except for those whom He approves﴾ means those who say, "There is no god but God." Know that this verse is among the strongest proofs for us in establishing intercession for the people of major sins. Its demonstration is that whoever says, "There is no god but God," God has approved of him in that, and when it is true that God has approved of him in that, it is true that God has approved of him, because whenever a composite is true, each of its parts is necessarily true. When it is established that God has approved of him, it is necessary that he fall under this verse. Thus it is established by the argument we have stated that this verse is among the strongest proofs for us, according to what Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, established.

The third issue: This verse indicates three matters. First: it indicates that the angels are accountable, from His saying: ﴿They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command,﴾ ﴿and they are fearful out of awe of Him,﴾ and from the threat. Second: it also indicates that the angels are infallible (ma'sumun), because He said: ﴿and they act by His command.﴾ Third: Qadi Abd al-Jabbar said: His saying ﴿Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers﴾ indicates that every wrongdoer will be recompensed by God with Hell, as He threatened the angels with it, and this necessitates a definite judgment that He, Exalted, does not forgive the people of major sins in the Hereafter. The answer: At most, this general wording suggests a threat, and it is counterbalanced by the general wordings of promise.
