(The second story: the story of Ibrahim, peace be upon him)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed We gave Ibrahim his guidance (rushd) before, and We were of him well-knowing.﴾ ﴿When he said to his father and his people, "What are these images (tamathil) to which you are devoted?"﴾ ﴿They said, "We found our fathers worshipping them."﴾ ﴿He said, "Indeed you have been, you and your fathers, in manifest error."﴾ ﴿They said, "Have you brought us the truth, or are you of those who play?"﴾

Know that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed We gave Ibrahim his guidance﴾ contains several issues:

The first issue: Concerning rushd (right guidance) there are two opinions. The first: it is prophethood, and they argued for this from His saying: ﴿and We were of him well-knowing.﴾ They said: because He, exalted is He, only singles out with prophethood the one whom He knows, from his state, will in the future uphold its right, avoid what does not befit it, and guard against what would repel his people from accepting him. The second: it is being guided to the aspects of goodness in religion and worldly life. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you perceive in them maturity (rushd), then hand over to them their property﴾ [An-Nisa: 6]. There is also a third opinion: that prophethood and guidance both fall under rushd, since it is not permissible for a prophet to be sent unless Allah, exalted is He, has guided him to His essence and attributes, and has also guided him to the welfare of himself and of his people, and all of that is rushd.

The second issue: Our companions (the Ash'arites) argued from this verse that faith is created by Allah, exalted is He. For if rushd is tawfiq (divine enabling) and clarification, then Allah, exalted is He, has done that for the disbelievers, so it must be that He has given them their rushd. Al-Ka'bi answered that this is said of the one who accepts, not of the one who rejects, like one who gives wealth to two sons, and one of them accepts it and makes it grow, while the other rejects it or takes it and then wastes it. It is said: "So-and-so enriched his son," regarding the one whose wealth bore fruit, and the same is not said regarding the one who wasted it. The response to this: this answer is complete only if we make his acceptance a part of the meaning of rushd, and that is invalid, because if the designated thing is composed of two parts, and one of them is not within the agent's power, it is not permissible to attribute that thing to that agent. It would then follow that it is not permissible to attribute rushd to Allah, exalted is He, in the sense of being the object (of giving). But the text, His saying: ﴿And indeed We gave Ibrahim his guidance﴾, is explicit that this rushd came from Allah, exalted is He, so what they said is refuted.

The third issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: it has been read as rashadahu, like 'adam and 'udm. The meaning of its attribution to Him is that it is rushd like Him, and that it is a rushd of significant standing.

As for His saying: ﴿from before (min qablu)﴾, there are several interpretations: First: We gave Ibrahim his prophethood and his guidance before the time of Musa, peace be upon him, related from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jarir. Second: in his childhood, before his maturity, when he was in the cave and the stars appeared to him, and he reasoned by them. This is according to the view of those who understood rushd as guidance; otherwise it would follow that one must judge him to be a prophet, peace be upon him, before maturity, related from Muqatil. Third: meaning when he was in the loins of Adam, peace be upon him, when Allah took the covenant of the prophets, related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, in the narration of al-Dahhak.

As for His saying: ﴿and We were of him well-knowing﴾, the meaning is that He, glorified is He, knew from him wondrous states, marvelous secrets and attributes with which He was pleased, until He qualified him to be a close friend (khalil) to Him. This is like your saying about a great man: "I know So-and-so," for this speech is more indicative of exalting him than if you were to describe the greatness of his perfection.

As for His saying: ﴿When he said to his father and his people﴾, the author of al-Kashshaf said: "idh" may relate either to "We gave" or to "his guidance," or to an implied verb, meaning: mention from the times of his guidance this time.

As for His saying: ﴿What are these images to which you are devoted?﴾, there are issues:

The first issue: timthal (image) is a name for a made thing presented as resembling one of the creations of Allah, exalted is He. Its root is from "mathhaltu al-shay' bi al-shay'," when you liken one thing to another, and the name of that likened thing is timthal.

The second issue: The people were worshippers of idols in particular forms, such as the form of a human or other than that. So he, peace be upon him, made this statement the opening of his speech in order to see what doubt they might bring forward, so that he could refute it for them.

The third issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: he did not intend an object for "al-'akifin" and treated it as an intransitive verb, as when you say "fa'iluna li al-'ukuf" or "waqifuna laha." He said: If you say, why was it not said "'alayha 'akifun," like His saying: ﴿they devote themselves to idols they have﴾ [Al-A'raf: 138]? I say: had he intended transitivity, he would have made it transitive with its proper preposition, which is "'ala."

As for His saying: ﴿They said, "We found our fathers worshipping them."﴾ know that the people found in their answer to him only the path of imitation (taqlid), which necessarily entails greater error, because if they were in error in their affair, the fact that their fathers too had followed this path did not protect them from this error. Therefore Ibrahim, peace be upon him, answered them with His saying: ﴿Indeed you have been, you and your fathers, in manifest error.﴾ Thus he made clear that falsehood does not become truth because of the multitude of those who cling to it. When he, peace be upon him, established this against them, and they found no escape from his words, and saw him steadfast in denunciation, firm of heart in it, and they found it improbable that such denunciation would be directed at them given their numbers and the long duration of their doctrine, then at that point they said to him: ﴿Have you brought us the truth, or are you of those who play?﴾, implying by this speech that it is far-fetched that he would proceed to denounce them seriously. Thereupon he, may peace be upon him, turned to explaining monotheism.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 21, verses 57–64:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "Rather, your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, who created them; and I am of those who bear witness to that."﴾ ﴿"And by Allah, I will surely plot against your idols after you have turned away and gone."﴾ ﴿So he reduced them to fragments, except a large one among them, that they might return to it.﴾ ﴿They said, "Who has done this to our gods? Indeed, he is of the wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿They said, "We heard a youth mention them, called Ibrahim."﴾

Know that when the people were led to suppose that he was joking in what he had said to them about their idols, peace be upon him made clear what would show them that he was earnest in manifesting the truth, which is tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness). This was done first by speech and second by action. As for the verbal method, it is his saying: ﴿Rather, your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, who created them.﴾ This argument indicates that the Creator who created the two for the benefit of the servants is the One who is fitting to be worshipped, because whoever has power over that also has power to harm and benefit in the Hereafter through punishment and reward. The outcome of this method thus returns to the method he mentioned to his father in his saying: ﴿O my father, why do you worship that which does not hear and does not see and cannot avail you at all?﴾ [Maryam: 42]. The author of al-Kashshaf said: the pronoun in ﴿fataranna﴾ ("who created them") refers either to the heavens and the earth or to the images, and its referring to the images is more effective in the argument against them.

As for his saying: ﴿and I am of those who bear witness to that,﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: what is intended by it is emphasis and affirmation, like the saying of a man when he exaggerates in praising or blaming someone: "I bear witness that he is generous" or "that he is blameworthy." The second: peace be upon him meant by his saying ﴿and I am of those who bear witness to that﴾ a claim that he is able to establish what he has mentioned by proof, and that I am not like you, who say what you cannot establish by proof, just as you have been unable to argue for your own doctrine, and you have added nothing beyond that you found your fathers doing so. As for the practical method, it is his saying: ﴿And by Allah, I will surely plot against your idols after you have turned away and gone.﴾ When the people did not benefit from the rational proof, he turned to showing them the uselessness of worshipping them. In this there are several issues (masa'il, points of discussion):

The first issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: Mu'adh ibn Jabal, may Allah be pleased with him, recited ﴿wa-billah﴾ ("and by Allah") and it was read ﴿tawallau﴾ with the meaning of ﴿tatawallau﴾ ("you turn away"), and his saying ﴿fa-tawallau 'anhu mudbirin﴾ ("so they turned away from him, retreating") strengthens it. If you ask: what is the difference between the bā' (ب) and the tā' (ت)? I say: the bā' is the original, and the tā' is a substitute for the wāw which was itself substituted; the tā' carries an added meaning, which is wonder, as if he marvelled at how easy the plot had become at his hand, because that was a matter regarded as despaired of due to its difficulty.

The second issue: If it is said: why did he say ﴿la-akidanna asnamakum﴾ ("I will surely plot against your idols"), while kayd (plotting) is outwitting another in a harm that the other does not perceive, and that cannot be done to idols? The answer: he said that by way of extension, since in their view harm could befall them. It was also said: the meaning is "I will surely plot against you concerning your idols," because by that act he had brought grief upon them.

The third issue: Regarding how the story begins, there are two views. One: al-Suddi said: when they returned from their festival they would enter upon the idols and prostrate to them, then return to their homes. When this time came, Azar said to Ibrahim, peace be upon him: "If only you would come out with us." So he came out with them, but when they were part of the way he threw himself down and said: "Indeed, I am sick; my leg is aching." When they had gone and only the weak among the people remained, he called out and said: ﴿And by Allah, I will surely plot against your idols.﴾ The one who holds this view takes as evidence the Most High's saying: ﴿They said, "We heard a youth mention them, called Ibrahim."﴾

The second: al-Kalbi said: Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was from a household that studied the stars, and when they went out to their festival they would leave behind none but the sick. When Ibrahim intended what he intended of breaking the idols, he looked at the sky before the day of the festival and said to his companions: "I see that I will be ill tomorrow." This is His saying: ﴿So he glanced at the stars, and said, "Indeed, I am sick."﴾ [al-Saffat: 88–89]. In the morning of the next day his head was bound, and the people went out to their festival, and none remained behind except him. He said: "By Allah, I will surely plot against your idols." One man among them heard this statement and memorized it, then that man informed others and it spread among a group; for this reason the Most High said: ﴿They said, "We heard a youth mention them."﴾ Know that both views are possible. Then the completion of the story is that when Ibrahim, peace be upon him, entered the house of the idols, he found seventy idols arranged in rows, and there was a great idol facing the door, which was of gold, and in its two eyes were two jewels that shone at night. He broke them all with an axe in his hand until none remained except the large one; then he hung the axe around its neck.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So he reduced them to fragments, except a large one among them, that they might return to it,﴾ there are several issues:

The first issue: If it is said: why did He say ﴿fa-ja'alahum judhadhan﴾ ("so he reduced them to fragments"), when this is a plural form that is appropriate only for people? The answer: it is because of their belief about them, that they were like people in being venerated and drawn near to; and perhaps among them were those who thought that they could harm and benefit.

The second issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: judhadhan means pieces, from al-jadhdh, which is cutting. It was read with a kasra and with a fatha, and it was read judhadhan as the plural of jadhidh, and jidhadhan as the plural of juddah.

The third issue: If it is said: what is the meaning of ﴿illa kabiran lahum﴾ ("except a large one among them")? We say: "kabir" may be understood in terms of physical size, or in terms of honour, or in both respects.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿that they might return to it,﴾ the return may be understood as their returning to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, or their returning to the large one. As for the first: its explanation is in two ways. The first: the meaning is that perhaps they would return to the statement of Ibrahim and turn away from falsehood. The second: he was overcome by the assumption that they would return to none but him, because of what they had heard of his denial of their religion and his reviling of their gods; so he rebuked them with the answer he gave: ﴿Rather, this was done by the largest of them; so ask them, if they can speak.﴾ [al-Anbiya': 63]. As for if we say the pronoun refers to the large one, there are two views. The first: the meaning is that perhaps they would return to it as one returns to a scholar to solve difficulties, so they would say: "What has happened to these, broken, while you are whole, with the axe on your shoulder?" This is the view of al-Kalbi, and he said this based on the abundance of their ignorance, so perhaps they believed about them that they would answer and speak. The second: he, peace be upon him, said that while knowing that they would not return to him, mocking them; and the proper measure of one who is worshipped and deemed fit for worship is that one should be returned to in solving difficulties.

The fourth issue: If it is said: those peoples, either it is said that they were rational or that they were not rational. If they were rational, it must be that they knew by necessity that those idols do not hear or see, nor benefit or harm, so what need was there to prove that by breaking them? At most one might say: the people were venerating them as one of us venerates the Qur'an, the mosque, or the prayer niche, and breaking them does not detract from their being venerated in this respect.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 21, verses 57–64:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "Rather, your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, who created them; and I am of those who bear witness to that."﴾ ﴿"And by Allah, I will surely plot against your idols after you have turned away and gone."﴾ ﴿So he reduced them to fragments, except a large one among them, that they might return to it.﴾ ﴿They said, "Who has done this to our gods? Indeed, he is of the wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿They said, "We heard a youth mention them, called Ibrahim."﴾

Know that when the people were led to suppose that he was joking in what he had said to them about their idols, peace be upon him made clear what would show them that he was earnest in manifesting the truth, which is tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness). This was done first by speech and second by action. As for the verbal method, it is his saying: ﴿Rather, your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, who created them.﴾ This argument indicates that the Creator who created the two for the benefit of the servants is the One who is fitting to be worshipped, because whoever has power over that also has power to harm and benefit in the Hereafter through punishment and reward. The outcome of this method thus returns to the method he mentioned to his father in his saying: ﴿O my father, why do you worship that which does not hear and does not see and cannot avail you at all?﴾ [Maryam: 42]. The author of al-Kashshaf said: the pronoun in ﴿fataranna﴾ ("who created them") refers either to the heavens and the earth or to the images, and its referring to the images is more effective in the argument against them.

As for his saying: ﴿and I am of those who bear witness to that,﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: what is intended by it is emphasis and affirmation, like the saying of a man when he exaggerates in praising or blaming someone: "I bear witness that he is generous" or "that he is blameworthy." The second: peace be upon him meant by his saying ﴿and I am of those who bear witness to that﴾ a claim that he is able to establish what he has mentioned by proof, and that I am not like you, who say what you cannot establish by proof, just as you have been unable to argue for your own doctrine, and you have added nothing beyond that you found your fathers doing so. As for the practical method, it is his saying: ﴿And by Allah, I will surely plot against your idols after you have turned away and gone.﴾ When the people did not benefit from the rational proof, he turned to showing them the uselessness of worshipping them. In this there are several issues (masa'il, points of discussion):

The first issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: Mu'adh ibn Jabal, may Allah be pleased with him, recited ﴿wa-billah﴾ ("and by Allah") and it was read ﴿tawallau﴾ with the meaning of ﴿tatawallau﴾ ("you turn away"), and his saying ﴿fa-tawallau 'anhu mudbirin﴾ ("so they turned away from him, retreating") strengthens it. If you ask: what is the difference between the bā' (ب) and the tā' (ت)? I say: the bā' is the original, and the tā' is a substitute for the wāw which was itself substituted; the tā' carries an added meaning, which is wonder, as if he marvelled at how easy the plot had become at his hand, because that was a matter regarded as despaired of due to its difficulty.

The second issue: If it is said: why did he say ﴿la-akidanna asnamakum﴾ ("I will surely plot against your idols"), while kayd (plotting) is outwitting another in a harm that the other does not perceive, and that cannot be done to idols? The answer: he said that by way of extension, since in their view harm could befall them. It was also said: the meaning is "I will surely plot against you concerning your idols," because by that act he had brought grief upon them.

The third issue: Regarding how the story begins, there are two views. One: al-Suddi said: when they returned from their festival they would enter upon the idols and prostrate to them, then return to their homes. When this time came, Azar said to Ibrahim, peace be upon him: "If only you would come out with us." So he came out with them, but when they were part of the way he threw himself down and said: "Indeed, I am sick; my leg is aching." When they had gone and only the weak among the people remained, he called out and said: ﴿And by Allah, I will surely plot against your idols.﴾ The one who holds this view takes as evidence the Most High's saying: ﴿They said, "We heard a youth mention them, called Ibrahim."﴾

The answer: it is because of their belief about them, that they were like people in being venerated and drawn near to; and perhaps among them were those who thought that they could harm and benefit.

The third issue: If it is said: what is the meaning of ﴿illa kabiran lahum﴾ ("except a large one among them")? We say: "kabir" may be understood in terms of physical size, or in terms of honour, or in both respects.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿that they might return to it,﴾ the return may be understood as their returning to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, or their returning to the large one. As for the first: its explanation is in two ways. The first: the meaning is that perhaps they would return to the statement of Ibrahim and turn away from falsehood. The second: he was overcome by the assumption that they would return to none but him, because of what they had heard of his denial of their religion and his reviling of their gods; so he rebuked them with the answer he gave: ﴿Rather, this was done by the largest of them; so ask them, if they can speak.﴾ [al-Anbiya': 63]. As for if we say the pronoun refers to the large one, there are two views. The first: the meaning is that perhaps they would return to it as one returns to a scholar to solve difficulties, so they would say: "What has happened to these, broken, while you are whole, with the axe on your shoulder?" This is the view of al-Kalbi, and he said this based on the abundance of their ignorance, so perhaps they believed about them that they would answer and speak. The second: he, peace be upon him, said that while knowing that they would not return to him, mocking them; and the proper measure of one who is worshipped and deemed fit for worship is that one should be returned to in solving difficulties.

The fourth issue: If it is said: those peoples, either it is said that they were rational or that they were not rational. If they were rational, it must be that they knew by necessity that those idols do not hear or see, nor benefit or harm, so what need was there to prove that by breaking them? At most one might say: the people were venerating them as one of us venerates the Qur'an, the mosque, or the prayer niche, and breaking them does not detract from their being venerated in this respect.

And if we say that they were not rational, it would follow that debate with them and sending messengers to them would not be fitting. The answer: they were rational, and they knew by necessity that they were inanimate objects; but perhaps they believed about them that they were images of the stars and that they were talismans placed in such a way that whoever worshipped them benefited by them, and whoever made light of them suffered from them a severe harm. As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said, "We heard a youth mention them, called Ibrahim."﴾ there are two issues:

The first issue: al-Zajjaj said: Ibrahim is in the nominative case in two ways. One: on the basis that the meaning is "it is said that he is Ibrahim." The second: on the basis of address, with the meaning "it is said to him: O Ibrahim." The author of al-Kashshaf said: the correct view is that it is the subject of yuqalu (it is said), because what is meant is the name, not the one named.

The second issue: The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that those who spoke were a group, not one person. It seems that they had previously come to know of him and heard what he said about their gods, so it became dominant in their hearts that he was the doer; and his saying alone, "What are these images?" would have been sufficient.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 21, verses 57–64:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "Rather, your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, who created them; and I am of those who bear witness to that."﴾ ﴿"And by Allah, I will surely plot against your idols after you have turned away and gone."﴾ ﴿So he reduced them to fragments, except a large one among them, that they might return to it.﴾ ﴿They said, "Who has done this to our gods? Indeed, he is of the wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿They said, "We heard a youth mention them, called Ibrahim."﴾

Know that when the people were led to suppose that he was joking in what he had said to them about their idols, peace be upon him made clear what would show them that he was earnest in manifesting the truth, which is tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness). This was done first by speech and second by action. As for the verbal method, it is his saying: ﴿Rather, your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, who created them.﴾ This argument indicates that the Creator who created the two for the benefit of the servants is the One who is fitting to be worshipped, because whoever has power over that also has power to harm and benefit in the Hereafter through punishment and reward. The outcome of this method thus returns to the method he mentioned to his father in his saying: ﴿O my father, why do you worship that which does not hear and does not see and cannot avail you at all?﴾ [Maryam: 42]. The author of al-Kashshaf said: the pronoun in ﴿fataranna﴾ ("who created them") refers either to the heavens and the earth or to the images, and its referring to the images is more effective in the argument against them.

As for his saying: ﴿and I am of those who bear witness to that,﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: what is intended by it is emphasis and affirmation, like the saying of a man when he exaggerates in praising or blaming someone: "I bear witness that he is generous" or "that he is blameworthy." The second: peace be upon him meant by his saying ﴿and I am of those who bear witness to that﴾ a claim that he is able to establish what he has mentioned by proof, and that I am not like you, who say what you cannot establish by proof, just as you have been unable to argue for your own doctrine, and you have added nothing beyond that you found your fathers doing so. As for the practical method, it is his saying: ﴿And by Allah, I will surely plot against your idols after you have turned away and gone.﴾ When the people did not benefit from the rational proof, he turned to showing them the uselessness of worshipping them. In this there are several issues (masa'il, points of discussion):

The first issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: Mu'adh ibn Jabal, may Allah be pleased with him, recited ﴿wa-billah﴾ ("and by Allah") and it was read ﴿tawallau﴾ with the meaning of ﴿tatawallau﴾ ("you turn away"), and his saying ﴿fa-tawallau 'anhu mudbirin﴾ ("so they turned away from him, retreating") strengthens it. If you ask: what is the difference between the bā' (ب) and the tā' (ت)? I say: the bā' is the original, and the tā' is a substitute for the wāw which was itself substituted; the tā' carries an added meaning, which is wonder, as if he marvelled at how easy the plot had become at his hand, because that was a matter regarded as despaired of due to its difficulty.

The second issue: If it is said: why did he say ﴿la-akidanna asnamakum﴾ ("I will surely plot against your idols"), while kayd (plotting) is outwitting another in a harm that the other does not perceive, and that cannot be done to idols? The answer: he said that by way of extension, since in their view harm could befall them. It was also said: the meaning is "I will surely plot against you concerning your idols," because by that act he had brought grief upon them.

The third issue: Regarding how the story begins, there are two views. One: al-Suddi said: when they returned from their festival they would enter upon the idols and prostrate to them, then return to their homes. When this time came, Azar said to Ibrahim, peace be upon him: "If only you would come out with us." So he came out with them, but when they were part of the way he threw himself down and said: "Indeed, I am sick; my leg is aching." When they had gone and only the weak among the people remained, he called out and said: ﴿And by Allah, I will surely plot against your idols.﴾ The one who holds this view takes as evidence the Most High's saying: ﴿They said, "We heard a youth mention them, called Ibrahim."﴾

The second: al-Kalbi said: Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was from a household that studied the stars, and when they went out to their festival they would leave behind none but the sick. When Ibrahim intended what he intended of breaking the idols, he looked at the sky before the day of the festival and said to his companions: "I see that I will be ill tomorrow." This is His saying: ﴿So he glanced at the stars, and said, "Indeed, I am sick."﴾ [al-Saffat: 88–89]. In the morning of the next day his head was bound, and the people went out to their festival, and none remained behind except him. He said: "By Allah, I will surely plot against your idols." One man among them heard this statement and memorized it, then that man informed others and it spread among a group; for this reason the Most High said: ﴿They said, "We heard a youth mention them."﴾ Know that both views are possible. Then the completion of the story is that when Ibrahim, peace be upon him, entered the house of the idols, he found seventy idols arranged in rows, and there was a great idol facing the door, which was of gold, and in its two eyes were two jewels that shone at night. The Almighty said: ﴿They said, "Then bring him before the eyes of the people, that they may bear witness."﴾ ﴿They said, "Did you do this to our gods, O Ibrahim?"﴾ He said, "Rather, this, their largest one, did it. So ask them, if they can speak." ﴿So they returned to themselves and said, "Indeed, you are the wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿Then they were overturned upon their heads: "You know that these do not speak."﴾ ﴿He said, "Do you then worship, instead of Allah, that which can neither benefit you at all nor harm you?"﴾ ﴿"Uff to you and to what you worship instead of Allah! Do you not reason?"﴾

Know that when the people witnessed the breaking of the idols, and it was said that its doer was Ibrahim (peace be upon him), they said among themselves: ﴿Then bring him before the eyes of the people.﴾ The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: "'Before the eyes of the people' is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: bring him as one who is seen, that is, in their sight and view. If you ask, what is the meaning of the sense of elevation in 'ala (upon)? I say: it comes as a figure of speech, meaning that his being established before the eyes is as firm as a rider's being established upon a mount."

As for His saying: ﴿that they may bear witness﴾, there are two views. The first: they disliked taking him without evidence, so they wanted to bring him before the eyes of the people so that they might bear witness against him for what he said, and it would then be a proof against him for what he did. This is the view of al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Suddi, Ata' and Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them).

The second, which is the view of Muhammad ibn Ishaq: that is, they would be present and see what is done to him, and this would deter them from committing the like of his act. There is a third view, which is the view of Muqatil and al-Kalbi: that the intended meaning is both views together, so they would bear witness against him for his act and witness his punishment.

As for His saying: ﴿Did you do this?﴾ know that there is an ellipsis in the speech, which is: so they brought him, and they said: "Did you do this?" They asked him to confess to that, so that they could proceed to harm him. But there appeared from him what turned the matter against them, until they wished to be rid of him. So he said: ﴿Rather, this, their largest one, did it,﴾ and he had hung the axe on his neck in order to produce this statement, so that their ignorance in worshipping idols would become apparent. If it is said: his saying "Rather, their largest one did it" is a lie, the scholars have two answers. The first, which is the view of the majority of the verifiers (muhaqqiqin), is that it is not a lie, and they mentioned several explanations for it.

One: Ibrahim (peace be upon him) did not intend to attribute the act that proceeded from him to the idol. Rather, he intended to affirm it for himself and to establish it for them by way of allusion (ta'ridi), by which he achieved his purpose of enforcing the proof upon them and rebuking them. This is like if your companion, when you have written a letter in a graceful hand, and you are famous for beautiful handwriting, says to you: "Did you write this?" while your companion is illiterate, unable to write well, and capable only of a corrupt scribble. You say to him: "Rather, you wrote it," as if your intention by this reply is to affirm it while mocking him, not to deny it from yourself and affirm it for the illiterate or the scribbler. For affirming it for one of two disputed parties when one of them is incapable is a mockery of him and an affirmation for the capable one.

Two: Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was enraged by those idols when he saw them lined up and adorned, and his anger at their largest one was greater because of what he saw of their increased veneration for it. So he ascribed the act to it, because it was the cause of his contempt for them and his smashing of them, and an act is ascribed both to its doer and to the one who prompted it.

Three: that it is a narration of what follows from their own doctrine, as if he said to them: "What is there to deny in its largest one doing this? For whoever is worshipped and called a god ought to be able to do this and more." These three aspects were mentioned by the author of al-Kashshaf.

Four: that it is a kinaya (indirect reference) to something unmentioned, meaning: whoever did it did it, and "their largest one, this" is the beginning of a new statement. It is related from al-Kisa'i that he would pause at His saying ﴿Rather, He did it﴾ and then begin with ﴿their largest one, this.﴾

Five: that it is permissible that there be a pause at His saying ﴿their largest one﴾, and then he begins: ﴿this, so ask them,﴾ and the meaning is: "Rather, their largest one did it," and he meant himself, because a human is greater than any idol.

Six: that there is an inversion (taqdim and ta'khir) in the speech, as if he said: "Rather, their largest one, this, did it, if they can speak, so ask them." Then the attribution of the act to their largest one is conditioned upon their being able to speak, and since they were unable to speak, it was impossible for them to be doers.

Seven: Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' read: "fa'allahu kabiruhum" (so perhaps its doer is their largest one), meaning: perhaps the doer is their largest one.

The second answer, which is the view of a group of narrators (ahl al-hikayat), is that it is a lie. They argued by what

[Page 161]

was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Ibrahim did not lie except three lies, all of them for the sake of Allah, Most High: his saying ﴿Indeed, I am sick﴾ [al-Saffat: 89], and his saying ﴿Rather, this, their largest one, did it,﴾ and his saying to Sarah: 'She is my sister.'" In another report: "When the people of the Standing (on the Day of Judgment) ask Ibrahim for intercession, he will say: 'Indeed, I have lied three lies.'"

Then they established their statement by reason, and said: lying is not evil in its essence. For when a prophet (peace be upon him) flees from a wrongdoer and hides in a person's house, and the wrongdoer comes and asks about his condition, it is obligatory to lie in that case. If that is so, then what is far-fetched in Allah, Most High, permitting that for a benefit which none knows but Him?

Know that this view is to be rejected. As for the first report, which they narrated: it is more fitting to attribute the lie to its narrators than to attribute it to the prophets (peace and blessings be upon them). The decisive proof against it is that if it were permissible for them to lie for a benefit, and Allah permitted it, then we would have to allow this possibility in everything they reported and everything Allah, Most High, reported. That would nullify trust in the revealed laws, and suspicion would fall upon all of them. Moreover, even if that report is authentic, it is to be understood as indirect speech (ma'arid), in accordance with his (peace be upon him) saying: "Indeed, in indirect speech there is a sufficient alternative to lying."

As for His saying ﴿Indeed, I am sick﴾, perhaps he had a slight ailment. A full discussion of this belongs in its proper place.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿Rather, this, their largest one, did it,﴾ the answer concerning it has already been given.

As for his saying to Sarah, "She is my sister," the intended meaning is that she is his sister in religion. And when it is possible to take the statement according to its apparent sense without attributing a lie to the prophets (peace be upon them), then no one attributes a lie to them except a heretic (zindiq).

As for His saying ﴿So they returned to themselves and said, "Indeed, you are the wrongdoers,"﴾ there are several views. The first: when Ibrahim (peace be upon him) alerted them, by what he presented to them, to the ugliness of their path, they became aware, and they knew that worshipping idols is false, and that they were in delusion and ignorance in this. The second: Muqatil said: "They returned to themselves and blamed themselves and said, 'Indeed, you are the wrongdoers' to Ibrahim, in that you claim he broke them, while the axe was between the hands of the largest idol." The third: the meaning is that you are the wrongdoers to yourselves, in that you asked him about this until he began to mock you in the answer. The nearer is the first.

As for His saying ﴿Then they were overturned upon their heads: "You know that these do not speak."﴾ the author of al-Kashshaf said: "nakkasahu" means he turned it over, making its bottom its top. And in this there are two issues.

First issue: regarding the meaning, there are several views. One: the intended meaning is that they were upright when they returned to themselves and brought forth sound reasoning, then they were overturned, turned away from that state, and took up argument with falsehood, and that these, despite their being far below the state of a rational speaking animal, are worshipped gods. Two: they were actually turned over upon their heads, due to the extreme lowering of their heads out of shame, humiliation and defeat, because of what Ibrahim had confounded them with, so they could find no answer except one which was a proof against them. Three: Ibn Jarir said: "Then they were overturned upon their heads" regarding the proof against them, when Ibrahim argued with them. That is, they were turned over in argument, and they argued against Ibrahim with what was in fact a proof for Ibrahim against them. So they said, ﴿You know that these do not speak,﴾ and they acknowledged this out of the bewilderment that befell them. He said: the meaning is that their argument was overturned, so the report about them was placed in the position of the report about their argument.

Second issue: it is read "nukkisu" (with shadda) and "nukisu" in the passive form (the subject not named), meaning they overturned themselves upon their heads. This is the reading of Ridwan ibn Abd al-Ma'bud.

[Page 162]

As for His saying ﴿He said, "Do you then worship, instead of Allah, that which can neither benefit you at all nor harm you?"﴾ ﴿"Uff to you and to what you worship instead of Allah! Do you not reason?"﴾ the meaning is clear. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Uff" is a sound which, when uttered, indicates that its utterer is vexed. Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was vexed by what he saw of their persistence in worshipping them after their excuse had ended, and after the truth had become clear and falsehood had vanished, so he said "uff" to them. Then it is possible he said this to them when they knew the correctness of his statement. It is also possible he said it to them when the proof had appeared, even though they did not understand. And this is the nearer view, given His saying ﴿Do you then worship?﴾ and His saying ﴿Do you not reason?﴾

Five: that it is permissible that there be a pause at His saying ﴿their largest one﴾, and then he begins: ﴿this, so ask them,﴾ and the meaning is: "Rather, their largest one did it," and he meant himself, because a human is greater than any idol.

Six: that there is an inversion (taqdim and ta'khir) in the speech, as if he said: "Rather, their largest one, this, did it, if they can speak, so ask them." Then the attribution of the act to their largest one is conditioned upon their being able to speak, and since they were unable to speak, it was impossible for them to be doers.

Seven: Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' read: "fa'allahu kabiruhum" (so perhaps its doer is their largest one), meaning: perhaps the doer is their largest one.

The second answer, which is the view of a group of narrators (ahl al-hikayat), is that it is a lie. They argued by what

[Page 161]

was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Ibrahim did not lie except three lies, all of them for the sake of Allah, Most High: his saying ﴿Indeed, I am sick﴾ [al-Saffat: 89], and his saying ﴿Rather, this, their largest one, did it,﴾ and his saying to Sarah: 'She is my sister.'" In another report: "When the people of the Standing (on the Day of Judgment) ask Ibrahim for intercession, he will say: 'Indeed, I have lied three lies.'"

Then they established their statement by reason, and said: lying is not evil in its essence. For when a prophet (peace be upon him) flees from a wrongdoer and hides in a person's house, and the wrongdoer comes and asks about his condition, it is obligatory to lie in that case. If that is so, then what is far-fetched in Allah, Most High, permitting that for a benefit which none knows but Him?

Know that this view is to be rejected. As for the first report, which they narrated: it is more fitting to attribute the lie to its narrators than to attribute it to the prophets (peace and blessings be upon them). The decisive proof against it is that if it were permissible for them to lie for a benefit, and Allah permitted it, then we would have to allow this possibility in everything they reported and everything Allah, Most High, reported. That would nullify trust in the revealed laws, and suspicion would fall upon all of them. Moreover, even if that report is authentic, it is to be understood as indirect speech (ma'arid), in accordance with his (peace be upon him) saying: "Indeed, in indirect speech there is a sufficient alternative to lying."

As for His saying ﴿Indeed, I am sick﴾, perhaps he had a slight ailment. A full discussion of this belongs in its proper place.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿Rather, this, their largest one, did it,﴾ the answer concerning it has already been given.

As for his saying to Sarah, "She is my sister," the intended meaning is that she is his sister in religion. And when it is possible to take the statement according to its apparent sense without attributing a lie to the prophets (peace be upon them), then no one attributes a lie to them except a heretic (zindiq).

As for His saying ﴿So they returned to themselves and said, "Indeed, you are the wrongdoers,"﴾ there are several views. The first: when Ibrahim (peace be upon him) alerted them, by what he presented to them, to the ugliness of their path, they became aware, and they knew that worshipping idols is false, and that they were in delusion and ignorance in this. The second: Muqatil said: "They returned to themselves and blamed themselves and said, 'Indeed, you are the wrongdoers' to Ibrahim, in that you claim he broke them, while the axe was between the hands of the largest idol." The third: the meaning is that you are the wrongdoers to yourselves, in that you asked him about this until he began to mock you in the answer. The nearer is the first.

First issue: regarding the meaning, there are several views. One: the intended meaning is that they were upright when they returned to themselves and brought forth sound reasoning, then they were overturned, turned away from that state, and took up argument with falsehood, and that these, despite their being far below the state of a rational speaking animal, are worshipped gods. Two: they were actually turned over upon their heads, due to the extreme lowering of their heads out of shame, humiliation and defeat, because of what Ibrahim had confounded them with, so they could find no answer except one which was a proof against them. Three: Ibn Jarir said: "Then they were overturned upon their heads" regarding the proof against them, when Ibrahim argued with them. That is, they were turned over in argument, and they argued against Ibrahim with what was in fact a proof for Ibrahim against them. So they said, ﴿You know that these do not speak,﴾ and they acknowledged this out of the bewilderment that befell them. He said: the meaning is that their argument was overturned, so the report about them was placed in the position of the report about their argument.

Second issue: it is read "nukkisu" (with shadda) and "nukisu" in the passive form (the subject not named), meaning they overturned themselves upon their heads. This is the reading of Ridwan ibn Abd al-Ma'bud.

As for His saying ﴿He said, "Do you then worship, instead of Allah, that which can neither benefit you at all nor harm you?"﴾ ﴿"Uff to you and to what you worship instead of Allah! Do you not reason?"﴾ the meaning is clear. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Uff" is a sound which, when uttered, indicates that its utterer is vexed. Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was vexed by what he saw of their persistence in worshipping them after their excuse had ended, and after the truth had become clear and falsehood had vanished, so he said "uff" to them. Then it is possible he said this to them when they knew the correctness of his statement. It is also possible he said it to them when the proof had appeared, even though they did not understand. And this is the nearer view, given His saying ﴿Do you then worship?﴾ and His saying ﴿Do you not reason?﴾

Do you not reason?"﴾

Know that when the people witnessed the breaking of the idols, and it was said that its doer was Ibrahim (peace be upon him), they said among themselves: ﴿Then bring him before the eyes of the people.﴾ The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: "'Before the eyes of the people' is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: bring him as one who is seen, that is, in their sight and view. If you ask, what is the meaning of the sense of elevation in 'ala (upon)? I say: it comes as a figure of speech, meaning that his being established before the eyes is as firm as a rider's being established upon a mount."

As for His saying: ﴿that they may bear witness﴾, there are two views. The first: they disliked taking him without evidence, so they wanted to bring him before the eyes of the people so that they might bear witness against him for what he said, and it would then be a proof against him for what he did. This is the view of al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Suddi, Ata' and Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them).

The second, which is the view of Muhammad ibn Ishaq: that is, they would be present and see what is done to him, and this would deter them from committing the like of his act. There is a third view, which is the view of Muqatil and al-Kalbi: that the intended meaning is both views together, so they would bear witness against him for his act and witness his punishment.

As for His saying: ﴿Did you do this?﴾ know that there is an ellipsis in the speech, which is: so they brought him, and they said: "Did you do this?" They asked him to confess to that, so that they could proceed to harm him. But there appeared from him what turned the matter against them, until they wished to be rid of him. So he said: ﴿Rather, this, their largest one, did it,﴾ and he had hung the axe on his neck in order to produce this statement, so that their ignorance in worshipping idols would become apparent. If it is said: his saying "Rather, their largest one did it" is a lie, the scholars have two answers. The first, which is the view of the majority of the verifiers (muhaqqiqin), is that it is not a lie, and they mentioned several explanations for it.

One: Ibrahim (peace be upon him) did not intend to attribute the act that proceeded from him to the idol. Rather, he intended to affirm it for himself and to establish it for them by way of allusion (ta'ridi), by which he achieved his purpose of enforcing the proof upon them and rebuking them. This is like if your companion, when you have written a letter in a graceful hand, and you are famous for beautiful handwriting, says to you: "Did you write this?" while your companion is illiterate, unable to write well, and capable only of a corrupt scribble. You say to him: "Rather, you wrote it," as if your intention by this reply is to affirm it while mocking him, not to deny it from yourself and affirm it for the illiterate or the scribbler. For affirming it for one of two disputed parties when one of them is incapable is a mockery of him and an affirmation for the capable one.

Two: Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was enraged by those idols when he saw them lined up and adorned, and his anger at their largest one was greater because of what he saw of their increased veneration for it. So he ascribed the act to it, because it was the cause of his contempt for them and his smashing of them, and an act is ascribed both to its doer and to the one who prompted it.

Three: that it is a narration of what follows from their own doctrine, as if he said to them: "What is there to deny in its largest one doing this? For whoever is worshipped and called a god ought to be able to do this and more." These three aspects were mentioned by the author of al-Kashshaf.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They said, "Burn him and support your gods, if you are going to act."﴾ ﴿We said, "O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham."﴾ ﴿They intended a scheme against him, but We made them the greatest losers.﴾ ﴿And We delivered him and Lot to the land which We had blessed for the worlds.﴾

Know that when Allah the Exalted had explained what Abraham, peace be upon him, had shown of the proofs of monotheism and the refutation of what they were upon of worshipping images, He followed it with what indicates their ignorance, and that they said: ﴿Burn him and support your gods.﴾ Here there are issues:

**The first issue:** The Qur'an does not say who said this. The well-known view is that it was Namrud ibn Kan'an ibn Sanjarib ibn Namrud ibn Kush ibn Ham ibn Nuh. Mujahid said: I heard Ibn Umar say: "The one who advised burning Abraham, peace be upon him, was a man from the Kurds, from the Bedouins of Persia." Ibn Jurayj narrated from Wahb, from Shu'ayb al-Jubba'i, who said: "The one who said, 'Burn him,' was a man named Hirin, and Allah caused the earth to swallow him, and he is still sinking into it until the Day of Resurrection."

**The second issue:** As for how the story happened, Muqatil said: When Namrud and his people gathered to burn Abraham, they imprisoned him in a house and built a structure like an enclosure. This is His saying: ﴿Build for him a structure and throw him into the blazing fire.﴾ [al-Saffat: 97]. Then they gathered a great quantity of firewood, so much so that if a woman fell ill she would say: "If Allah restores my health, I will surely make firewood for Abraham." They carried the firewood on animals for forty days. When the fire blazed, it grew intense, and the air became such that if a bird passed through the furthest reaches of the air, it would be burned. Then they took Abraham, peace be upon him, raised him to the top of the structure, and bound him. Then they made a catapult, placed him in it bound and shackled. The heavens, the earth, and whoever is in them of the angels, except the two species (humans and jinn), cried out with one cry: "Our Lord, there is no one on Your earth who worships You except Abraham, and he is being burned for Your sake, so permit us to support him." He, glorified is He, said: "If he calls upon anyone among you, then help him; but if he does not call upon anyone other than Me, then I know about him, and I am his Protector. So leave him between Me and him."

When they wanted to throw him into the fire, the keeper of the winds came to him and said: "If you wish, I will make the fire fly into the air." Abraham, peace be upon him, said: "I have no need of you." Then he raised his head to the sky and said: "O Allah, You are the One in the heavens, and I am the one on the earth. There is no one on the earth who worships You other than me. You are sufficient for us, and the best Disposer of affairs." It was also said that when he was thrown into the fire he said: "There is no god but You, glory be to You, Lord of the worlds, to You is all praise and to You is all sovereignty, You have no partner." Then they placed him in the catapult and threw him into the fire. Jibril, peace be upon him, came to him and said: "O Abraham, do you have any need?" He said: "As for to you, no." He said: "Then ask your Lord." He said: "My knowledge of my condition is enough for me as a request." So Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham.﴾

Al-Suddi said: It was Jibril, peace be upon him, who said that. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said in the narration of Mujahid: "Had He not followed 'coolness' with 'safety,' Abraham would have died from its cold." He said: "On that day, no fire remained in the world but it was extinguished." Then al-Suddi said: The angels took Abraham by his armpits and seated him on the ground, and there was a spring of sweet water, a red rose, and narcissus. The fire burned nothing of him except his bonds. Al-Minhal ibn Amr said: "I was told that when Abraham, peace be upon him, was thrown into the fire, he remained in it for either forty days or fifty days, and he said: 'I never had days more pleasant in life than those I spent in it.'" Ibn Ishaq said: Allah sent the angel of shade in the form of Abraham, and he sat beside Abraham to keep him company. Jibril brought him a shirt of silk from Paradise and said: "O Abraham, your Lord says: 'Do you not know that the fire does not harm My beloved?'" Then Namrud looked out from a palace of his and gazed upon Abraham, and he saw him sitting in a garden, and he saw the angel sitting beside him, and around him was fire burning the firewood. Namrud called out: "O Abraham, can you come out of it?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Get up and come out." So he got up walking until he came out of it. When he came out, Namrud said to him: "Who was the man I saw with you in your form?" He said: "That was the angel of shade, whom my Lord sent to keep me company in it." Namrud said: "I will offer a sacrifice to your Lord, because of what I saw of His power and might in what He did for you. I will slaughter for Him four thousand cows." Abraham, peace be upon him, said: "Allah will not accept from you while you are upon your religion." Namrud said: "I cannot give up my kingdom, but I will slaughter them for Him." Then he slaughtered them for Him and ceased harming Abraham, peace be upon him.

This story has also been narrated in another form: they built a structure for Abraham and threw him into it, then they kindled the fire upon him for seven days, then they sealed it over him, then they opened it on the next day, and he was found unburned, sweating profusely. Haran, the father of Lot, said to them: "The fire does not burn him, because he has performed magic upon the fire. Rather, place him on something and light a fire beneath it, for the smoke will kill him." So they put him over a well and lit a fire beneath him, and a spark flew and landed in the beard of Haran's son, Lot, and burned him.

**The third issue:** They chose punishment by fire only because it is the most severe of punishments. For this reason it was said: ﴿if you are going to act﴾, meaning: if you are going to support your gods with a strong support, so they chose the most severe punishment, which is burning.

* * *

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We said, "O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham."﴾, there are issues in it:

**The first issue:** Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, in explaining His saying: ﴿We said, "O fire, be coolness,"﴾, said: The meaning is that He, glorified is He, made the fire coolness and safety, and that there was no actual speech, like His saying: ﴿that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾, meaning, He brings it into being. It has been argued against this that fire is inanimate, so addressing it is not permissible. Most scholars hold that this speech did occur. Then these have two views: the first, which is the view of al-Suddi, is that the one speaking was Jibril, peace be upon him. The second, which is the view of most scholars, is that the one speaking was Allah the Exalted, and this is the more fitting and closer to the apparent meaning. As for the claim that fire is inanimate, so addressing it serves no purpose, we say: why could the purpose of that command not be a benefit returning to the angels?

**The second issue:** They differed about how the fire became cool, in three views. The first: Allah the Exalted removed from it the heat and burning, and left what it had of light and brilliance, and Allah has power over all things. The second: Allah the Exalted created in Abraham's body a condition that prevents the harm of the fire from reaching him, as He does with the guardians of Hell in the Hereafter, and just as He constructed the body of the ostrich so that swallowing a heated iron does not harm it, and the body of the salamander so that remaining in fire does not harm it. The third: He, glorified is He, created between him and the fire a barrier that prevents the effect of the fire from reaching him. The scholars who investigate said: The first is more preferable, because the apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿We said, "O fire, be coolness,"﴾ is that the fire itself became cool, so that Abraham was safe from its effect, not that the fire remained as it was. If it is said: fire is a body characterized by heat and subtlety; if heat is part of the definition of fire, it is impossible for fire to be cool. Therefore it must be said that what is meant by "fire" is the body which is one of the components of the definition of fire, and that is a metaphor (*majaz*, figurative usage). Why, then, is your metaphor preferable to the other two metaphors? We say: the metaphor we mentioned allows coolness to remain, whereas in the two metaphors you mentioned, that does not remain. So our metaphor is preferable.

As for His saying: ﴿be coolness and safety upon Abraham﴾, the meaning is that if coolness becomes excessive, it destroys just as heat does; rather, moderation is necessary. Then, in achieving moderation there are three aspects:

The first: Allah the Exalted determines its coolness at the degree that does not affect.

The second: some of the fire became cool and some of it remained at its heat, so heat and coolness balanced each other.

The third: He, exalted is He, placed in his body an extra measure of heat, so he was safe from that coldness; rather, he even benefited from it and enjoyed it.

Then here there are questions:

**The first question:** Did all the fire cease and become coolness? The answer: "fire" is the name of the reality (*māhiyya*, quiddity), so this coolness must occur in the reality, and it necessarily follows that it applies to every individual of the reality. It was also said: rather, it was specific to that fire, because the purpose only concerned the coolness of that fire, and fire has benefits for creation, so it is not permissible to render it useless, and the intention was the deliverance of Abraham, peace be upon him, not inflicting harm on the rest of creation.

**The second question:** Is it permissible what is narrated from al-Hasan, that it was a greeting of safety from Allah the Exalted upon Abraham, peace be upon him? The apparent answer: just as He made the fire cool, He made it safety for him so that he would be spared; so what he said is far-fetched, and it involves scattering the ordered speech.

**The third question:** Is it permissible what is narrated, that if He had not said "and safety," the coldness would have reached him? The answer: that is far-fetched, because the coldness of the fire did not come from it; it came from Allah the Exalted, and He is capable of both heat and cold, so it is not permissible to say: the coldness would have intensified had it not been for His saying "safety."

**The fourth question:** Is it permissible what is said, that he was in the fire more pleasantly than in all his other states? The answer: this is not impossible, because of the increase and completion of blessing it contains for him; and it is possible that he became more pleasant in life there because of the greatness of the joy he received from his deliverance from that great matter, and because of the greatness of his joy at his victory over his enemies and at what he manifested of the religion of Allah the Exalted.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They intended a scheme against him, but We made them the greatest losers.﴾, meaning: they wanted to plot against him, but they were nothing but defeated. They overcame him with argument, so Allah the Exalted taught him the conclusive proof. Then they abandoned force and tyranny, so He gave him victory and strengthened him over them. Then He, glorified is He, completed the blessing upon him by delivering him and delivering Lot along with him, and he was his nephew, Lot ibn Haran, to the land which He blessed for the worlds. In reports it is mentioned that this event took place within the borders of Babylon, so Allah the Exalted delivered him from that place to the blessed land. It was then said that it is Mecca; it was also said it is the land of Sham, because of His saying: ﴿to the farthest mosque whose surroundings We have blessed﴾ [al-Isra: 1]. As for the reason for its blessing: regarding religion, most of the prophets, peace be upon them, were sent from it, and their laws and religious traces spread there. As for worldly matters, Allah the Exalted blessed it with abundance of water, trees, fruit, fertility, and pleasant living. It was also said: there is no sweet water but that its source gushes from beneath the rock that is in Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem).

It has been argued against this that fire is inanimate, so addressing it is not permissible. Most scholars hold that this speech did occur. Then these have two views: the first, which is the view of al-Suddi, is that the one speaking was Jibril, peace be upon him. The second, which is the view of most scholars, is that the one speaking was Allah the Exalted, and this is the more fitting and closer to the apparent meaning. As for the claim that fire is inanimate, so addressing it serves no purpose, we say: why could the purpose of that command not be a benefit returning to the angels?

**The second issue:** They differed about how the fire became cool, in three views. The first: Allah the Exalted removed from it the heat and burning, and left what it had of light and brilliance, and Allah has power over all things. The second: Allah the Exalted created in Abraham's body a condition that prevents the harm of the fire from reaching him, as He does with the guardians of Hell in the Hereafter, and just as He constructed the body of the ostrich so that swallowing a heated iron does not harm it, and the body of the salamander so that remaining in fire does not harm it. The third: He, glorified is He, created between him and the fire a barrier that prevents the effect of the fire from reaching him. If it is said: fire is a body characterized by heat and subtlety; if heat is part of the definition of fire, it is impossible for fire to be cool. Therefore it must be said that what is meant by "fire" is the body which is one of the components of the definition of fire, and that is a metaphor (*majaz*, figurative usage). Why, then, is your metaphor preferable to the other two metaphors? We say: the metaphor we mentioned allows coolness to remain, whereas in the two metaphors you mentioned, that does not remain. So our metaphor is preferable.

As for His saying: ﴿be coolness and safety upon Abraham﴾, the meaning is that if coolness becomes excessive, it destroys just as heat does; rather, moderation is necessary. Then, in achieving moderation there are three aspects:

The first: Allah the Exalted determines its coolness at the degree that does not affect.

The second: some of the fire became cool and some of it remained at its heat, so heat and coolness balanced each other.

The third: He, exalted is He, placed in his body an extra measure of heat, so he was safe from that coldness; rather, he even benefited from it and enjoyed it.

Then here there are questions:

**The first question:** Did all the fire cease and become coolness? The answer: "fire" is the name of the reality (*māhiyya*, quiddity), so this coolness must occur in the reality, and it necessarily follows that it applies to every individual of the reality. It was also said: rather, it was specific to that fire, because the purpose only concerned the coolness of that fire, and fire has benefits for creation, so it is not permissible to render it useless, and the intention was the deliverance of Abraham, peace be upon him, not inflicting harm on the rest of creation.

**The second question:** Is it permissible what is narrated from al-Hasan, that it was a greeting of safety from Allah the Exalted upon Abraham, peace be upon him? The apparent answer: just as He made the fire cool, He made it safety for him so that he would be spared; so what he said is far-fetched, and it involves scattering the ordered speech.

The answer: that is far-fetched, because the coldness of the fire did not come from it; it came from Allah the Exalted, and He is capable of both heat and cold, so it is not permissible to say: the coldness would have intensified had it not been for His saying "safety."

The answer: this is not impossible, because of the increase and completion of blessing it contains for him; and it is possible that he became more pleasant in life there because of the greatness of the joy he received from his deliverance from that great matter, and because of the greatness of his joy at his victory over his enemies and at what he manifested of the religion of Allah the Exalted.

It was also said: there is no sweet water but that its source gushes from beneath the rock that is in Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem).
