**The first issue:** Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, in explaining His saying: ﴿We said, "O fire, be coolness,"﴾, said: The meaning is that He, glorified is He, made the fire coolness and safety, and that there was no actual speech, like His saying: ﴿that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾, meaning, He brings it into being. It has been argued against this that fire is inanimate, so addressing it is not permissible. Most scholars hold that this speech did occur. Then these have two views: the first, which is the view of al-Suddi, is that the one speaking was Jibril, peace be upon him. The second, which is the view of most scholars, is that the one speaking was Allah the Exalted, and this is the more fitting and closer to the apparent meaning. As for the claim that fire is inanimate, so addressing it serves no purpose, we say: why could the purpose of that command not be a benefit returning to the angels?

**The second issue:** They differed about how the fire became cool, in three views. The first: Allah the Exalted removed from it the heat and burning, and left what it had of light and brilliance, and Allah has power over all things. The second: Allah the Exalted created in Abraham's body a condition that prevents the harm of the fire from reaching him, as He does with the guardians of Hell in the Hereafter, and just as He constructed the body of the ostrich so that swallowing a heated iron does not harm it, and the body of the salamander so that remaining in fire does not harm it. The third: He, glorified is He, created between him and the fire a barrier that prevents the effect of the fire from reaching him. The scholars who investigate said: The first is more preferable, because the apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿We said, "O fire, be coolness,"﴾ is that the fire itself became cool, so that Abraham was safe from its effect, not that the fire remained as it was. If it is said: fire is a body characterized by heat and subtlety; if heat is part of the definition of fire, it is impossible for fire to be cool. Therefore it must be said that what is meant by "fire" is the body which is one of the components of the definition of fire, and that is a metaphor (*majaz*, figurative usage). Why, then, is your metaphor preferable to the other two metaphors? We say: the metaphor we mentioned allows coolness to remain, whereas in the two metaphors you mentioned, that does not remain. So our metaphor is preferable.

As for His saying: ﴿be coolness and safety upon Abraham﴾, the meaning is that if coolness becomes excessive, it destroys just as heat does; rather, moderation is necessary. Then, in achieving moderation there are three aspects:

The first: Allah the Exalted determines its coolness at the degree that does not affect.

The second: some of the fire became cool and some of it remained at its heat, so heat and coolness balanced each other.

The third: He, exalted is He, placed in his body an extra measure of heat, so he was safe from that coldness; rather, he even benefited from it and enjoyed it.

Then here there are questions:

**The first question:** Did all the fire cease and become coolness? The answer: "fire" is the name of the reality (*māhiyya*, quiddity), so this coolness must occur in the reality, and it necessarily follows that it applies to every individual of the reality. It was also said: rather, it was specific to that fire, because the purpose only concerned the coolness of that fire, and fire has benefits for creation, so it is not permissible to render it useless, and the intention was the deliverance of Abraham, peace be upon him, not inflicting harm on the rest of creation.

**The second question:** Is it permissible what is narrated from al-Hasan, that it was a greeting of safety from Allah the Exalted upon Abraham, peace be upon him? The apparent answer: just as He made the fire cool, He made it safety for him so that he would be spared; so what he said is far-fetched, and it involves scattering the ordered speech.

**The third question:** Is it permissible what is narrated, that if He had not said "and safety," the coldness would have reached him? The answer: that is far-fetched, because the coldness of the fire did not come from it; it came from Allah the Exalted, and He is capable of both heat and cold, so it is not permissible to say: the coldness would have intensified had it not been for His saying "safety."

**The fourth question:** Is it permissible what is said, that he was in the fire more pleasantly than in all his other states? The answer: this is not impossible, because of the increase and completion of blessing it contains for him; and it is possible that he became more pleasant in life there because of the greatness of the joy he received from his deliverance from that great matter, and because of the greatness of his joy at his victory over his enemies and at what he manifested of the religion of Allah the Exalted.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They intended a scheme against him, but We made them the greatest losers.﴾, meaning: they wanted to plot against him, but they were nothing but defeated. They overcame him with argument, so Allah the Exalted taught him the conclusive proof. Then they abandoned force and tyranny, so He gave him victory and strengthened him over them. Then He, glorified is He, completed the blessing upon him by delivering him and delivering Lot along with him, and he was his nephew, Lot ibn Haran, to the land which He blessed for the worlds. In reports it is mentioned that this event took place within the borders of Babylon, so Allah the Exalted delivered him from that place to the blessed land. It was then said that it is Mecca; it was also said it is the land of Sham, because of His saying: ﴿to the farthest mosque whose surroundings We have blessed﴾ [al-Isra: 1]. As for the reason for its blessing: regarding religion, most of the prophets, peace be upon them, were sent from it, and their laws and religious traces spread there. As for worldly matters, Allah the Exalted blessed it with abundance of water, trees, fruit, fertility, and pleasant living. It was also said: there is no sweet water but that its source gushes from beneath the rock that is in Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem).

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 21, verses 72–73:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob as an additional gift, and We made each of them righteous﴾ ﴿And We made them leaders guiding by Our command, and We revealed to them the doing of good deeds, the establishment of prayer, and the giving of zakat; and they were worshippers of Us﴾

Know that after He, exalted is He, mentioned His favour upon Abraham and upon Lot, by delivering the two of them to the blessed land, He followed it with the mention of other blessings. He joined the two of them together because Lot's being with him, along with the kinship between them and their sharing in prophethood, is an additional favour. Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the blessings He bestowed upon Abraham, peace be upon him, and then the blessings He bestowed upon Lot. As for the first, it is in several aspects:

The first: ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob as an additional gift﴾. Know that al-nafilah (the additional gift) means a gift specifically, and likewise al-nafl, and a man who gives many gifts is called nawfal. Then there are two positions of the exegetes here:

The first: that it is here a verbal noun (masdar) from "We gave him", a masdar from a word other than its own verb, and there is no difference between this and His saying ﴿and We gave him﴾ as a gift, meaning: We gave them both to him as a gift and a bounty, not as a deserved reward. This is the view of Mujahid and Ata'.

The second, which is the view of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj: when Abraham, peace be upon him, asked God for a child, he said: ﴿My Lord, grant me [a child] from among the righteous﴾ [al-Saffat: 100], God answered his supplication, and He gave him Isaac, and bestowed upon him Jacob without his asking. So this was ﴿an additional gift﴾, like a voluntary matter from human beings. It is as if He said: ﴿And We gave him Isaac﴾ in answer to his supplication; and We gave him ﴿Jacob as an additional gift﴾ beyond what he asked, like the voluntary prayer which is an addition to the obligatory one. According to this, the additional gift is Jacob alone.

The first aspect is closer, because He, exalted is He, joined the two together and then mentioned the word ﴿additional﴾; so when it is suitable to be a description of both of them, that is more appropriate.

The second blessing: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and We made each of them righteous﴾, meaning, each of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, were prophets sent. This is the view of al-Dahhak. Others said: acting in obedience to God, mighty and majestic, avoiding His prohibitions.

The second aspect is closer, because the word al-salah (righteousness) encompasses all of them; for He, glorified is He, said after this verse: ﴿and We revealed to them the doing of good deeds﴾; so if we took righteousness to mean prophethood, repetition would arise. Our companions (the Ash'arites) used this verse as evidence that the actions of servants are created by God, the Exalted, because His saying ﴿and We made each of them righteous﴾ indicates that this righteousness is from Him. Al-Jubba'i answered that if it were so, He would not have described them as righteous, nor as leaders, nor as worshippers, nor would He have praised them for that, nor commended them for it. And if that is established, then interpretation is necessary, and it is of two aspects:

The first: that what is meant is that He, glorified is He, gave them, out of His kindness and enabling grace, that by which they became righteous.

The second: that what is meant is that He named them by that, as one says: Zayd declared Fulan to be a sinner (fasiq), misguided him, and declared him an unbeliever (kafir), when he describes him with that and is believed by the people; and as one says of a judge: he certified Fulan, deemed him trustworthy, or discredited him, when he rules thus.

Know that these aspects are flawed. As for their reliance on praise and blame, the customary answer is that we counter it with the two issues of the supplicant and of knowledge. As for the reading of it as kindness, it is invalid, because the act of bestowing kindness is general with respect to the responsible persons, so this specification requires additional benefit. Also, his saying "I made him righteous" is like his saying "I made him moving"; so reading it as attaining something other than righteousness abandons the apparent meaning. As for reading it as naming, it too is a metaphor; at most it is resorted to in cases of necessity in some places, and here there is no necessity, unless they return once more to the issue of praise and blame, and then we also return to the two issues of the supplicant and of knowledge.

The third blessing: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We made them leaders guiding by Our command﴾. In it there are two views:

One: meaning, We made them leaders calling people to the religion of God, exalted is He, and to good deeds, by Our command and permission.

The second: the view of Abu Muslim that this leadership (imamah) is prophethood.

The first is preferable, so as to avoid repetition. Our companions used this verse as evidence for two matters:

One: for the creation of actions, by His saying ﴿and We made them leaders﴾, and its establishment is as previously mentioned.

The second: that calling to truth and forbidding falsehood is not permissible except by the command of God, exalted is He; for if the command were not relevant, there would be no benefit in His saying "by Our command".

The fourth blessing: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and We revealed to them the doing of good deeds﴾. This indicates that He, glorified is He, singled them out with the honour of prophethood, and that is among the greatest blessings upon a father. Al-Zajjaj said: the ha' was omitted from iqamat al-salah (the establishment of prayer), because the idafah (construct phrase) is a substitute for it. Others said: al-iqam and al-iqamah are verbal nouns. Abu al-Qasim al-Ansari said: prayer is the most noble of the physical acts of worship, and it was legislated for the remembrance of God, exalted is He; and zakat is the most noble of the financial acts of worship; and their combination is the magnification of God's command and compassion toward God's creation.

Know that He, glorified is He, first described them with righteousness, because it is the first of the stages of those journeying to God, exalted is He; then He ascended and described them with imamah; then He ascended further and described them with prophethood and revelation. And since righteousness, which is infallibility (ismah), is the first stage of prophethood, this indicates that the prophets are infallible, for one deprived of the first stage is more deserving of being deprived of the final one. Then, just as He, glorified is He, explained the kinds of His blessings upon them, He afterward explained their occupation with His worship, saying: ﴿and they were worshippers of Us﴾. It is as if He, glorified and exalted is He, when He fulfilled the covenant of lordship in beneficence and bounty, they likewise fulfilled the covenant of servanthood, which is occupation with obedience and worship.

(The Third Story: the story of Lot, peace be upon him)

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And Lot—We gave him judgment and knowledge, and We delivered him from the town that was committing abominations. Indeed, they were a people of evil, defiantly disobedient.﴾ ﴿And We admitted him into Our mercy. Indeed, he was of the righteous.﴾

Know that after He mentioned what He bestowed upon Abraham, peace be upon him, He followed it with the mention of His blessings upon Lot, peace be upon him, since He had joined the two of them earlier. Here there are two issues:

The first issue: concerning the waw in His words ﴿And Lot﴾, there are two opinions:

One of them, which is the view of al-Zajjaj, is that it is coordinated (ʿatf) with His words ﴿And We revealed to them﴾.

The second, which is the view of Abu Muslim, is that it is coordinated with His words ﴿We gave Abraham his right guidance﴾. There must be a pronoun in His words ﴿And Lot﴾, so it is as if He said: "And We gave Lot," and the verb's object was omitted.

[Page 167]

The second issue: concerning the kinds of blessings, which are four aspects:

The first of them is judgment (ḥukm), that is, wisdom (ḥikmah), which is what must be done, or the settling of disputes between adversaries. It has also been said that it is prophethood.

The second is knowledge (ʿilm). Know that the addition of tanwin to both of them indicates the elevated rank of that knowledge and that judgment.

The third is His words: ﴿and We delivered him from the town that was committing abominations﴾. The intended meaning is the people of the town, because it is they who committed the abominations, not the town itself; and because the destruction came upon them, and God, exalted be He, delivered him from that. Then, exalted and high be He, clarified by His words ﴿Indeed, they were a people of evil, defiantly disobedient﴾ what He meant by the abominations; and their affair in what they used to undertake is evident.

The fourth is His words: ﴿And We admitted him into Our mercy. Indeed, he was of the righteous﴾. Concerning the interpretation of mercy (raḥmah) there are two opinions:

The first: that it is prophethood, meaning that since he was fit for prophethood, God admitted him into His mercy so that he would discharge its duty. This is reported from Muqatil.

The second: that it is reward, reported from Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Dahhak. It may be said: when God gave him judgment and knowledge, and he was freed from evil companions, the doors of unveilings (mukashafat) were opened to him, and the lights of divinity became manifest to him, and these are a sea without shore, and they are mercy in reality.

(The Fourth Story: the story of Noah, peace be upon him)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Noah, when he called out before; so We responded to him and delivered him and his family from the great distress. And We helped him against the people who denied Our signs. Indeed, they were a people of evil, so We drowned them all.﴾

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿when he called out before﴾, there are two issues in it:

The first issue: There is no doubt that what is meant by this call is his supplication against his people for punishment. This is confirmed by Allah's account of it, sometimes in summary, in His saying: ﴿So he prayed to his Lord, "I am overpowered, so give me victory."﴾ [al-Qamar: 10], and sometimes in detail, in His saying: ﴿And Noah said, "My Lord, do not leave upon the earth from among the disbelievers an inhabitant."﴾ [Nuh: 26]. It also indicates this that Allah, exalted is He, answered him with His saying: ﴿so We responded to him and delivered him and his family from the great distress.﴾ This response indicates that the deliverance mentioned in it was what was requested in the petition, so this shows that his call and supplication was that He would deliver him from what befell him from them of kinds of harm through denial and rejection of him, and that He would grant him victory over them and destroy them. Therefore, after it He said: ﴿And We helped him against the people who denied Our signs.﴾

The second issue: The scholars (muhaqqiqun) agreed that this call was by the command of Allah, exalted is He; for if it were not by His command, it could not be assured that the good would not be to refrain from answering it, which would then become a cause for diminishing the standing of the prophets. And because undertaking such petitions without command would be exaggeration in harm. Others said: he, peace be upon him, was not authorized in that. Abu Umamah said: No one among the creatures of Allah, exalted is He, has grieved as Adam and Noah grieved: Adam's grief was over accepting the whisper of Iblis, and Noah's grief was over his supplication against his people. So Allah, exalted is He, revealed to him: "Do not grieve, for your supplication matched My decree."

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and delivered him and his family from the great distress﴾, the "family" here means the people of his religion. And regarding the explanation of "distress" there are several views:

The first: that it is the punishment descending upon the disbelievers, which is the drowning, and this is the view of most exegetes.

The second: that it is the denial of his people toward him and the harm he suffered from them.

The third: that it is the combination of both matters, and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, and it is the closest, because he, peace be upon him, had invited them to Allah, exalted is He, for a long period, and he would receive from them every hateful thing, and the grief would increase because of that. And when Allah, exalted is He, informed him that He would drown them and commanded him to build the ark, he was also in grief and fear, not knowing who would be saved from the drowning and who would drown. So Allah, exalted is He, removed from him the great distress by delivering him from all of that, and delivering all who believed in him along with him.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We helped him against the people﴾, the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b is "And We helped him against the people." Then al-Mubarrad said: its estimated sense is "And We helped him from the harm of the people." And Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Who will help us against the might of Allah?﴾ [Ghafir: 29], meaning, who will protect us from His punishment. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "min" here carries the meaning of "'ala" (against). The author of al-Kashshaf said: nasara is the verb whose reflexive form is intasara (to take revenge/be victorious), and I heard a Hudhali man supplicating against a thief: "O Allah, grant them victory over him," meaning, make them victorious over him.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, they were a people of evil﴾, the meaning is that they were a people of evil because of their rejection of him and their denial of him, so We drowned them all. Thus He explained the aspect by which He delivered him from them.

This is confirmed by Allah's account of it, sometimes in summary, in His saying: ﴿So he prayed to his Lord, "I am overpowered, so give me victory."﴾ [al-Qamar: 10], and sometimes in detail, in His saying: ﴿And Noah said, "My Lord, do not leave upon the earth from among the disbelievers an inhabitant."﴾ [Nuh: 26]. It also indicates this that Allah, exalted is He, answered him with His saying: ﴿so We responded to him and delivered him and his family from the great distress.﴾ This response indicates that the deliverance mentioned in it was what was requested in the petition, so this shows that his call and supplication was that He would deliver him from what befell him from them of kinds of harm through denial and rejection of him, and that He would grant him victory over them and destroy them. Therefore, after it He said: ﴿And We helped him against the people who denied Our signs.﴾

The second issue: The scholars (muhaqqiqun) agreed that this call was by the command of Allah, exalted is He; for if it were not by His command, it could not be assured that the good would not be to refrain from answering it, which would then become a cause for diminishing the standing of the prophets. And because undertaking such petitions without command would be exaggeration in harm. Others said: he, peace be upon him, was not authorized in that. Abu Umamah said: No one among the creatures of Allah, exalted is He, has grieved as Adam and Noah grieved: Adam's grief was over accepting the whisper of Iblis, and Noah's grief was over his supplication against his people. So Allah, exalted is He, revealed to him: "Do not grieve, for your supplication matched My decree."

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and delivered him and his family from the great distress﴾, the "family" here means the people of his religion. And regarding the explanation of "distress" there are several views:

The first: that it is the punishment descending upon the disbelievers, which is the drowning, and this is the view of most exegetes.

The second: that it is the denial of his people toward him and the harm he suffered from them.

The third: that it is the combination of both matters, and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, and it is the closest, because he, peace be upon him, had invited them to Allah, exalted is He, for a long period, and he would receive from them every hateful thing, and the grief would increase because of that. And when Allah, exalted is He, informed him that He would drown them and commanded him to build the ark, he was also in grief and fear, not knowing who would be saved from the drowning and who would drown. So Allah, exalted is He, removed from him the great distress by delivering him from all of that, and delivering all who believed in him along with him.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We helped him against the people﴾, the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b is "And We helped him against the people." Then al-Mubarrad said: its estimated sense is "And We helped him from the harm of the people." And Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Who will help us against the might of Allah?﴾ [Ghafir: 29], meaning, who will protect us from His punishment. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "min" here carries the meaning of "'ala" (against). The author of al-Kashshaf said: nasara is the verb whose reflexive form is intasara (to take revenge/be victorious), and I heard a Hudhali man supplicating against a thief: "O Allah, grant them victory over him," meaning, make them victorious over him.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, they were a people of evil﴾, the meaning is that they were a people of evil because of their rejection of him and their denial of him, so We drowned them all. Thus He explained the aspect by which He delivered him from them.

The fifth story: the story of Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them both.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Dawud and Sulayman, when they judged concerning the tilth, when the sheep of certain people grazed in it by night, and We were witnesses to their judgment. And We gave understanding of it to Sulayman; and to each We gave judgment and knowledge, and We subjected the mountains to glorify along with Dawud, and the birds; and We were doers. And We taught him the making of coats of mail for you, to protect you from your violence; so will you be grateful? And to Sulayman the wind, blowing violently, running by his command toward the land which We had blessed; and We are Knower of all things. And among the devils were those who dived for him and did work other than that; and We were their guardians.﴾

Know that His saying, "And Dawud, and Sulayman, and Ayyub, and Zakariyya, and Dhu al-Nun," is all in sequence with what preceded it from His saying: ﴿And We gave Ibrahim his rectitude before,﴾ and from His saying: ﴿And Lut – We gave him judgment and knowledge﴾. Know that the purpose is to mention the blessings of God Most High upon Dawud and Sulayman. He first mentioned the blessing they shared, then mentioned what is specific to each of them from among the blessings. As for the shared blessing, it is the story mentioned, namely the story of the judgment, and the aspect of the blessing in it is that God Most High adorned both of them with knowledge and understanding in His saying: ﴿And to each We gave judgment and knowledge.﴾ Then in this there is an indication that knowledge is the most excellent and greatest of perfections, because God Most High mentioned it first here before the other great blessings, such as the subjugation of the mountains, the birds, the wind, and the jinn. And if knowledge is placed before such things, what then do you think of other things? There are issues in this:

The first issue: Ibn al-Sikkit said: "al-nafsh" is that sheep scatter at night, grazing without a shepherd, and this is the view of the majority of the commentators. According to al-Hasan, it is permitted for this to happen by night and by day.

The second issue: Most commentators hold that al-harth (tilth) is crops; some said it is a vineyard, and the first is closer to common usage.

The third issue: Whoever holds that the least plural is two argued from His saying: ﴿and We were witnesses to their judgment﴾, although the intended ones are Dawud and Sulayman? The answer: just as judgment is attributed to the judge, it may also be attributed to the one in whose favour it is given. So when judgment is attributed to the litigants, the group is more than two. It has also been read as "wa kunna li-hukmihima shahidin" (and We were witnesses to their two judgments).

The fourth issue: Regarding the manner of the story there are two views:

The first: Most commentators said: two men entered upon Dawud, peace be upon him, one of them the owner of a tilth and the other the owner of sheep. The owner of the tilth said: "The sheep of this man entered my tilth and left nothing of it." Dawud, peace be upon him, said: "Go, for the sheep are yours." They left and passed by Sulayman, who said: "How did he judge between you?" They informed him. He said: "If I were the judge, I would have judged otherwise." Dawud, peace be upon him, was informed of that, so he summoned him and said: "How would you judge between them?" He said: "I would give the sheep to the owner of the tilth, so that he benefits from their milk, offspring and wool until the tilth returns in the coming year to the state it was in on the day it was eaten. Then I would return the sheep to their owners, and the owner of the tilth would receive his tilth."

The second: Ibn Mas'ud, Shurayh and Muqatil, may God have mercy on them, said: a shepherd once stopped for the night beside a vineyard, and the sheep entered the vineyard while he was unaware; they ate the vine shoots and ruined the vineyard. The owner of the vineyard went the next day to Dawud, peace be upon him, and he judged in his favour that the sheep be given to him, because there was no difference between the value of the vineyard and the value of the sheep. They went out and passed by Sulayman, who said to them: "How did he judge between you?" They told him, and he said: "Other than this is more gentle to both parties." Dawud, peace be upon him, was informed of that; so he summoned Sulayman and said to him: "By the right of fatherhood and prophethood, tell me what is more gentle to both parties." He said: "You hand the sheep over to the owner of the vineyard so that he may benefit from their produce, and the shepherd works at restoring the vineyard until it becomes as it was; then you return the sheep to their owner." Dawud, peace be upon him, said: "The judgment is only what you have decided," and he ruled accordingly.

* * *

Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with him both, said: Sulayman judged with that when he was eleven years old. There are matters here that must be discussed.

The first question: Is there in the verse an indication that the two of them, peace be upon them, differed in the judgment or not? Abu Bakr al-Asamm said: they did not differ at all, and God Most High clarified the judgment for them, but He clarified it through the tongue of Sulayman, peace be upon him. The answer: the correct view is that they differed, and the evidence is the consensus of the Companions and the Successors, may God be pleased with them, as we have narrated. Also, God Most High said: ﴿and We were witnesses to their judgment﴾, then He said: ﴿And We gave understanding of it to Sulayman﴾, and the "fa" indicates sequence, so that judgment must have preceded this understanding. That prior judgment either is said to have been agreed upon by both or to have been disputed. If they agreed on it, there remains no benefit in His saying: ﴿And We gave understanding of it to Sulayman﴾; and if they differed on it, then that is what is sought.

The second question: Granting that they differed in the judgment, were the two judgments issued from the text or from ijtihad (independent reasoning)? The answer: both possibilities are permissible in our view. Al-Jubba'i claimed that both were issued from the text. Then he at one time based that on the view that ijtihad is not permitted for prophets, and at another time on the view that although ijtihad is generally permitted for them, it is not permitted in this matter.

As for the first argument: we have discussed it in general in our book called al-Mahsul fi al-Usul, and let us here mention the fundamentals of the discussion from both sides. Al-Jubba'i argued that ijtihad is not permitted for the prophets, peace be upon them, on several grounds:

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: It is not for me to change it of my own accord; I follow only what is revealed to me﴾ [Yunus: 15], and His saying: ﴿Nor does he speak of his own desire﴾ [al-Najm: 3].

The second: ijtihad's method is conjecture, while he is able to grasp it with certainty, so it is not permissible for him to resort to conjecture, like one who sees the qibla directly, for whom it is not permissible to make ijtihad.

The third: opposing the Messenger entails disbelief, by His saying: ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge in what is disputed among them﴾ [al-Nisa': 65], whereas opposing what is conjectural and matters of ijtihad does not entail disbelief.

The fourth: If it were permissible for him to exercise ijtihad in rulings, he would not have hesitated in any of them; yet he hesitated in the matter of zihar and li'an until revelation came down, which shows that ijtihad was not permissible for him.

The fifth: ijtihad is only resorted to when the text is absent, but the absence of the text with regard to the Messenger is as if impossible; therefore ijtihad must not be permissible for him.

The sixth: If ijtihad were permissible for the Messenger, it would also be permissible for Jibril, peace be upon him, and then there would be no assurance that these laws he brought are from the texts of God Most High or from the ijtihad of Jibril.

The answer to the first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Say: It is not for me to change it of my own accord; I follow only what is revealed to me﴾ does not support your view, because it concerns replacing one verse with another, since it comes after His saying: ﴿Those who do not hope for meeting Us said: Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it﴾ [Yunus: 15], and there is no room for ijtihad in that. As for His saying: ﴿Nor does he speak of his own desire﴾, it is far-fetched; for whoever permits ijtihad for him says: what I exercise ijtihad in is from revelation in general, even if not in detail, and the verse concerns conveying from God Most High, not His ruling which is by reason.

The answer to the second: When God Most High says to him: "If it becomes predominant in your opinion that the ruling in the original case is grounded in such and such a cause, and then it becomes predominant in your opinion that this cause exists in another case, then judge accordingly," then here the ruling is certain, and conjecture does not enter into the ruling itself but into the means to it.

The answer to the third: We do not grant that opposing matters of ijtihad is permitted absolutely; rather, the permissibility of opposing them is conditional on their issuing from someone other than the infallible. The proof of this is that the community may agree on a ijtihad, and then their opposition becomes forbidden; and the position of the Messenger is even more binding.

The answer to the fourth: Perhaps he, peace be upon him, was forbidden from ijtihad in some kinds, or was permitted absolutely but the basis of ijtihad did not appear to him in that particular case, and therefore he hesitated.

The answer to the fifth: Why should it not be permissible that the text be withheld from him in some cases? Then the condition for the permissibility of ijtihad is fulfilled.

The answer to the sixth: This possibility is rejected by the consensus of the community against it.

This is the answer to the doubts of those who deny it. The following are the arguments that show ijtihad is permitted for them:

The first: when, if he, peace be upon him, becomes predominantly of the view that the ruling in the original case is grounded in a certain meaning, and then he knows or conjectures that this meaning exists in another case, it is necessary that it becomes predominant in his view that the ruling of God Most High in this case is like that in the original. He has a certain premise, namely that opposing the ruling of God Most High is a cause for deserving punishment; from these two premises there arises the conjecture of deserving punishment for opposing this conjectured ruling.

At this point, either he proceeds to act and to refrain at the same time, which is impossible because two contradictories cannot be combined; or he refrains from both, which is impossible because it is impossible to be free of both contradictories; or he gives preference to the less probable over the more probable, which is false by the self-evidence of reason; or he gives preference to the more probable over the less probable, and that is acting by analogy (qiyas). This point is the one on which reliance is placed for acting by analogy, and it also applies to the prophets, peace be upon them. This applies to the permissibility of ijtihad from Jibril, peace be upon him.

The second: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So take warning, O people of insight﴾ [al-Hashr: 2] is an address to all to take warning, so it is necessary that the Messenger, peace be upon him, be included in it, because he is the leader of those who take warning and the best of them.

The third: that inference (istinbat) is among the highest ranks of scholars, so it is necessary that the Messenger have a share in it; otherwise each individual of the ijtihad scholars would be superior to him in this domain. If it is said: this would only follow if there were no rank higher than taking warning, and the matter is not so, because he would have received the rulings by revelation with certainty, and so he would be of a higher rank than ijtihad which at most yields only conjecture. We say: it is not impossible that he did not find the text in some places; if he were unable to exercise ijtihad, he would be of lower rank than the mujtahid who can arrive at that ruling through ijtihad. Also, we have shown that when God Most High commanded him to exercise ijtihad, that itself was useful for certainty about the ruling.

The fourth: he, peace be upon him, said: "The scholars are the heirs of the prophets," so it is necessary that the rank of ijtihad be established for the prophets, so that the scholars may inherit that from them. This is the complete statement on this issue.

The fifth: God Most High said: ﴿God pardon you! Why did you grant them permission?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 43]. If that permission was by God's permission, it is impossible that He would say: "Why did you grant them permission?" If it was by the inclination of the soul, that is not permissible, and if it was by ijtihad, then that is what is sought.

The second source: al-Jubba'i said: If we permit ijtihad for the prophets, peace be upon them, then in this matter it must be impermissible, for several reasons:

The first: what reached the owner of the tilth from the milk of the livestock and their benefits is of unknown amount, so how is it permissible in ijtihad to make one of them a substitute for the other?

Second, if Dawud's ijtihad (independent legal reasoning) was correct, then it should not have been overturned, since ijtihad is not overturned by ijtihad. And if it was an error, then God, exalted is He, should have made His repentance clear, as with the other errors He related about the prophets, peace be upon them. When He praised both of them by saying, ﴿And to each We gave judgment and knowledge﴾, this shows that no error occurred on Dawud's part.

Third, if he ruled by ijtihad, then what he attained there would be conjecture (zann), not knowledge (ilm), because God, exalted is He, said, ﴿And to each We gave judgment and knowledge﴾.

Fourth, how could it be based on ijtihad given His saying, ﴿So We gave Sulayman the understanding of it﴾?

As for the first objection, the uncertainty about the amount does not prevent ijtihad, as in the case of the reward for a stipulated task (ju'ala) and the ruling on the musarrah (a she-camel or ewe whose udder was tied to deceive the buyer about its milk yield).

As for the second, perhaps it was an error of the minor sins (saghair).

As for the third, we have explained that whoever adheres to analogy (qiyas), the conjecture occurs in the means of establishing the ruling, but the ruling itself is definite.

As for the fourth, when he reflected and exerted effort, and his ijtihad led him to what we have mentioned, God had given him understanding by showing him the path to that. This is the summary of the discussion showing that it is not impossible that the disagreement between Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them, regarding that ruling was due to ijtihad. As for showing that it is also not impossible that their disagreement about it was due to an explicit text (nass), the method is to say: Dawud, peace be upon him, had been commanded by God, exalted is He, in this matter to rule as he did. Then God, glorified is He, abrogated (naskh) that by revelation to Sulayman, peace be upon him, alone, and commanded him to inform Dawud of it. So that ruling became the ruling of both of them. His saying, ﴿So We gave Sulayman the understanding of it﴾ means: We revealed it to him. If it is said: this is invalid for two reasons:

The first: when God, exalted is He, sent down the first ruling to Dawud, its abrogation should also have been sent down to Dawud, not to Sulayman.

The second: God, exalted is He, praised each of them for understanding. If that had been by way of explicit text, there would be no great praise in his understanding. The great praise is rather for the strength of insight and acuity in deduction (istinbat).

[Page 172]

The third question: If you have established that their disagreement could have been due to an explicit text (nass), and could have been due to ijtihad (independent legal reasoning), then which of the two opinions is more likely? The answer: ijtihad is more likely, for several reasons.

The first: many reports state that Dawud, peace be upon him, had not yet issued his ruling in the matter until he heard from Sulayman that another ruling was better. In some reports, Dawud, peace be upon him, adjured him to state what he had. None of this fits with an explicit text, for if it had been an explicit text, he would have made it known and would not have concealed it.

The fourth question: Explain how ijtihad was carried out. The answer: the basis of the ijtihad in it is what Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, mentioned, that Dawud, peace be upon him, assessed the value of the damage to the vineyard, and it equalled the value of the sheep. He therefore judged that the required compensation for that damage was to be removed by an equivalent benefit, so he handed the sheep over to the injured party. This is like what Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, said about a slave who causes a death: his owner must either surrender him or ransom him. As for Sulayman, peace be upon him, his ijtihad led him to hold that principal property should be matched against principal property and accessory gains against accessory gains. Matching principal property against accessory gains is not permitted, for it entails injustice and oppression. Perhaps the benefits of the sheep in that year were equal to the benefits of the vineyard, so he ruled accordingly. This is like what al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said about one who usurps a slave who then escapes from his hand: he must pay the value, so that the one from whom it was usurped may benefit from it in return for the benefits of the slave which the usurper deprived him of. When the slave is found, they both return what they took.

The fifth question: Assuming it is established with certainty that that disagreement was based on ijtihad, does this story indicate that only one is correct (al-musib wahid), or that all are correct (al-kull musibun)?

The answer: As for those who hold that only one is correct, some of them argued with the words of the Exalted: ﴿So We gave Sulayman the understanding of it﴾. They said: If all were correct, singling out Sulayman, peace be upon him, for this understanding would serve no purpose. As for those who hold that all are correct, some of them argued with His words: ﴿And to each We gave judgement and knowledge﴾. They said: If only one were correct and his opponent in error, it would not be proper to say: ﴿And to each We gave judgement and knowledge﴾. Know that both arguments are weak.

As for the first: Allah, the Exalted, did not say that He gave him the correct understanding. It is possible that He gave him the abrogating ruling (al-nasikh) which had not reached Dawud, peace be upon him. Each of them was correct in what he judged. Moreover, the most that the verse indicates is that Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them both, were not both correct, and that does not necessitate that the matter is the same in our law.

As for the second: He, the Exalted, did not say that to each We gave judgement and knowledge of what he ruled. Rather, it is possible that He gave each of them judgement and knowledge of the methods of ijtihad and the ways of deriving rulings. Furthermore, it does not follow that because every mujtahid was correct in their law, the matter is the same in our law.

* * *

The sixth question: If this incident had occurred in our law, what would its ruling be? The answer: al-Hasan al-Basri said: This verse is muhkam (clear and not abrogated), and judges judge by it until the Day of Resurrection. Know that many scholars claim it has been abrogated by ijma' (scholarly consensus). Then they differed about its ruling. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: If it happened by day, there is no liability, because the owner of livestock may let his livestock graze by day, and the guarding of the crops by day falls on their owner. If it happened by night, liability is required, because guarding them at night falls on him. Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, said: There is no liability on him, whether by night or by day, if he did not transgress by releasing them. This is based on his, peace be upon him, saying: "The wound caused by an animal is unpunishable." Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, relied on what was narrated from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, who said: "A she-camel that was in the habit of trespassing entered an orchard and damaged it. The people mentioned that to the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, and he ruled that guarding orchards by day is the responsibility of their owners, and guarding livestock by night is the responsibility of their owners, and that the owners of livestock are responsible for what their livestock damage by night." This completes the discussion on this verse.

* * *

Then Allah, the Exalted, mentioned after that two of the blessings with which He favoured Dawud, peace be upon him:

The first: His words, the Exalted: ﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify [Us] along with Dawud, and the birds, and We were ever doing [that]﴾. In it there are issues.

[Page 173]

Issue one: Regarding the interpretation of this glorification, there are two views.

One of them: that the mountains did glorify [Allah]. Then they mentioned several interpretations:

First: Muqatil said: When Dawud, peace be upon him, remembered his Lord, the mountains and the birds remembered their Lord along with him.

Second: al-Kalbi said: When Dawud glorified [Allah], the mountains answered him.

Third: Sulayman ibn Hayyan said: When Dawud, peace be upon him, felt a slackening, Allah, the Exalted, commanded the mountains, and they glorified [Allah], and he grew in vigour and yearning.

The second view, which is the choice of some of the scholars of meanings (ashab al-ma'ani): It is possible that the glorification of the mountains and birds is like His words: ﴿And there is not a thing but glorifies Him with His praise﴾ [al-Isra' 17:44]. Dawud, peace be upon him, was singled out for this because he, peace be upon him, knew this by necessity, and thus his certainty and reverence increased. The first view is closer to the truth, because there is no necessity to turn the wording away from its apparent meaning.

As for the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist theological school), they said: If speech came from the mountain, it would come either by its own act or by Allah's act in it. The first is impossible, because the structure of a mountain cannot bear life, knowledge, and power, and whatever is not living, knowing, and powerful cannot perform an act. The second is also impossible, because the speaker, in their view, is one who produces speech, not one in whom speech occurs. So if the one who produces that speech were Allah, the Exalted, then the speaker would be Allah, the Exalted, not the mountain. Thus it is established that it cannot be taken according to its apparent meaning. At this point they said that in: ﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify [Us] along with Dawud﴾, and the similar verse: ﴿O mountains, echo with him﴾ [Saba' 34:10], the meaning is: move with him and travel at his command. And "yusabbihna" (glorify) derives from sabh, which is swimming, and the wording was used in the intensive form. Had it not intended intensity, it would have been said "yasbahna". When it was intensified, it was said "yusabbihna ma'ahu", meaning: travel with him. This is like His words: ﴿Indeed, for you in the day is a long sabh﴾ [al-Muzzammil 73:7], meaning: movement and course of action. Having established this, we say: their movement is the glorification, because it indicates the power of Allah, the Exalted, and His transcendence above all that is ascribed to Him. Know that the basis of this view rests on the claim that the structure of a mountain does not accept life, and this is disputed; and on the claim that speech is an act of Allah, which is also disputed.

Issue two: As for the birds, there is no impossibility that speech should come from them. However, the community (ummah) has agreed that the mukallafun (those bound by legal obligation) are either jinn, humans, or angels. It is therefore impossible for birds to reach the level of intellect required for obligation. Rather, they are in a state like that of a child, in that they can be commanded and forbidden, though they are not obligated. This became a miracle, in that He made them in understanding like an adolescent. Moreover, it is also an indication of the power of Allah, the Exalted, and of His transcendence above what is not permissible. So the discussion regarding them is like the discussion regarding the mountains.

Issue three: The author of al-Kashshaf said: "yusabbihna" is a circumstantial clause (hal) in the sense of "musabbihat" (glorifying), or it is a new statement (isti'naf), as if someone asked: "How did He subject them?" and it was answered: "They glorify." "Wal-tayr" (and the birds) is either conjoined to "al-jibal" (the mountains) or is an object "ma'ahu" (with him). If you ask: Why were the mountains mentioned before the birds? I say: Because their subjugation and their glorification is more wondrous, more indicative of power, and more compelling as a miracle, since they are inanimate, whereas the birds are living, speaking beings.

As for His words: ﴿And We were ever doing [that]﴾, the meaning is: We are able to do this, even though it is a wonder in your eyes. It was also said: We do that for the prophets, peace be upon them.

The second blessing: His words, the Exalted: ﴿And We taught him the making of chainmail for you, to protect you from your violence. Then, are you grateful?﴾ In it there are issues.

Issue one: al-libas (lubus) means clothing. [A poet] said: "Wear for every situation its garment."

Issue two: "Li-tuhsinakum" has been read with the letter nun, the letter ya', and the letter ta', and with the sad both light and doubled. The nun refers to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The ta' refers to the craft or to the chainmail, understood as the coat of mail. The ya' refers to Allah, the Exalted, or to Dawud, or to the chainmail.

[Page 174]

Issue three: Qatadah said: The first to make the coat of mail was Dawud, peace be upon him. Before him they were plates; he was the first to interlace them and make them into rings. al-Hasan mentioned that Luqman the Wise, peace be upon him, was present when he was making the coat of mail. Luqman wished to ask about what he was doing, but he kept silent until he finished it and wore it himself. Then he said: "Silence is wisdom, but few practise it." They said: Allah, the Exalted, softened the iron for him, so he worked it without fire, as if it were clay.

Issue four: Here "al-ba's" means war, although it can apply to all kinds of harm. The meaning is: to prevent and guard you from your violence, that is, from wounding, killing, the sword, the arrow, and the spear.

Issue five: This indicates that the first to make the coat of mail was Dawud, and then people learned it from him. People inherited it from him, and the blessing thereby encompassed every fighter among creation until the end of time. Therefore they are obliged to thank Allah, the Exalted, for the blessing. So He said: ﴿Then, are you grateful?﴾, that is: Give thanks to Allah for what He has made easy for you of this craft. Know that when He, glorified is He, mentioned the blessings with which He favoured Dawud, He then mentioned the blessings with which He favoured Sulayman, peace be upon him. Qatadah said: Allah, the Exalted, made Sulayman inherit from Dawud his kingdom and his prophethood, and added to him two things: He subjected the wind and the devils to him.

The first blessing: His words, the Exalted: ﴿And to Sulayman [We subjected] the wind, violent, running by his command﴾. That is: We made it obedient and submissive to him, in the sense that if he willed it to be violent, it would be violent, and if he willed it to be gentle, it would be gentle, and Allah, the Exalted, subjected it in both states. If it is said: "al-'asif" means the one of severe blowing, yet Allah, the Exalted, described it as gentle in His words: ﴿Gentle, wherever he directed it﴾ [Sad 38:36]. How then can the two be combined? The answer is in two ways:

First: In itself it was gentle and pleasant, like a breeze. When it passed by his throne, it carried him far in a short time, as He said: ﴿Its morning course was a month's journey, and its evening course a month's journey﴾ [Saba' 34:12]. It combined the two: gentleness in its own nature, and violence in its action, together with its obedience to Sulayman, peace be upon him. Its blowing followed what he willed and decreed, sign after sign, and miracle after miracle.

Second: It was gentle at one time and violent at another, depending on its blowing according to his will.

Issue six: "al-Rih" and "al-Riyah" have been read in both the nominative and accusative in both forms. The nominative is on the basis of the subject (ibtida'), and the accusative is by conjunction with "al-jibal" (the mountains). If it is said: He said regarding Dawud: ﴿And We subjected the mountains along with Dawud﴾, and regarding Sulayman: ﴿And to Sulayman the wind﴾, mentioning it for Dawud with the word "ma'a" (with) and for Sulayman with the preposition "li-" (to). He also observed this order in His words: ﴿O mountains, echo with him and the birds﴾ [Saba' 34:10], and He said: ﴿So We subjected to him the wind, running by his command﴾ [Sad 38:36]. What is the point of singling out Dawud with the word "ma'a" and Sulayman with "li-"? We say: It is possible that because the mountain was occupied with glorification, it attained a kind of honour, so what is attributed to it is attributed with the preposition of ownership (lam al-tamlik). As for the wind, nothing proceeded from it except what functions as service, so for this reason it is attributed to Sulayman with the preposition of ownership. This is my persuasive view.

* * *

As for His words: ﴿To the land which We had blessed for the worlds﴾, that is: to proceeding to Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). al-Kalbi said: It would travel from Istakhr to Syria, with Sulayman and his companions riding upon it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 21, verses 79–82 (part 2 of 2):

As for His saying, ﴿And We were Knowers of all things﴾, meaning: because of Our knowledge of things, it was valid for Us to arrange this arrangement among Our messengers, and in Our creation, and to perform these overpowering miracles.

The second favour: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And of the devils were those who dived for him and did other work than that. And We were guardians over them﴾. There are several issues concerning it.

The first issue: the meaning is that they dived for him in the seas and extracted pearls, and went beyond that to crafts and trades, the building of cities and palaces, and the invention of wondrous industries, as He said: ﴿They made for him whatever he willed: sanctuaries, statues, and basins﴾ [Saba': 13]. As for the industries, they include the making of baths, depilatory lime, mills, glass vessels and soap.

The second issue: His saying, ﴿And of the devils were those who dived for him﴾, means: "And We subjected to Solomon from among the devils those who dived for him." Thus it is in the position of the accusative (nasb, the grammatical case of the object) in coordination with "the wind". Al-Zajjaj said: "It may also be in the position of the nominative (raf', the grammatical case of the subject) in two ways:
One of them: coordination with "the wind", so that the meaning is: 'And for Solomon is the wind, and for him are those devils who dive for him.' It may also be nominative by way of inception (ibtida'), with "lahu" (for him) being the predicate (khabar)."

The third issue: it is possible that those among them who dived are the same ones who did all the other works, and it is possible that they were a separate group, all of them being included in the word "man" (those who). The first, however, is closer.

The fourth issue: the outward meaning says only that He subjected them to him. However, it has been narrated that He, exalted is He, subjected their disbelievers and not the believers, and this is closer for two reasons:
One of them: the unrestricted use of the word "devils".
The second: His saying, ﴿And We were guardians over them﴾, for a believer, when subjected to a task, does not need to be guarded lest he corrupt it; guarding is required only for the disbeliever.

The fifth issue: concerning His saying, ﴿And We were guardians over them﴾, there are several explanations:
The first: He, exalted is He, appointed over them a group of angels, or a group of believing jinn.
The second: Allah, exalted is He, subjected them by making His obedience beloved to them and making them fear disobedience to Him.
The third: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "It means that His authority remains over them, and He does to them what He wills."
If it is said: "From what were they guarded?" We say: there are three possibilities:
The first: He, exalted is He, was guarding them for him, lest they flee and leave him.
The second: al-Kalbi said: He was guarding them from stirring up anyone during his time.
The third: He was guarding them from corrupting what they had made, for their habit was to work by day and then corrupt it at night.

The sixth issue: al-Jubba'i asked himself and said: "How could these works come about for them, when their bodies are subtle and they cannot perform heavy labour, and they can only whisper?" He answered that He, glory be to Him, made their bodies dense specifically and strengthened them and increased their size, so that this would be a miracle for Solomon, peace be upon him. When Solomon died, Allah returned them to their original creation, because if He had left them in the second creation, it would have become a confusion for people, and if a pretender to prophethood had claimed prophethood and made it a proof, it would have been like the miracles of the messengers. Therefore He returned them to their original creation.
Know that this speech is invalid for several reasons:
The first: Why do you say that the jinn are bodies? Why is it not possible that there exists a created thing that is neither spatially located (mutahayyiz) nor subsisting in something spatially located, and the jinn are among such things? If you say: "If the matter were so, they would be a likeness to the Creator, exalted is He," I say: this is weak, because sharing in positive necessary attributes does not indicate sharing in what they necessitate, so how much less does sharing in negative attributes.
Granted that they are bodies, yet it is not possible for the capacity for these arduous works to be present in a subtle body. His speech is based on the premise that structure (bunyah) is a condition, and in his hand there is only weak inductive reasoning.
Granted that there must be densifying of their bodies, why do you say that there must be their return to the original creation after the death of Solomon, peace be upon him? If he says: "So that it does not lead to deception (talbis)," we say: deception does not necessarily follow, because if a pretender makes that a miracle for himself, the claimant may say: "Why is it not possible to say that the strength of their bodies was a miracle of another prophet before you?" And with the existence of this possibility, the pretender cannot use it as evidence.

Know that the bodies of this world are either dense or subtle. As for the dense, the densest bodies are stones and iron, and Allah, exalted is He, made both of them a miracle for David, peace be upon him: He made the stone speak and softened the iron. Each of them, just as it indicates monotheism and prophethood, indicates the validity of resurrection (hashr), for since He was able to bring stones to life, what is the distance in bringing bones that have decayed back to life? And since He was able to place in the finger of David, peace be upon him, the power of fire while the finger is extremely subtle, what is the distance in making dry earth into a living animal body?
The subtlest things in this world are air and fire, and Allah made both of them a miracle for Solomon, peace be upon him. As for air, it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We subjected the wind to him﴾ [Sad: 36]. As for fire, it is because the devils were created from it, and Allah, exalted is He, subjected them, so he would command them to dive into the waters, while fire is extinguished by water, yet this did not harm them. This indicates His power to bring forth the opposite from its opposite.

[Page 172]

The third question: If you have established that their disagreement could have been due to an explicit text (nass), and could have been due to ijtihad (independent legal reasoning), then which of the two opinions is more likely? The answer: ijtihad is more likely, for several reasons.

The first: many reports state that Dawud, peace be upon him, had not yet issued his ruling in the matter until he heard from Sulayman that another ruling was better. In some reports, Dawud, peace be upon him, adjured him to state what he had. None of this fits with an explicit text, for if it had been an explicit text, he would have made it known and would not have concealed it.

The fourth question: Explain how ijtihad was carried out. The answer: the basis of the ijtihad in it is what Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, mentioned, that Dawud, peace be upon him, assessed the value of the damage to the vineyard, and it equalled the value of the sheep. He therefore judged that the required compensation for that damage was to be removed by an equivalent benefit, so he handed the sheep over to the injured party. This is like what Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, said about a slave who causes a death: his owner must either surrender him or ransom him. As for Sulayman, peace be upon him, his ijtihad led him to hold that principal property should be matched against principal property and accessory gains against accessory gains. Matching principal property against accessory gains is not permitted, for it entails injustice and oppression. Perhaps the benefits of the sheep in that year were equal to the benefits of the vineyard, so he ruled accordingly. This is like what al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said about one who usurps a slave who then escapes from his hand: he must pay the value, so that the one from whom it was usurped may benefit from it in return for the benefits of the slave which the usurper deprived him of. When the slave is found, they both return what they took.

The fifth question: Assuming it is established with certainty that that disagreement was based on ijtihad, does this story indicate that only one is correct (al-musib wahid), or that all are correct (al-kull musibun)?

The answer: As for those who hold that only one is correct, some of them argued with the words of the Exalted: ﴿So We gave Sulayman the understanding of it﴾. They said: If all were correct, singling out Sulayman, peace be upon him, for this understanding would serve no purpose. As for those who hold that all are correct, some of them argued with His words: ﴿And to each We gave judgement and knowledge﴾. They said: If only one were correct and his opponent in error, it would not be proper to say: ﴿And to each We gave judgement and knowledge﴾. Know that both arguments are weak.

As for the first: Allah, the Exalted, did not say that He gave him the correct understanding. It is possible that He gave him the abrogating ruling (al-nasikh) which had not reached Dawud, peace be upon him. Each of them was correct in what he judged. Moreover, the most that the verse indicates is that Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them both, were not both correct, and that does not necessitate that the matter is the same in our law.

As for the second: He, the Exalted, did not say that to each We gave judgement and knowledge of what he ruled. Rather, it is possible that He gave each of them judgement and knowledge of the methods of ijtihad and the ways of deriving rulings. Furthermore, it does not follow that because every mujtahid was correct in their law, the matter is the same in our law.

* * *

The sixth question: If this incident had occurred in our law, what would its ruling be? The answer: al-Hasan al-Basri said: This verse is muhkam (clear and not abrogated), and judges judge by it until the Day of Resurrection. Know that many scholars claim it has been abrogated by ijma' (scholarly consensus). Then they differed about its ruling. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: If it happened by day, there is no liability, because the owner of livestock may let his livestock graze by day, and the guarding of the crops by day falls on their owner. If it happened by night, liability is required, because guarding them at night falls on him. Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, said: There is no liability on him, whether by night or by day, if he did not transgress by releasing them. This is based on his, peace be upon him, saying: "The wound caused by an animal is unpunishable." Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, relied on what was narrated from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, who said: "A she-camel that was in the habit of trespassing entered an orchard and damaged it. The people mentioned that to the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, and he ruled that guarding orchards by day is the responsibility of their owners, and guarding livestock by night is the responsibility of their owners, and that the owners of livestock are responsible for what their livestock damage by night." This completes the discussion on this verse.

* * *

Then Allah, the Exalted, mentioned after that two of the blessings with which He favoured Dawud, peace be upon him:

The first: His words, the Exalted: ﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify [Us] along with Dawud, and the birds, and We were ever doing [that]﴾. In it there are issues.

[Page 173]

Issue one: Regarding the interpretation of this glorification, there are two views.

One of them: that the mountains did glorify [Allah]. Then they mentioned several interpretations:

First: Muqatil said: When Dawud, peace be upon him, remembered his Lord, the mountains and the birds remembered their Lord along with him.

Second: al-Kalbi said: When Dawud glorified [Allah], the mountains answered him.

Third: Sulayman ibn Hayyan said: When Dawud, peace be upon him, felt a slackening, Allah, the Exalted, commanded the mountains, and they glorified [Allah], and he grew in vigour and yearning.

The second view, which is the choice of some of the scholars of meanings (ashab al-ma'ani): It is possible that the glorification of the mountains and birds is like His words: ﴿And there is not a thing but glorifies Him with His praise﴾ [al-Isra' 17:44]. Dawud, peace be upon him, was singled out for this because he, peace be upon him, knew this by necessity, and thus his certainty and reverence increased. The first view is closer to the truth, because there is no necessity to turn the wording away from its apparent meaning.

As for the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist theological school), they said: If speech came from the mountain, it would come either by its own act or by Allah's act in it. The first is impossible, because the structure of a mountain cannot bear life, knowledge, and power, and whatever is not living, knowing, and powerful cannot perform an act. The second is also impossible, because the speaker, in their view, is one who produces speech, not one in whom speech occurs. So if the one who produces that speech were Allah, the Exalted, then the speaker would be Allah, the Exalted, not the mountain. Thus it is established that it cannot be taken according to its apparent meaning. At this point they said that in: ﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify [Us] along with Dawud﴾, and the similar verse: ﴿O mountains, echo with him﴾ [Saba' 34:10], the meaning is: move with him and travel at his command. And "yusabbihna" (glorify) derives from sabh, which is swimming, and the wording was used in the intensive form. Had it not intended intensity, it would have been said "yasbahna". When it was intensified, it was said "yusabbihna ma'ahu", meaning: travel with him. This is like His words: ﴿Indeed, for you in the day is a long sabh﴾ [al-Muzzammil 73:7], meaning: movement and course of action. Having established this, we say: their movement is the glorification, because it indicates the power of Allah, the Exalted, and His transcendence above all that is ascribed to Him. Know that the basis of this view rests on the claim that the structure of a mountain does not accept life, and this is disputed; and on the claim that speech is an act of Allah, which is also disputed.

Issue two: As for the birds, there is no impossibility that speech should come from them. However, the community (ummah) has agreed that the mukallafun (those bound by legal obligation) are either jinn, humans, or angels. It is therefore impossible for birds to reach the level of intellect required for obligation. Rather, they are in a state like that of a child, in that they can be commanded and forbidden, though they are not obligated. This became a miracle, in that He made them in understanding like an adolescent. Moreover, it is also an indication of the power of Allah, the Exalted, and of His transcendence above what is not permissible. So the discussion regarding them is like the discussion regarding the mountains.

Issue three: The author of al-Kashshaf said: "yusabbihna" is a circumstantial clause (hal) in the sense of "musabbihat" (glorifying), or it is a new statement (isti'naf), as if someone asked: "How did He subject them?" and it was answered: "They glorify." "Wal-tayr" (and the birds) is either conjoined to "al-jibal" (the mountains) or is an object "ma'ahu" (with him). If you ask: Why were the mountains mentioned before the birds? I say: Because their subjugation and their glorification is more wondrous, more indicative of power, and more compelling as a miracle, since they are inanimate, whereas the birds are living, speaking beings.

As for His words: ﴿And We were ever doing [that]﴾, the meaning is: We are able to do this, even though it is a wonder in your eyes. It was also said: We do that for the prophets, peace be upon them.

The second blessing: His words, the Exalted: ﴿And We taught him the making of chainmail for you, to protect you from your violence. Then, are you grateful?﴾ In it there are issues.

Issue one: al-libas (lubus) means clothing. [A poet] said: "Wear for every situation its garment."

Issue two: "Li-tuhsinakum" has been read with the letter nun, the letter ya', and the letter ta', and with the sad both light and doubled. The nun refers to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The ta' refers to the craft or to the chainmail, understood as the coat of mail. The ya' refers to Allah, the Exalted, or to Dawud, or to the chainmail.
