As for Sulayman, peace be upon him, his ijtihad led him to hold that principal property should be matched against principal property and accessory gains against accessory gains. Matching principal property against accessory gains is not permitted, for it entails injustice and oppression. Perhaps the benefits of the sheep in that year were equal to the benefits of the vineyard, so he ruled accordingly. This is like what al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said about one who usurps a slave who then escapes from his hand: he must pay the value, so that the one from whom it was usurped may benefit from it in return for the benefits of the slave which the usurper deprived him of. When the slave is found, they both return what they took.

The fifth question: Assuming it is established with certainty that that disagreement was based on ijtihad, does this story indicate that only one is correct (al-musib wahid), or that all are correct (al-kull musibun)?

The answer: As for those who hold that only one is correct, some of them argued with the words of the Exalted: ﴿So We gave Sulayman the understanding of it﴾. They said: If all were correct, singling out Sulayman, peace be upon him, for this understanding would serve no purpose. As for those who hold that all are correct, some of them argued with His words: ﴿And to each We gave judgement and knowledge﴾. They said: If only one were correct and his opponent in error, it would not be proper to say: ﴿And to each We gave judgement and knowledge﴾. Know that both arguments are weak.

As for the first: Allah, the Exalted, did not say that He gave him the correct understanding. It is possible that He gave him the abrogating ruling (al-nasikh) which had not reached Dawud, peace be upon him. Each of them was correct in what he judged. Moreover, the most that the verse indicates is that Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them both, were not both correct, and that does not necessitate that the matter is the same in our law.

As for the second: He, the Exalted, did not say that to each We gave judgement and knowledge of what he ruled. Rather, it is possible that He gave each of them judgement and knowledge of the methods of ijtihad and the ways of deriving rulings. Furthermore, it does not follow that because every mujtahid was correct in their law, the matter is the same in our law.

* * *

The sixth question: If this incident had occurred in our law, what would its ruling be? The answer: al-Hasan al-Basri said: This verse is muhkam (clear and not abrogated), and judges judge by it until the Day of Resurrection. Know that many scholars claim it has been abrogated by ijma' (scholarly consensus). Then they differed about its ruling. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: If it happened by day, there is no liability, because the owner of livestock may let his livestock graze by day, and the guarding of the crops by day falls on their owner. If it happened by night, liability is required, because guarding them at night falls on him. Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, said: There is no liability on him, whether by night or by day, if he did not transgress by releasing them. This is based on his, peace be upon him, saying: "The wound caused by an animal is unpunishable." Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, relied on what was narrated from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, who said: "A she-camel that was in the habit of trespassing entered an orchard and damaged it. The people mentioned that to the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, and he ruled that guarding orchards by day is the responsibility of their owners, and guarding livestock by night is the responsibility of their owners, and that the owners of livestock are responsible for what their livestock damage by night." This completes the discussion on this verse.

* * *

Then Allah, the Exalted, mentioned after that two of the blessings with which He favoured Dawud, peace be upon him:

The first: His words, the Exalted: ﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify [Us] along with Dawud, and the birds, and We were ever doing [that]﴾. In it there are issues.

[Page 173]

Issue one: Regarding the interpretation of this glorification, there are two views.

One of them: that the mountains did glorify [Allah]. Then they mentioned several interpretations:

First: Muqatil said: When Dawud, peace be upon him, remembered his Lord, the mountains and the birds remembered their Lord along with him.

Second: al-Kalbi said: When Dawud glorified [Allah], the mountains answered him.

Third: Sulayman ibn Hayyan said: When Dawud, peace be upon him, felt a slackening, Allah, the Exalted, commanded the mountains, and they glorified [Allah], and he grew in vigour and yearning.

The second view, which is the choice of some of the scholars of meanings (ashab al-ma'ani): It is possible that the glorification of the mountains and birds is like His words: ﴿And there is not a thing but glorifies Him with His praise﴾ [al-Isra' 17:44]. Dawud, peace be upon him, was singled out for this because he, peace be upon him, knew this by necessity, and thus his certainty and reverence increased. The first view is closer to the truth, because there is no necessity to turn the wording away from its apparent meaning.

As for the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist theological school), they said: If speech came from the mountain, it would come either by its own act or by Allah's act in it. The first is impossible, because the structure of a mountain cannot bear life, knowledge, and power, and whatever is not living, knowing, and powerful cannot perform an act. The second is also impossible, because the speaker, in their view, is one who produces speech, not one in whom speech occurs. So if the one who produces that speech were Allah, the Exalted, then the speaker would be Allah, the Exalted, not the mountain. Thus it is established that it cannot be taken according to its apparent meaning. At this point they said that in: ﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify [Us] along with Dawud﴾, and the similar verse: ﴿O mountains, echo with him﴾ [Saba' 34:10], the meaning is: move with him and travel at his command. And "yusabbihna" (glorify) derives from sabh, which is swimming, and the wording was used in the intensive form. Had it not intended intensity, it would have been said "yasbahna". When it was intensified, it was said "yusabbihna ma'ahu", meaning: travel with him. This is like His words: ﴿Indeed, for you in the day is a long sabh﴾ [al-Muzzammil 73:7], meaning: movement and course of action. Having established this, we say: their movement is the glorification, because it indicates the power of Allah, the Exalted, and His transcendence above all that is ascribed to Him. Know that the basis of this view rests on the claim that the structure of a mountain does not accept life, and this is disputed; and on the claim that speech is an act of Allah, which is also disputed.

Issue two: As for the birds, there is no impossibility that speech should come from them. However, the community (ummah) has agreed that the mukallafun (those bound by legal obligation) are either jinn, humans, or angels. It is therefore impossible for birds to reach the level of intellect required for obligation. Rather, they are in a state like that of a child, in that they can be commanded and forbidden, though they are not obligated. This became a miracle, in that He made them in understanding like an adolescent. Moreover, it is also an indication of the power of Allah, the Exalted, and of His transcendence above what is not permissible. So the discussion regarding them is like the discussion regarding the mountains.

Issue three: The author of al-Kashshaf said: "yusabbihna" is a circumstantial clause (hal) in the sense of "musabbihat" (glorifying), or it is a new statement (isti'naf), as if someone asked: "How did He subject them?" and it was answered: "They glorify." "Wal-tayr" (and the birds) is either conjoined to "al-jibal" (the mountains) or is an object "ma'ahu" (with him). If you ask: Why were the mountains mentioned before the birds? I say: Because their subjugation and their glorification is more wondrous, more indicative of power, and more compelling as a miracle, since they are inanimate, whereas the birds are living, speaking beings.

As for His words: ﴿And We were ever doing [that]﴾, the meaning is: We are able to do this, even though it is a wonder in your eyes. It was also said: We do that for the prophets, peace be upon them.

The second blessing: His words, the Exalted: ﴿And We taught him the making of chainmail for you, to protect you from your violence. Then, are you grateful?﴾ In it there are issues.

Issue one: al-libas (lubus) means clothing. [A poet] said: "Wear for every situation its garment."

Issue two: "Li-tuhsinakum" has been read with the letter nun, the letter ya', and the letter ta', and with the sad both light and doubled. The nun refers to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The ta' refers to the craft or to the chainmail, understood as the coat of mail. The ya' refers to Allah, the Exalted, or to Dawud, or to the chainmail.

[Page 174]

Issue three: Qatadah said: The first to make the coat of mail was Dawud, peace be upon him. Before him they were plates; he was the first to interlace them and make them into rings. al-Hasan mentioned that Luqman the Wise, peace be upon him, was present when he was making the coat of mail. Luqman wished to ask about what he was doing, but he kept silent until he finished it and wore it himself. Then he said: "Silence is wisdom, but few practise it." They said: Allah, the Exalted, softened the iron for him, so he worked it without fire, as if it were clay.

Issue four: Here "al-ba's" means war, although it can apply to all kinds of harm. The meaning is: to prevent and guard you from your violence, that is, from wounding, killing, the sword, the arrow, and the spear.

Issue five: This indicates that the first to make the coat of mail was Dawud, and then people learned it from him. People inherited it from him, and the blessing thereby encompassed every fighter among creation until the end of time. Therefore they are obliged to thank Allah, the Exalted, for the blessing. So He said: ﴿Then, are you grateful?﴾, that is: Give thanks to Allah for what He has made easy for you of this craft. Know that when He, glorified is He, mentioned the blessings with which He favoured Dawud, He then mentioned the blessings with which He favoured Sulayman, peace be upon him. Qatadah said: Allah, the Exalted, made Sulayman inherit from Dawud his kingdom and his prophethood, and added to him two things: He subjected the wind and the devils to him.

The first blessing: His words, the Exalted: ﴿And to Sulayman [We subjected] the wind, violent, running by his command﴾. That is: We made it obedient and submissive to him, in the sense that if he willed it to be violent, it would be violent, and if he willed it to be gentle, it would be gentle, and Allah, the Exalted, subjected it in both states. If it is said: "al-'asif" means the one of severe blowing, yet Allah, the Exalted, described it as gentle in His words: ﴿Gentle, wherever he directed it﴾ [Sad 38:36]. How then can the two be combined? The answer is in two ways:

First: In itself it was gentle and pleasant, like a breeze. When it passed by his throne, it carried him far in a short time, as He said: ﴿Its morning course was a month's journey, and its evening course a month's journey﴾ [Saba' 34:12]. It combined the two: gentleness in its own nature, and violence in its action, together with its obedience to Sulayman, peace be upon him. Its blowing followed what he willed and decreed, sign after sign, and miracle after miracle.

Second: It was gentle at one time and violent at another, depending on its blowing according to his will.

Issue six: "al-Rih" and "al-Riyah" have been read in both the nominative and accusative in both forms. The nominative is on the basis of the subject (ibtida'), and the accusative is by conjunction with "al-jibal" (the mountains). If it is said: He said regarding Dawud: ﴿And We subjected the mountains along with Dawud﴾, and regarding Sulayman: ﴿And to Sulayman the wind﴾, mentioning it for Dawud with the word "ma'a" (with) and for Sulayman with the preposition "li-" (to). He also observed this order in His words: ﴿O mountains, echo with him and the birds﴾ [Saba' 34:10], and He said: ﴿So We subjected to him the wind, running by his command﴾ [Sad 38:36]. What is the point of singling out Dawud with the word "ma'a" and Sulayman with "li-"? We say: It is possible that because the mountain was occupied with glorification, it attained a kind of honour, so what is attributed to it is attributed with the preposition of ownership (lam al-tamlik). As for the wind, nothing proceeded from it except what functions as service, so for this reason it is attributed to Sulayman with the preposition of ownership. This is my persuasive view.

* * *

As for His words: ﴿To the land which We had blessed for the worlds﴾, that is: to proceeding to Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). al-Kalbi said: It would travel from Istakhr to Syria, with Sulayman and his companions riding upon it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 21, verses 79–82 (part 2 of 2):

As for His saying, ﴿And We were Knowers of all things﴾, meaning: because of Our knowledge of things, it was valid for Us to arrange this arrangement among Our messengers, and in Our creation, and to perform these overpowering miracles.

The second favour: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And of the devils were those who dived for him and did other work than that. And We were guardians over them﴾. There are several issues concerning it.

The first issue: the meaning is that they dived for him in the seas and extracted pearls, and went beyond that to crafts and trades, the building of cities and palaces, and the invention of wondrous industries, as He said: ﴿They made for him whatever he willed: sanctuaries, statues, and basins﴾ [Saba': 13]. As for the industries, they include the making of baths, depilatory lime, mills, glass vessels and soap.

The second issue: His saying, ﴿And of the devils were those who dived for him﴾, means: "And We subjected to Solomon from among the devils those who dived for him." Thus it is in the position of the accusative (nasb, the grammatical case of the object) in coordination with "the wind". Al-Zajjaj said: "It may also be in the position of the nominative (raf', the grammatical case of the subject) in two ways:
One of them: coordination with "the wind", so that the meaning is: 'And for Solomon is the wind, and for him are those devils who dive for him.' It may also be nominative by way of inception (ibtida'), with "lahu" (for him) being the predicate (khabar)."

The third issue: it is possible that those among them who dived are the same ones who did all the other works, and it is possible that they were a separate group, all of them being included in the word "man" (those who). The first, however, is closer.

The fourth issue: the outward meaning says only that He subjected them to him. However, it has been narrated that He, exalted is He, subjected their disbelievers and not the believers, and this is closer for two reasons:
One of them: the unrestricted use of the word "devils".
The second: His saying, ﴿And We were guardians over them﴾, for a believer, when subjected to a task, does not need to be guarded lest he corrupt it; guarding is required only for the disbeliever.

The fifth issue: concerning His saying, ﴿And We were guardians over them﴾, there are several explanations:
The first: He, exalted is He, appointed over them a group of angels, or a group of believing jinn.
The second: Allah, exalted is He, subjected them by making His obedience beloved to them and making them fear disobedience to Him.
The third: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "It means that His authority remains over them, and He does to them what He wills."
If it is said: "From what were they guarded?" We say: there are three possibilities:
The first: He, exalted is He, was guarding them for him, lest they flee and leave him.
The second: al-Kalbi said: He was guarding them from stirring up anyone during his time.
The third: He was guarding them from corrupting what they had made, for their habit was to work by day and then corrupt it at night.

The sixth issue: al-Jubba'i asked himself and said: "How could these works come about for them, when their bodies are subtle and they cannot perform heavy labour, and they can only whisper?" He answered that He, glory be to Him, made their bodies dense specifically and strengthened them and increased their size, so that this would be a miracle for Solomon, peace be upon him. When Solomon died, Allah returned them to their original creation, because if He had left them in the second creation, it would have become a confusion for people, and if a pretender to prophethood had claimed prophethood and made it a proof, it would have been like the miracles of the messengers. Therefore He returned them to their original creation.
Know that this speech is invalid for several reasons:
The first: Why do you say that the jinn are bodies? Why is it not possible that there exists a created thing that is neither spatially located (mutahayyiz) nor subsisting in something spatially located, and the jinn are among such things? If you say: "If the matter were so, they would be a likeness to the Creator, exalted is He," I say: this is weak, because sharing in positive necessary attributes does not indicate sharing in what they necessitate, so how much less does sharing in negative attributes.
Granted that they are bodies, yet it is not possible for the capacity for these arduous works to be present in a subtle body. His speech is based on the premise that structure (bunyah) is a condition, and in his hand there is only weak inductive reasoning.
Granted that there must be densifying of their bodies, why do you say that there must be their return to the original creation after the death of Solomon, peace be upon him? If he says: "So that it does not lead to deception (talbis)," we say: deception does not necessarily follow, because if a pretender makes that a miracle for himself, the claimant may say: "Why is it not possible to say that the strength of their bodies was a miracle of another prophet before you?" And with the existence of this possibility, the pretender cannot use it as evidence.

Know that the bodies of this world are either dense or subtle. As for the dense, the densest bodies are stones and iron, and Allah, exalted is He, made both of them a miracle for David, peace be upon him: He made the stone speak and softened the iron. Each of them, just as it indicates monotheism and prophethood, indicates the validity of resurrection (hashr), for since He was able to bring stones to life, what is the distance in bringing bones that have decayed back to life? And since He was able to place in the finger of David, peace be upon him, the power of fire while the finger is extremely subtle, what is the distance in making dry earth into a living animal body?
The subtlest things in this world are air and fire, and Allah made both of them a miracle for Solomon, peace be upon him. As for air, it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We subjected the wind to him﴾ [Sad: 36]. As for fire, it is because the devils were created from it, and Allah, exalted is He, subjected them, so he would command them to dive into the waters, while fire is extinguished by water, yet this did not harm them. This indicates His power to bring forth the opposite from its opposite.

[Page 172]

The third question: If you have established that their disagreement could have been due to an explicit text (nass), and could have been due to ijtihad (independent legal reasoning), then which of the two opinions is more likely? The answer: ijtihad is more likely, for several reasons.

The first: many reports state that Dawud, peace be upon him, had not yet issued his ruling in the matter until he heard from Sulayman that another ruling was better. In some reports, Dawud, peace be upon him, adjured him to state what he had. None of this fits with an explicit text, for if it had been an explicit text, he would have made it known and would not have concealed it.
