Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 21, verses 87–88 (part 1 of 2):

[The Eighth Story: the story of Yunus (peace be upon him)]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Dhu'l-Nun, when he went off in anger, thinking that We would not decree against him; so he called out in the darknesses, "There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been among the wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿So We answered him and delivered him from distress, and thus do We deliver the believers.﴾ Know that here there are several issues:

The first issue: There is no disagreement that Dhu'l-Nun is Yunus (peace be upon him), because al-Nun is the fish (al-samakah). We have mentioned that when a name lies between being a purely epithetic designation (laqab mahd) and being meaningful, it is more appropriate to take it as meaningful, especially when the benefit that suits that description is known.

The second issue: They differed over whether his (peace be upon him) being in the belly of the fish occurred before he was occupied with conveying the message of God, exalted is He, or after it.

As for the first view: Ibn Abbas (may God be pleased with him) said: Yunus (peace be upon him) and his people lived in Filastin (Palestine). A king attacked them and took captive nine and a half tribes, and two and a half tribes remained. God, exalted is He, revealed to Shu'ayb the Prophet (peace be upon him) that he should go to Hizqil the king and say to him: "Until he appoints a strong, trustworthy prophet, for I will cast into the hearts of those people that they send Bani Isra'il with him." The king said to him: "Whom do you see?" In his kingdom there were five prophets. He said: "Yunus ibn Matta, for he is strong and trustworthy." The king summoned Yunus and ordered him to go forth. Yunus said: "Has God commanded you to expel me?" He said: "No." He said: "Has He named me to you?" He said: "No." He said: "There are other prophets besides me here." They pressed him, so he went forth in anger at the king and his people. He came to the Sea of the Romans and found a people who had prepared a ship, so he boarded with them. When the ship was tossed by the waves and tilted with them, and they nearly drowned, the sailors said: "There is a disobedient man here, or a runaway slave, for a ship does not do this without wind unless there is a disobedient man in it. It is our custom that when we are afflicted with such a calamity, we cast lots, and whoever the lot falls upon, we throw into the sea; for one man drowning is better than the ship sinking." They cast lots three times, and the lot fell each time upon Yunus (peace be upon him). He said: "I am the disobedient man and the runaway slave," and he threw himself into the sea. A whale came and swallowed him. God, exalted is He, revealed to the whale: "Do not harm a single hair of him, for I have made your belly a prison for him, and I did not make him food for you." Then, when God, exalted is He, delivered him from the belly of the whale, He cast him out onto the open ground like a plucked fledgling, with no hair or skin upon him. God caused a gourd plant to grow over him, under which he sheltered and ate of its fruit until he grew strong. When the plant dried up, Yunus (peace be upon him) grieved over it. It was said to him: "Do you grieve over a plant, yet you did not grieve over a hundred thousand or more, since you did not go to them and did not seek their comfort?" Then God revealed to him and commanded him to go to them. Yunus (peace be upon him) set out toward them until he entered their land, and they were not far from him. Yunus (peace be upon him) came to them and said to their king: "God, exalted is He, has sent me to you so that you may send Bani Isra'il with me." They said: "We do not know what you are saying. Had we known that you were truthful, we would have done it. We came to you in your homes and took you captive, so if what you say were true, God would have protected you from us." He circulated among them for three days, calling them to this, but they refused him. God, exalted is He, revealed to him: "Say to them: If you do not believe, the punishment will come upon you." He conveyed this to them, but they refused. He left from among them, and when they lost him, they regretted their action. They set out seeking him but could not find him. Then they mentioned their matter and Yunus's matter to the scholars who were in their religion, and they said: "Look and seek him in the city; if he is in it, then nothing of what he mentioned about the descent of the punishment will happen; and if he has gone out, then it is as he said." They sought him, and it was said to them: "He went out in the evening." When they despaired, they closed the gate of their city, so their cattle and their sheep did not enter, and they separated the mothers from their young, and likewise the children and the mothers. Then they stood waiting for dawn. When the dawn broke, they saw the punishment descending from the sky. They tore their collars, the pregnant women delivered what was in their bellies, the children cried out, and the sheep and cattle bellowed. God, exalted is He, then lifted the punishment from them.

[Page 185]

They sent to Yunus (peace be upon him), and they believed in him, and they sent Bani Isra'il with him. According to this view, Yunus's prophetic mission was after he was cast out by the whale. The evidence for this view is the saying of God, exalted is He, in Surat al-Saffat: ﴿So We cast him onto the open ground while he was ailing﴾ ﴿and We caused a gourd plant to grow over him﴾ ﴿and We sent him to a hundred thousand or more﴾ [al-Saffat: 145].

There is another narration in this view, namely that Jibril (peace be upon him) said to Yunus (peace be upon him): "Go to the people of Nineveh and warn them that the punishment has drawn near to them." Yunus (peace be upon him) said: "Shall I seek an animal (to ride)?" He said: "The matter is more urgent than that." So he became angry and set out to the ship, and the rest of the story is as has passed until the whale swallowed him, and he went on until he reached Nineveh, and there it threw him up.

As for the second view: that the story of the whale occurred after his calling the people of Nineveh and conveying God's message to them. They said: When they did not believe, he threatened them with the punishment; then, when the punishment was removed from them after he had threatened them with it, he went out from among them in anger. Then they mentioned several matters concerning the cause of his departure and his anger:

First: that he felt shy to be among a people who had tested him as a liar.

Second: that it was their custom to kill the liar.

Third: that he was seized by pride.

Fourth: because the punishment did not descend upon those people.

Most scholars hold that the story of the whale and Yunus's departure in anger occurred after God had sent him to them, and after the punishment had been lifted from them.

* * *

The third issue: Those who argue for the permissibility of sin on the prophets (peace be upon them) have adduced this verse in several ways:

First: most exegetes hold that Yunus went off in anger at his Lord. It is said this is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Wahb, and the choice of Ibn Qutaybah and Muhammad ibn Jarir. If that is so, it follows that his anger toward God, exalted is He, is among the greatest sins. Furthermore, even on the supposition that this anger was not directed at God, exalted is He, but at that king or at the people, it too would be forbidden, because God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So be patient for the judgment of your Lord, and do not be like the companion of the whale﴾ [al-Qalam: 48], and this indicates that that act of Yunus was forbidden.

Second: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿thinking that We would not decree against him﴾, and this indicates that he doubted the power of God, exalted is He.

Third: His saying: ﴿indeed I have been among the wrongdoers﴾, and wrongdoing is among the names of blame, according to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Surely the curse of God is upon the wrongdoers﴾ [Hud: 18].

Fourth: If no sin had proceeded from him, why did God punish him by casting him into the belly of the whale?

Fifth: His saying, exalted is He, in another verse: ﴿So the whale swallowed him while he was blameworthy﴾ [al-Saffat: 142], and the one who is blameworthy is one deserving of blame, and whoever is so is a sinner.

Sixth: His saying: ﴿and do not be like the companion of the whale﴾. If the companion of the whale was not sinful, the prohibition against resembling him would not be proper; and if he was sinful, the purpose has been achieved.

Seventh: that He said: ﴿and do not be like the companion of the whale﴾ and He said: ﴿so be patient as the steadfast messengers were patient﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35]; it follows that Yunus was not among the steadfast messengers (ulu al-'azm). Moses was among the steadfast messengers, and then (the Prophet ﷺ) said about him: "If Ibn Imran were alive, he would have had no choice but to follow me," and he said about Yunus: "Do not prefer me over Yunus ibn Matta." This is outside the explanation of the verse. As for the answer to the first point: there is no mention in the verse of who angered him, but we affirm that it is not permissible for a prophet of God to be angry with his Lord, for that is the attribute of one who is ignorant that God is the owner of command and prohibition, and one ignorant of God is not a believer, let alone a prophet. As for what is narrated, that he went out angry over a matter concerning the postponement of his mission and the taking of a supererogatory matter, this is among the matters from which the rank of the prophets (peace be upon them) is elevated; for when God commands them to do something, it is not permissible for them to oppose it, according to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when God and His Messenger have decided a matter, to have any choice in their affair﴾ [al-Ahzab: 36], and His saying: ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge in what is disputed between them, then they find within themselves no discomfort at what you have decided﴾ [al-Nisa': 65]. If there was opposition in the postponement, it is not permissible for that to occur from them. And when it is established that this anger cannot be attributed to God, exalted is He, it must be that he went out angry at other than God. The usual pattern is that one is angry with the one who disobeys him in what he commands; so it may be his people, or the king, or both of them together. The meaning of his anger toward his people is that he angered them by leaving, because they feared the punishment would descend upon them at that time. Abu Sharaf read "mughdaban" (with a different vowelling).

As for the claim that the anger toward the people was also forbidden, because of His saying: ﴿and do not be like the companion of the whale﴾, we say: we do not concede that it was forbidden. God, exalted is He, commanded him to convey that message to them, and He did not command him to remain with them forever; the apparent sense of a command does not imply repetition. Therefore his leaving from among them was not disobedience. As for the anger, we do not concede that it was disobedience, because since he had not been forbidden from it before, he thought it permissible, inasmuch as he did it only in anger for God, exalted is He, out of zeal for His religion, and hatred of disbelief and its people. Rather, the better course for him would have been to endure and wait for permission from God, exalted is He, to migrate from them. For this reason God, exalted is He, said: ﴿and do not be like the companion of the whale,﴾ as if God, exalted is He, intended for Muhammad ﷺ the highest and most exalted ranks.

As for the answer to the second objection, namely the reliance on His saying: ﴿thinking that We would not decree against him﴾: we say that whoever thinks that God, exalted is He, is incapable is a disbeliever, and there is no disagreement that such a thing cannot be attributed to ordinary believers, so how could it be attributed to the prophets (peace be upon them)? Therefore there must be an interpretation, and there are several:

First: ﴿thinking that We would not decree against him﴾ means "We would not constrict him" (lan nudayyiqa 'alayhi). This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿God extends provision to whom He wills of His servants, and restricts it (yaqdiru)﴾ [al-Ankabut: 62], i.e., constricts; ﴿and whoever has his provision restricted (qudira 'alayhi rizquh)﴾ [al-Talaq: 7], i.e., constricted; ﴿but when He tries him and restricts his provision (faqadara 'alayhi rizqahu)﴾ [al-Fajr: 16], i.e., constricted. Its meaning is: that We would not constrict him.

Know that according to this interpretation the verse becomes a proof for us, because Yunus (peace be upon him) thought that he had the choice: if he wished he could remain, and if he wished he could leave, and that God, exalted is He, would not constrict him in his choice. Yet it was known that the good lay in delaying his departure. This statement from God, exalted is He, is an explanation of what serves as an excuse for him in the matter of his leaving, not as a deliberate intent to disobey; but because he thought that the matter of leaving was flexible, that one could advance or delay it, whereas the good lay otherwise.

Second: that this is a figure of speech (min bab al-tamthil), meaning: his state was depicted as the state of one who thought that We would not decree against him in leaving his people without waiting for God's command, exalted is He.

Third, the power (qudra) may be interpreted as decree (qadaa), so the meaning is: "he thought that We would not decree upon him with hardship." This is the view of Mujahid, Qatada, al-Dahhak, al-Kalbi, and it is related from al-Awfi on the authority of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both; it is also the preference of al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. Al-Zajjaj said: "naqdira" means "nuqaddira" (We would decree). It is said: "Allah decreed (qadara) the thing, a decree (qadran), and He ordained it (qaddarahu) with an ordainment (taqdiran)." So al-Qadr means at-Taqdir. Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz and al-Zuhri read "fa-zanna an lan nuqaddira alayhi" with a damma on the nun and shaddah, from at-taqdir. Ubayd ibn Umayr read it with shaddah in the passive voice, and Ya'qub read "yuqdaru alayhi" with the lightened form in the passive voice.

It is related that Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, entered upon Mu'awiya, may Allah be pleased with him, and Mu'awiya said: "The waves of the Qur'an struck me last night and I was drowned in them, and I found no deliverance for myself except through you." He said: "And what is it?" He said: "Does the Prophet of Allah think that Allah will not have power over him?" Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "This is from qadr (decree), not from qudra (power)."

Fourth: "an lan naqdira" means: "he thought that We would not act," because there is a relation between power and action, so it is not far-fetched to make one of them a metaphor for the other.

Fifth: it is an interrogative with the meaning of rebuke, its meaning being: "Did he think that We would not have power over him?" This is related from Ibn Zayd.

Sixth: according to the view of those who say that this incident occurred before the mission of Yunus, peace be upon him, this thought was present before the mission. It is not far-fetched, regarding those other than prophets and messengers, that this thought might occur to his mind through the whispering of Satan, and then he would repel it with proof and evidence.

As for the answer to the third objection, which is the reliance on His saying: ﴿Indeed, I was of the wrongdoers﴾, we say: if we take it to refer to what preceded prophethood, then there is no discussion; and if we take it to refer to what followed it, then interpretation is necessary.

صفحة ١٨٧

For if we let it stand on its apparent meaning, it would necessarily follow that the Prophet deserved blame, and no Muslim says this. And since interpretation is necessary, we say: there is no doubt that he had left what is better while being able to attain what is better, and so that was a wrong.

As for the answer to the fourth objection: we do not grant that this was a punishment, since prophets cannot be punished; rather, what is meant is a trial (mihna). However, many commentators mention for every harm inflicted because of a sin that it is a punishment.

As for the answer to the fifth objection: the blame was because of leaving what is better.

* * *

The fourth issue: the author of al-Kashshaf said: "In the darknesses" means in the intense, dense darkness within the belly of the fish, as in His saying: ﴿Allah took away their light and left them in darknesses﴾ [al-Baqara: 17], and His saying: ﴿They bring them out from the light into the darknesses﴾ [al-Baqara: 257]. Some have considered different kinds of darkness: if the calling was at night, there is the darkness of the night, the sea, and the belly of the fish; and if it was in the day, the darkness of the fish's intestines is added to it. Or [it is said] that a fish swallowed the fish which was in its belly. Or [it is said] that when the fish dives deeply into the depths of the sea, the water above it becomes darkness upon darkness. As for the view of one who says that the fish which swallowed him dove into the seventh earth, if this is established by a report then there is no discussion; and if it is said for the sake of his call occurring in the darknesses, then what we have already mentioned suffices for that.

As for His saying: ﴿that there is no god but You﴾, the meaning is "that there is no god but You," or it is in the sense of "i.e.". It is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "No distressed person supplicates with this supplication except that it is answered for him." It is related from al-Hasan: "Allah did not save him except by his acknowledgment of his own wrongdoing."

As for His saying: ﴿Glory be to You﴾, it is a declaration of His transcendence above all deficiencies, including incapacity. This indicates that what he intended by His saying: ﴿and thought that We would not have power over him﴾ was not that he thought of incapacity. Rather, he said "Glory be to You" because its implication is: "Glory be to You that You would do that out of injustice, or a desire for vengeance, or incapacity to free me from this confinement; rather, You did it by right of divinity and in accordance with wisdom."

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, I was of the wrongdoers﴾, the meaning is: "I wronged myself by fleeing from my people without Your permission," as if he said: "I was of the wrongdoers, and I am now of the repentant regretful ones, so remove from me the trial." This is indicated by His saying: ﴿So We answered him﴾. There is another aspect to it: that he, peace be upon him, described Him with His saying: ﴿There is no god but You﴾ with perfection of lordship, and described himself with His saying: ﴿Indeed, I was of the wrongdoers﴾ with human weakness and shortcoming in fulfilling the right of lordship. This degree suffices in asking, as al-Mutanabbi said:

*"There are needs in the soul, and in You is discernment; my silence is speech in its presence, and address."*

Abdullah ibn Rafi', freedman of Umm Salama, related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "When Allah wished to confine Yunus, peace be upon him, He revealed to the fish: 'Take him, but do not scratch his flesh or break his bone.' So it took him and plunged with him to the bottom of the sea. Yunus, peace be upon him, heard a sound and said to himself: 'What is this?' Allah revealed to him: 'This is the glorification of the creatures of the sea.' He said: so he glorified, and the angels heard his glorification and said the same."

As for His saying: ﴿And We saved him from the distress﴾, meaning from his distress because of being in the belly of the fish and because of his error. Just as We saved Yunus, peace be upon him, from the affliction of confinement when he called upon Us: ﴿And thus do We save the believers﴾ from their affliction when they seek Our aid. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The supplication of Dhu'l-Nun in the belly of the fish: 'There is no god but You, glory be to You, indeed I was of the wrongdoers'; no Muslim servant has ever supplicated with it while in distress except that Allah answers his supplication."

The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Nunjī, nunajjī and najjā" have been read, and the nun is not assimilated into the jim. As for one who strained to make it correct by taking it as "fa'ala" and saying: "najjā" [with the verb being] "al-najā'" (the deliverance), and he made the yā' (ي) go and attributed it to its verbal noun, and put "al-mu'minīn" in the accusative by "al-najā'," he indulged in the coldest kind of strained interpretation.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 21, verses 87–88 (part 1 of 2):

[The Eighth Story: the story of Yunus (peace be upon him)]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Dhu'l-Nun, when he went off in anger, thinking that We would not decree against him; so he called out in the darknesses, "There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been among the wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿So We answered him and delivered him from distress, and thus do We deliver the believers.﴾ Know that here there are several issues:

The first issue: There is no disagreement that Dhu'l-Nun is Yunus (peace be upon him), because al-Nun is the fish (al-samakah). We have mentioned that when a name lies between being a purely epithetic designation (laqab mahd) and being meaningful, it is more appropriate to take it as meaningful, especially when the benefit that suits that description is known.

The second issue: They differed over whether his (peace be upon him) being in the belly of the fish occurred before he was occupied with conveying the message of God, exalted is He, or after it.

As for the first view: Ibn Abbas (may God be pleased with him) said: Yunus (peace be upon him) and his people lived in Filastin (Palestine). A king attacked them and took captive nine and a half tribes, and two and a half tribes remained. God, exalted is He, revealed to Shu'ayb the Prophet (peace be upon him) that he should go to Hizqil the king and say to him: "Until he appoints a strong, trustworthy prophet, for I will cast into the hearts of those people that they send Bani Isra'il with him." The king said to him: "Whom do you see?" In his kingdom there were five prophets. He said: "Yunus ibn Matta, for he is strong and trustworthy." The king summoned Yunus and ordered him to go forth. Yunus said: "Has God commanded you to expel me?" He said: "No." He said: "Has He named me to you?" He said: "No." He said: "There are other prophets besides me here." They pressed him, so he went forth in anger at the king and his people. He came to the Sea of the Romans and found a people who had prepared a ship, so he boarded with them. When the ship was tossed by the waves and tilted with them, and they nearly drowned, the sailors said: "There is a disobedient man here, or a runaway slave, for a ship does not do this without wind unless there is a disobedient man in it. It is our custom that when we are afflicted with such a calamity, we cast lots, and whoever the lot falls upon, we throw into the sea; for one man drowning is better than the ship sinking." They cast lots three times, and the lot fell each time upon Yunus (peace be upon him). He said: "I am the disobedient man and the runaway slave," and he threw himself into the sea. A whale came and swallowed him. God, exalted is He, revealed to the whale: "Do not harm a single hair of him, for I have made your belly a prison for him, and I did not make him food for you." Then, when God, exalted is He, delivered him from the belly of the whale, He cast him out onto the open ground like a plucked fledgling, with no hair or skin upon him. God caused a gourd plant to grow over him, under which he sheltered and ate of its fruit until he grew strong. When the plant dried up, Yunus (peace be upon him) grieved over it. It was said to him: "Do you grieve over a plant, yet you did not grieve over a hundred thousand or more, since you did not go to them and did not seek their comfort?" Then God revealed to him and commanded him to go to them. Yunus (peace be upon him) set out toward them until he entered their land, and they were not far from him. Yunus (peace be upon him) came to them and said to their king: "God, exalted is He, has sent me to you so that you may send Bani Isra'il with me." They said: "We do not know what you are saying. Had we known that you were truthful, we would have done it. We came to you in your homes and took you captive, so if what you say were true, God would have protected you from us." He circulated among them for three days, calling them to this, but they refused him. God, exalted is He, revealed to him: "Say to them: If you do not believe, the punishment will come upon you." He conveyed this to them, but they refused. He left from among them, and when they lost him, they regretted their action. They set out seeking him but could not find him. Then they mentioned their matter and Yunus's matter to the scholars who were in their religion, and they said: "Look and seek him in the city; if he is in it, then nothing of what he mentioned about the descent of the punishment will happen; and if he has gone out, then it is as he said." They sought him, and it was said to them: "He went out in the evening." When they despaired, they closed the gate of their city, so their cattle and their sheep did not enter, and they separated the mothers from their young, and likewise the children and the mothers. Then they stood waiting for dawn. When the dawn broke, they saw the punishment descending from the sky. They tore their collars, the pregnant women delivered what was in their bellies, the children cried out, and the sheep and cattle bellowed. God, exalted is He, then lifted the punishment from them.

[Page 185]

They sent to Yunus (peace be upon him), and they believed in him, and they sent Bani Isra'il with him. According to this view, Yunus's prophetic mission was after he was cast out by the whale. The evidence for this view is the saying of God, exalted is He, in Surat al-Saffat: ﴿So We cast him onto the open ground while he was ailing﴾ ﴿and We caused a gourd plant to grow over him﴾ ﴿and We sent him to a hundred thousand or more﴾ [al-Saffat: 145].

There is another narration in this view, namely that Jibril (peace be upon him) said to Yunus (peace be upon him): "Go to the people of Nineveh and warn them that the punishment has drawn near to them." Yunus (peace be upon him) said: "Shall I seek an animal (to ride)?" He said: "The matter is more urgent than that." So he became angry and set out to the ship, and the rest of the story is as has passed until the whale swallowed him, and he went on until he reached Nineveh, and there it threw him up.

As for the second view: that the story of the whale occurred after his calling the people of Nineveh and conveying God's message to them. They said: When they did not believe, he threatened them with the punishment; then, when the punishment was removed from them after he had threatened them with it, he went out from among them in anger. Then they mentioned several matters concerning the cause of his departure and his anger:

First: that he felt shy to be among a people who had tested him as a liar.

Second: that it was their custom to kill the liar.

Third: that he was seized by pride.

Fourth: because the punishment did not descend upon those people.

Most scholars hold that the story of the whale and Yunus's departure in anger occurred after God had sent him to them, and after the punishment had been lifted from them.

* * *

The third issue: Those who argue for the permissibility of sin on the prophets (peace be upon them) have adduced this verse in several ways:

First: most exegetes hold that Yunus went off in anger at his Lord. It is said this is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Wahb, and the choice of Ibn Qutaybah and Muhammad ibn Jarir. If that is so, it follows that his anger toward God, exalted is He, is among the greatest sins. Furthermore, even on the supposition that this anger was not directed at God, exalted is He, but at that king or at the people, it too would be forbidden, because God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So be patient for the judgment of your Lord, and do not be like the companion of the whale﴾ [al-Qalam: 48], and this indicates that that act of Yunus was forbidden.

Second: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿thinking that We would not decree against him﴾, and this indicates that he doubted the power of God, exalted is He.

Third: His saying: ﴿indeed I have been among the wrongdoers﴾, and wrongdoing is among the names of blame, according to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Surely the curse of God is upon the wrongdoers﴾ [Hud: 18].

Fourth: If no sin had proceeded from him, why did God punish him by casting him into the belly of the whale?

Fifth: His saying, exalted is He, in another verse: ﴿So the whale swallowed him while he was blameworthy﴾ [al-Saffat: 142], and the one who is blameworthy is one deserving of blame, and whoever is so is a sinner.

Sixth: His saying: ﴿and do not be like the companion of the whale﴾. If the companion of the whale was not sinful, the prohibition against resembling him would not be proper; and if he was sinful, the purpose has been achieved.

Seventh: that He said: ﴿and do not be like the companion of the whale﴾ and He said: ﴿so be patient as the steadfast messengers were patient﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35]; it follows that Yunus was not among the steadfast messengers (ulu al-'azm). The meaning of his anger toward his people is that he angered them by leaving, because they feared the punishment would descend upon them at that time. As for the claim that the anger toward the people was also forbidden, because of His saying: ﴿and do not be like the companion of the whale﴾, we say: we do not concede that it was forbidden. God, exalted is He, commanded him to convey that message to them, and He did not command him to remain with them forever; the apparent sense of a command does not imply repetition. Therefore his leaving from among them was not disobedience. As for the anger, we do not concede that it was disobedience, because since he had not been forbidden from it before, he thought it permissible, inasmuch as he did it only in anger for God, exalted is He, out of zeal for His religion, and hatred of disbelief and its people. The fourth issue: the author of al-Kashshaf said: "In the darknesses" means in the intense, dense darkness within the belly of the fish, as in His saying: ﴿Allah took away their light and left them in darknesses﴾ [al-Baqara: 17], and His saying: ﴿They bring them out from the light into the darknesses﴾ [al-Baqara: 257]. Some have considered different kinds of darkness: if the calling was at night, there is the darkness of the night, the sea, and the belly of the fish; and if it was in the day, the darkness of the fish's intestines is added to it. Or [it is said] that a fish swallowed the fish which was in its belly. Or [it is said] that when the fish dives deeply into the depths of the sea, the water above it becomes darkness upon darkness. As for the view of one who says that the fish which swallowed him dove into the seventh earth, if this is established by a report then there is no discussion; and if it is said for the sake of his call occurring in the darknesses, then what we have already mentioned suffices for that.

As for His saying: ﴿that there is no god but You﴾, the meaning is "that there is no god but You," or it is in the sense of "i.e.". It is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "No distressed person supplicates with this supplication except that it is answered for him." It is related from al-Hasan: "Allah did not save him except by his acknowledgment of his own wrongdoing."

As for His saying: ﴿Glory be to You﴾, it is a declaration of His transcendence above all deficiencies, including incapacity. This indicates that what he intended by His saying: ﴿and thought that We would not have power over him﴾ was not that he thought of incapacity. Rather, he said "Glory be to You" because its implication is: "Glory be to You that You would do that out of injustice, or a desire for vengeance, or incapacity to free me from this confinement; rather, You did it by right of divinity and in accordance with wisdom."

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, I was of the wrongdoers﴾, the meaning is: "I wronged myself by fleeing from my people without Your permission," as if he said: "I was of the wrongdoers, and I am now of the repentant regretful ones, so remove from me the trial." This is indicated by His saying: ﴿So We answered him﴾. There is another aspect to it: that he, peace be upon him, described Him with His saying: ﴿There is no god but You﴾ with perfection of lordship, and described himself with His saying: ﴿Indeed, I was of the wrongdoers﴾ with human weakness and shortcoming in fulfilling the right of lordship. This degree suffices in asking, as al-Mutanabbi said:

*"There are needs in the soul, and in You is discernment; my silence is speech in its presence, and address."*

Abdullah ibn Rafi', freedman of Umm Salama, related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "When Allah wished to confine Yunus, peace be upon him, He revealed to the fish: 'Take him, but do not scratch his flesh or break his bone.' So it took him and plunged with him to the bottom of the sea. Yunus, peace be upon him, heard a sound and said to himself: 'What is this?' Allah revealed to him: 'This is the glorification of the creatures of the sea.' He said: so he glorified, and the angels heard his glorification and said the same."

As for His saying: ﴿And We saved him from the distress﴾, meaning from his distress because of being in the belly of the fish and because of his error. Just as We saved Yunus, peace be upon him, from the affliction of confinement when he called upon Us: ﴿And thus do We save the believers﴾ from their affliction when they seek Our aid. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The supplication of Dhu'l-Nun in the belly of the fish: 'There is no god but You, glory be to You, indeed I was of the wrongdoers'; no Muslim servant has ever supplicated with it while in distress except that Allah answers his supplication."

The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Nunjī, nunajjī and najjā" have been read, and the nun is not assimilated into the jim. As for one who strained to make it correct by taking it as "fa'ala" and saying: "najjā" [with the verb being] "al-najā'" (the deliverance), and he made the yā' (ي) go and attributed it to its verbal noun, and put "al-mu'minīn" in the accusative by "al-najā'," he indulged in the coldest kind of strained interpretation.

[The Ninth Story: the story of Zakariyya (peace be upon him)]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Zakariyya, when he called out to his Lord, "My Lord, do not leave me alone (without an heir), and You are the best of inheritors."﴾ ﴿So We responded to him and gave him Yahya, and We made his wife fit for him. Indeed, they used to hasten to good deeds, and they called upon Us in hope and in fear, and they were humbly submissive to Us.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, explained Zakariyya's (peace be upon him) turning to his Lord, exalted is He, when harm touched him by his being alone, and he loved one who would be a companion to him and strengthen him in the affairs of his religion and his worldly life, and who would stand in his place after his death. So he called upon Allah, exalted is He, with the supplication of one who is sincere and knows that He is able to do that, even though his situation and that of his wife had reached the point of despair of that, by the ordinary course of things, because of old age and other factors. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: his age was a hundred, and his wife's age was ninety-nine.

As for His saying, ﴿and You are the best of inheritors﴾, there are two interpretations:

The first: he (peace be upon him) mentioned it within his supplication, in the manner of praise of his Lord, in order to reveal his knowledge that the final outcome of affairs belongs to Allah, exalted is He.

The second: it is as if he (peace be upon him) said: "If You do not grant me one who inherits from me, then I do not mind, for You are the best of inheritors."

* * *
As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So We responded to him﴾, meaning: We did what he wanted in answer to his request. In this there is a magnification of him; therefore the scholars say that responding (to supplication) is a reward, because of the honour it contains.
* * *
As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and We gave him Yahya﴾, it is like an explanation of the responding. Regarding His saying ﴿and We made his wife fit for him﴾, there are three opinions:

The first: He made her fit for childbearing by removing from her the impediment of custom, and this is the most fitting to the story.

The second: He made her good in her character, for she had been upon a manner of bad temper and sharp tongue that hurt him, and He counted that among His favours upon him.

The third: that He, glorified is He, made her a source of reform in religion, for her righteousness in religion is among the greatest helpers of his being a caller to Allah, exalted is He. So it is as if he (peace be upon him) asked his Lord for help in religion and in worldly life through both the child and the family together. This is closer to the apparent meaning, because when it is said, "Allah reformed so-and-so," the most apparent meaning concerns what relates to religion. Know that His saying, ﴿and We gave him Yahya and We made his wife fit for him﴾, indicates that the conjunction "wa" does not signify sequence, because the reform of the wife precedes the granting of the child, although He, exalted is He, placed it later in the wording. And He, exalted is He, showed the confirmation of what we have mentioned, saying: ﴿Indeed, they used to hasten to good deeds﴾, and by this He meant Zakariyya, his son and his family. He explained that He gave them what they asked for, and He strengthened some of them by means of others, since their way was that they hastened to good deeds. Hastening in obedience to Allah, exalted is He, is among the greatest qualities for which a person is praised, because it indicates a great eagerness for obedience.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and they called upon Us in hope and in fear﴾, it was recited as "raghaban wa rahaban," and it is like His saying: ﴿who fears the Hereafter and hopes for the mercy of his Lord﴾ [az-Zumar: 9]. The meaning is that they joined to the performance of acts of obedience and hastening in them two matters:

The first: resorting to Allah, exalted is He, out of desire for His reward and fear of His punishment.

The second: khushu' (humble submission), which is the fear firmly lodged in the heart, so the one who is khashi' is the cautious one who does not relax in affairs out of fear of sin.

[The Tenth Story: the story of Maryam, peace be upon her]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And she who guarded her chastity, so We breathed into her of Our Spirit and made her and her son a sign for the worlds.﴾

Know that the implied meaning is: "Mention her who guarded her chastity." Then there are two opinions concerning it.

The first: she guarded her chastity completely, from both the lawful and the unlawful alike, as she said: ﴿No man has touched me, and I have not been unchaste﴾ [Maryam: 20].

The second: [it refers to] the breathing of Jibril (peace be upon him), in that she prevented him from [reaching] the opening of her garment before she recognized him. The first is preferable, because it is the apparent meaning of the wording.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿So We breathed into her of Our Spirit﴾, one may say: breathing the spirit into a body is an expression for giving it life. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My Spirit﴾ [al-Hijr: 29], meaning "I gave him life." If this is established, then His saying ﴿So We breathed into her of Our Spirit﴾ is clearly problematic, because it would indicate the giving of life to Maryam (peace be upon her). The answer comes in several ways:

First: its meaning is "So We breathed the spirit into Isa within her," that is, We gave him life in her womb, just as a piper says, "I blew into the house of so-and-so," meaning into the flute in his house.

Second: We made the breathing into Maryam (peace be upon her) come from Our Spirit, which is Jibril (peace be upon him), for he breathed into the opening of her garment, and the breath reached her womb. Then, Exalted is He, stated in the briefest words the signs that were specific to Maryam and Isa (peace be upon them both), saying: ﴿And We made her and her son a sign for the worlds.﴾ As for Maryam, her signs are many:

One: the pregnancy appeared in her without a male, and this became a sign and a miracle outside the ordinary custom.

Two: her provision used to come to her from Paradise brought by the angels, as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Where has this come to you from? She said: It is from Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 37].

Third and fourth: al-Hasan said: she never once took a breast, and she spoke in her childhood just as Isa (peace be upon him) spoke. As for the signs of Isa (peace be upon him), their explanation has already passed. So He, glory be to Him, made clear that He made the two of them a sign for people, that they might reflect upon what they were singled out with of signs, and derive from them evidence of His power and wisdom, glory be to Him and exalted is He. If it is said: why was it not said "two signs," as He said: ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs﴾ [al-Isra: 12]? We say: because their condition together is one sign, namely her giving birth to him without a father. Here ends the stories.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 21, verses 93–95:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, this community of yours is one community, and I am your Lord, so worship Me.﴾ ﴿But they divided their affair among themselves into sects; each of them will return to Us.﴾

The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Ummah" means millah (religious community, path), and this refers to the millat al-Islam (the religion of Islam), meaning: the religion of Islam is your religion, which you must adhere to, referred to as one religion, not divided. And I am your God, one God, so worship Me. Al-Hasan read "ummatakum" in the accusative as a badal (substitute) of "hadhihi," and read "ummatun" in the nominative as the predicate (khabar). It is also reported from him that both were read in the nominative as two predicates, or that he intended a mubtada' (subject) for the second.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But they divided their affair among themselves﴾, the original form is "wa-taqatta'tum," but the speech has been turned to the third person by way of iltifat (shift of pronoun); as if He is conveying to others what they have corrupted, and disapproving of their action in their presence, saying to them: Do you not see the great thing these people have committed? The meaning is: they made the matter of their religion among themselves into pieces, just as a group distributes a thing and divides it, so that this one gets a share and that one gets a share, as a figure of speech for their disagreement about it and their becoming sects and diverse parties.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿each of them will return to Us﴾, He has threatened them that these divided sects will return to Him, so He will hold them to account and recompense them. It is related from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he said: "The Children of Israel split into seventy-one sects; seventy of them perished and one sect was saved. And my community will split into seventy-two sects; seventy-one will perish and one sect will be saved." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, who is that saved sect?" He said: "The Jama'ah (the main body), the Jama'ah, the Jama'ah."

From this report it becomes clear that what is meant by His saying: ﴿Indeed, this community of yours﴾ is the Jama'ah that holds fast to what Allah the Exalted has explained in this surah of tawhid and prophethood. And that in the Messenger's saying ﷺ about the saved sect, that it is the Jama'ah, is an indication that by it he pointed to the community of faith. Otherwise his saying, in defining the saved sect, that it is the Jama'ah would be meaningless, since there is no sect that adheres to falsehood or truth except that it is a group in terms of number.

Some have criticized the soundness of this report, saying: If by the seventy-two sects he means the principles of the religions, they do not reach this number; and if he means the branches, they exceed this number many times over. It has also been said: the opposite has been reported, namely that they are all saved except one sect. The answer: the meaning is that my community will split in a certain state, and there is no indication in it that it will split in all states; it is not permissible that the number should increase or decrease.

[p. 191]

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So whoever does righteous deeds while being a believer, there will be no denial of his effort, and indeed We are recording it for him.﴾ ﴿And it is forbidden for a city which We have destroyed that they will not return.﴾ ﴿Until, when Gog and Magog are released, and they swarm from every elevated place.﴾ ﴿And the true promise has drawn near, and behold, the eyes of those who disbelieved will stare fixedly. "O woe to us! We were certainly heedless of this; rather, we were wrongdoers."﴾

Know that He, glorified is He, when He mentioned the matter of the community earlier, and mentioned their dispersal, and that they would all return to the place where there is no command except His, followed that with His words: ﴿So whoever does righteous deeds while being a believer, there will be no denial of his effort.﴾ He explained that whoever combines being a believer with doing righteous deeds, then the first (being a believer) includes knowledge and affirmation of Allah and His Messenger, and the second (righteous deeds) includes performing the obligations and abstaining from the prohibited acts. ﴿There will be no denial of his effort﴾, meaning there will be no nullification of the reward for his deed. This is like His words, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it, while being a believer, those are the ones whose effort is appreciated.﴾ [al-Isra' 19]. So "kufran" (denial, ingratitude) is a metaphor for the deprivation of reward, and "shukr" (gratitude) is a metaphor for its granting. His words ﴿there will be no denial﴾ mean the negation of the genus, so that it is in the utmost emphasis, because negating the essence (māhiyyah) necessitates negating all its individual instances.

* * *

As for His words, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed We are recording it for him﴾, the meaning is "and indeed We are recording for his effort." It has been said: the meaning is "guarding it, so that We may reward him for it." It has also been said: "recording it," either in the Mother of the Book (umm al-kitab) or in the scrolls which will be displayed on the Day of Resurrection. The purpose of this is to encourage the servants to hold fast to obedience to Allah, exalted is He.

As for the first, the meaning is: that their non-return is forbidden, i.e., impossible (mumtani'). If their non-return is impossible, then their return is obligatory. This return either means return to the Hereafter or return to this world. As for the first: the meaning is that their return to life in the Abode of the Hereafter is obligatory, and the purpose of this is to refute the view of those who deny resurrection, and to confirm what preceded: that there is no denial of anyone's effort, for He will surely give him the reward for it on the Day of Resurrection. This is the interpretation of Abu Muslim ibn Bahr.

As for the second: the meaning is that their return to this world is obligatory. But it is known that they did not return to this world, so at this point the exegetes mentioned two views.

The first: that "haram" may come with the meaning of "wajib" (obligatory). The evidence for this is the Qur'an, usage, and poetry. As for poetry, the verse of al-Khansa':

"And indeed, forbidden (i.e., obligatory) is it that I do not see the days weeping over their grief except that I weep over 'Amr."

That is, "wa-inna wajiban" (and indeed obligatory). As for usage: naming one of two opposites by the name of the other is a well-known figure of speech (majaz), such as His words: ﴿And the recompense for an evil deed is an evil deed like it﴾ [al-Shura 40]. If this is established, then the meaning is: it is obligatory upon the people of every city which We have destroyed that they will not return. Then they mentioned two matters in explaining the return:

The first: that they will not return from polytheism, nor turn away from it. This is the view of Mujahid and al-Hasan.

The second: that they will not return to this world. This is the view of Qatadah and Muqatil.

The second view: that His words "wa-haram" be left in its apparent sense, and that in His words "la yarji'un" (they do not return) an extra particle (silah za'idah) be taken, just as it is an extra particle in His words: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating?﴾ [al-A'raf 12]. The meaning is: "Forbidden upon a city which We have destroyed is their return to this world," like His words: ﴿So they will not be able to make a bequest, nor return to their families﴾ [Ya-Sin 50]. Or the meaning may be: "and forbidden upon them is their return from polytheism and abandoning faith." This is the view of a group of exegetes. All of this applies if we make His words "﴿And forbidden﴾" the predicate of His words ﴿that they will not return﴾. But if we make it the predicate of something else, then the meaning is: "And forbidden upon a city which We have destroyed is that," referring to what is mentioned in the preceding verse of righteous deeds and appreciated effort which is not denied. Then He gave a reason, saying: ﴿that they do not return﴾ from disbelief, so how could that not be prevented? This is according to the reading "innahum" with a kasrah. The reading with a fathah ("annahum") can also be taken in this sense, meaning "that they do not return."

As for His words, exalted is He: ﴿Until, when Gog and Magog are released, and they swarm from every elevated place. And the true promise has drawn near, and behold, the eyes of those who disbelieved will stare fixedly﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: "hatta" (until) is connected to "haram." As for Abu Muslim's interpretation, the meaning is that their return to the Hereafter is obligatory, to the extent that its obligation reaches the point where, when Gog and Magog are released and the true promise draws near, then behold, the eyes of those who disbelieved will stare fixedly. The meaning is that they will be the first of people present at the assembly of Resurrection. So "hatta" is connected to "haram," and it is its limit (ghayah), but it is a limit of the same kind as the thing, like your saying: "The pilgrims entered, even the pedestrians." Here "hatta" is the one after which speech is related (yuhka). The related speech is this sentence of condition and consequence, namely His words: ﴿when Gog and Magog are released﴾ and ﴿the true promise has drawn near﴾. There the staring of the eyes of those who disbelieved takes place. This is not permissible, because the condition only occurs at the end of the days of this world, while the consequence occurs on the Day of Resurrection, and the condition and the consequence must be close to each other. We say: a slight difference is considered as non-existent. As for the remaining interpretations, the meaning is that the impossibility of their return does not cease until the Hour is established.

The second issue: His words ﴿until, when it is released﴾ mean: the barrier of Gog and Magog is breached. The noun was omitted, and the feminine marker was attached to "futihat" (was released) after the noun was omitted, because Gog and Magog are feminine, being like two tribes. It has also been said: "until, when the direction of Gog was opened."

The third issue: they are two tribes from the kind of mankind. It is said: people are ten parts; nine of them are Gog and Magog, who will come out when the barrier is opened.

The fourth issue: it has been said: the barrier is opened by Allah, exalted is He, directly. It has also been said: rather, when Allah, exalted is He, makes the earth level (dakkan), the hardness is removed from the parts of the earth, and then the barrier will open.

As for His words, exalted is He: ﴿And they swarm from every elevated place﴾, it is an insertion in the middle of the speech. The meaning is: when Gog is released and the true promise draws near, the eyes of those who disbelieved will stare fixedly. "Al-hadab" is a raised place on the earth, and from it comes "hadabat al-ard" (a hump of the earth), and from it "hadabat al-zahr" (a hump of the back). It was also read with a damma on the sin. "Nasala" and "‘asala" mean he hastened. Then there are two views. Most exegetes said: it is a metaphor for Gog and Magog. Mujahid said: it is a metaphor for all the accountable beings, meaning they come out of their graves from every place, and are gathered to the station of reckoning. The first is the more apparent, otherwise the arrangement of the discourse would be disjointed. As for His words, exalted is He: ﴿And the true promise has drawn near﴾, there is no doubt that the promise mentioned is the Day of Resurrection.

As for His words: ﴿Then behold, they﴾, know that "idha" here is for suddenness (lil-mufaja'ah). The appointed time is called a promise figuratively. Know that before His words "O woe to us" there must be an omission, and the estimated speech is: they say: "O woe to us."

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So whoever does righteous deeds while being a believer, there will be no denial of his effort, and indeed We are recording it for him.﴾ ﴿And it is forbidden for a city which We have destroyed that they will not return.﴾ ﴿Until, when Gog and Magog are released, and they swarm from every elevated place.﴾ ﴿And the true promise has drawn near, and behold, the eyes of those who disbelieved will stare fixedly. "O woe to us! We were certainly heedless of this; rather, we were wrongdoers."﴾

Know that He, glorified is He, when He mentioned the matter of the community earlier, and mentioned their dispersal, and that they would all return to the place where there is no command except His, followed that with His words: ﴿So whoever does righteous deeds while being a believer, there will be no denial of his effort.﴾ He explained that whoever combines being a believer with doing righteous deeds, then the first (being a believer) includes knowledge and affirmation of Allah and His Messenger, and the second (righteous deeds) includes performing the obligations and abstaining from the prohibited acts. ﴿There will be no denial of his effort﴾, meaning there will be no nullification of the reward for his deed. This is like His words, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it, while being a believer, those are the ones whose effort is appreciated.﴾ [al-Isra' 19]. So "kufran" (denial, ingratitude) is a metaphor for the deprivation of reward, and "shukr" (gratitude) is a metaphor for its granting. His words ﴿there will be no denial﴾ mean the negation of the genus, so that it is in the utmost emphasis, because negating the essence (māhiyyah) necessitates negating all its individual instances.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 21, verses 98–100:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell; you will be going into it.﴾ ﴿Had these been gods, they would not have entered it, but all of them will abide therein.﴾ ﴿For them therein is a moaning, and they therein will not hear.﴾

Know that His saying ﴿Indeed, you﴾ is addressed to the polytheists of Makkah and the worshippers of idols.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and what you worship besides Allah﴾, it has been narrated that he (ﷺ) entered the mosque while the chieftains of Quraysh were in al-Hatim and around the Ka'bah were three hundred and sixty idols. He sat down with them, and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith met him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spoke with him and silenced him. Then he recited to them: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾, the verse. Then 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zib'ara came and saw them whispering to one another, and said: "What is this discussion of yours?" Al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah informed him of the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). 'Abd Allah said: "By Allah, if I had found him, I would have refuted him. So call him." He (ﷺ) was called, and Ibn al-Zib'ara said: "Did you say that?" He said: "Yes." He said: "I have refuted you, by the Lord of the Ka'bah. Did not the Jews worship 'Uzayr, the Christians worship the Messiah, and the sons of Malih worship the angels?"

Then two narrations are related concerning this:

The first: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) remained silent and did not answer, so the people laughed, and there was revealed His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when the son of Mary is cited as an example, behold, your people turn away from it.﴾ ﴿And they say, "Are our gods better, or is he?" They do not strike it for you except for argument. Rather, they are a quarrelsome people.﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 57–58] And there was revealed concerning 'Isa and the angels: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best reward has preceded from Us﴾ [al-Anbiya': 101], the verse. This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second narration: that he (ﷺ) did answer and said: "Rather, they worshipped the devils, who commanded them to do so." So Allah, glorified is He, revealed: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best reward has preceded from Us﴾ [al-Anbiya': 101], the verse; meaning 'Uzayr, the Messiah and the angels.

Know that the objection of Ibn al-Zib'ara is invalid in several respects:

First: His saying ﴿Indeed, you﴾ is a direct address, and it was with the polytheists of Makkah, who worshipped only idols.

Second: He did not say "those whom you worship" (man), but said "what you worship" (ma), and the word "ma" does not apply to rational beings.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By the sky and He who constructed it﴾ [al-Shams: 5], and His saying: ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ [al-Kafirun: 2], it is taken to refer to "thing." Its parallel here would be to say: "Indeed, you and the thing you worship besides Allah." But the word "thing" does not imply generality, so Ibn al-Zib'ara's objection does not apply.

Third: whoever worships the angels does not claim that they are gods, and He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Had these been gods, they would not have entered it.﴾

Fourth: Grant that generality is established, it is nonetheless specified by rational and revealed proofs regarding the angels, the Messiah and 'Uzayr, for their freedom from sins and transgressions, and Allah promised them every honour. This is what is meant by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best reward has preceded from Us, those will be kept far from it﴾ [al-Anbiya': 101].

Fifth: the answer which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave, namely that they worshipped the devils. If it is said: the devils are rational beings, and the word "ma" does not include them, so how did the Messenger (ﷺ) say that? We say: it is as if he (ﷺ) said: "Even if it is established for you that it includes rational beings, your objection is also not binding from this aspect." As for what is said, that he (ﷺ) remained silent when Ibn al-Zib'ara raised this objection, that is an error; for at the very least he (ﷺ) would have been alert to these answers which the exegetes mention, since he (ﷺ) was more knowledgeable than them in the language and in the interpretation of the Qur'an. How could these answers become apparent to others while none of them became apparent to him (ﷺ)? If it is said: they allowed that he (ﷺ) might remain silent while awaiting clarification, we say: since the clarification was present with him, silence was not permissible for him, lest it be supposed that he had broken off from answering them. Some people answered Ibn al-Zib'ara's objection by saying: Allah, exalted is He, will fashion for them in the Fire an angel in the form of those they worshipped, and then the verse remains upon its apparent meaning. Know that this is weak in two respects:

The first: the people did not worship that image, but worshipped something else which was not present with them in the Fire.

The second: that the angel does not in reality become fuel of Hell, even if it is valid that he enters it, for the guardians of the Fire enter it, yet they are not the fuel of Hell.

Second question: the wisdom in their being mentioned together with their gods in several matters:

First: they will not cease, by being in each other's company, to increase in grief and regret, for they only fell into that punishment because of them, and looking at the face of an enemy is a kind of punishment.

Second: the people had assumed that they would intercede for them in the Hereafter to avert the punishment; when they find the matter the opposite of what they had assumed, nothing will be more hateful to them than them.

Third: casting them into the Fire is in the manner of mockery of their worshippers.

Fourth: it has been said: whatever of them was stone or iron will be heated and stuck to their worshippers, and whatever was wood will be made into live coals with which its worshipper is tormented.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿fuel of Hell﴾, the meaning is that they will be hurled into the Fire of Hell. He likened them to the pebbles with which a thing is struck; so when they are hurled as pebbles are hurled, he made them "fuel of Hell" by way of comparison. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "al-Hasb" means throwing. It was read with a sukun on the sad as a verbal noun used as a description, and it was read "hatab" and "hadab" with the dotted dad, vowelled and unvowelled.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿you will be going into it﴾, the preposition in "lahā" (to it) is permitted because it precedes the verb; you say: "You are for Zayd a striker," as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who are for their trusts and their covenant﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 8], ﴿and those who are for their private parts﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 5], meaning: you are entering it. The meaning is that you must go into it, and there is no escape for you from entering it.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Had these been gods, they would not have entered it﴾, know that His saying ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah﴾ is more fitting for idols because of the use of the word "ma", while this statement is more fitting for the devils because of His saying "these" (hā'ulā'). It is possible that He intends both the devils and the idols, and then the masculine rational form prevails, so that they are mentioned with the expression of rational beings. Allah, exalted is He, drew attention to the fact that whoever is cast into the Fire cannot be a god.

Here there is a question: His saying ﴿Had these been gods, they would not have entered it﴾ is an argument, but they did enter it, so they are not gods. This argument is either something He mentioned for Himself or for others. If He mentioned it for Himself, there is no benefit in it, since He knew that they were not gods. If He mentioned it for others, either He mentions it to one who believes in his prophethood or to one who denies his prophethood. If He mentions it to one who believes in his prophethood, there is no need for this argument, for everyone who believes in his prophethood does not say that these idols are divine. If He mentions it to one who denies his prophethood, that denier does not concede that those gods enter the Fire, and he would deny him in that, so mentioning this argument was futile in any case. Moreover, those who affirm their divinity did not believe that they govern the world, otherwise they would be mad; rather, they believed them to be images of the stars or likenesses of intercessors, and that does not prevent their entering the Fire.

He sat down with them, and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith met him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spoke with him and silenced him. Then he recited to them: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾, the verse. The first: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) remained silent and did not answer, so the people laughed, and there was revealed His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when the son of Mary is cited as an example, behold, your people turn away from it.﴾ ﴿And they say, "Are our gods better, or is he?" They do not strike it for you except for argument. Rather, they are a quarrelsome people.﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 57–58] And there was revealed concerning 'Isa and the angels: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best reward has preceded from Us﴾ [al-Anbiya': 101], the verse. The second narration: that he (ﷺ) did answer and said: "Rather, they worshipped the devils, who commanded them to do so." So Allah, glorified is He, revealed: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best reward has preceded from Us﴾ [al-Anbiya': 101], the verse; meaning 'Uzayr, the Messiah and the angels.

Third: whoever worships the angels does not claim that they are gods, and He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Had these been gods, they would not have entered it.﴾
