Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 21, verses 105–111 (part 1 of 2):

Allah's words: ﴿On the day We roll up the heaven like the rolling up of a written scroll for documents. As We originated the first creation, We shall repeat it; a promise binding upon Us. Indeed, We are ever doing it.﴾ ﴿And We had already written in the Zabur, after the Dhikr, that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants.﴾ ﴿Indeed, in this is a message for a people who worship.﴾ ﴿And We have not sent you, [O Muhammad], except as a mercy to the worlds.﴾

Know that the implied meaning is: "They will not be grieved by the greatest terror on the day We roll up the heaven," or: "and the angels will receive them on the day We roll up the heaven." It is also read as ﴿On the day the heaven is rolled up﴾ in the passive voice. "Al-sijill" is on the pattern of "al-'itill," and "al-sajl" is on the pattern of "al-dalw," and a vowel with kasra is also reported in it. Regarding "al-sijill" there are two opinions:

The first: It is a name for the scroll (tumar) in which things are written. "Al-kitab" originally is a verbal noun like "al-bina'," and then it is applied to what is written. Whoever reads it as a plural (al-kutub) means "for the written things," i.e., for the many meanings written in it. So the meaning of "rolling up the sijill for the kitab" is that the sijill covers that writing and conceals it, because rolling up is the opposite of unfolding, which reveals. The meaning is: We shall roll up the heaven as the scroll in which things are written is rolled up.

The second opinion: It is not a name for the scroll. Then Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "Al-sijill is the name of an angel who rolls up the books of the children of Adam when they are raised to him." This is also related from 'Ali, peace be upon him. Abu al-Jawza' related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it is the name of a scribe who belonged to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This is far-fetched, because the scribes of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were well known, and none of them was named this. Al-Zajjaj said: "It is the man, in the Abyssinian language." On these views, it is like saying "as Zayd rolls up the book," and the lam in "lil-kitab" is extra, as in His words "radifa lakum." If we say that the intended meaning of al-sijill is the scroll, then the verbal noun, which is rolling (tayy), is in the genitive form with the object, and the agent is omitted; the meaning is "like the rolling of the one who rolls the scroll." This last opinion is that of the majority.

Regarding His words: ﴿As We originated the first creation, We shall repeat it﴾ there are several issues:

The first issue: Al-Farra' said: the speech ends at His words "al-kutub," then He begins: ﴿As We originated﴾. Some said: when He said ﴿And the angels will receive them, saying: "This is your day which you were promised"﴾, He followed it with ﴿On the day We roll up the heaven like the rolling up of a written scroll for documents﴾, so He described the day with that, then described it with another description, saying: ﴿As We originated the first creation, We shall repeat it﴾.

The second issue: The author of "al-Kashshaf," may Allah have mercy on him, said: ﴿first creation﴾ is the object of "nu'id" (We shall repeat), which is explained by "nu'iduhu." The kaf is restrained by "ma," and the meaning is: We shall repeat the first of creation as We originated it, likening repetition to origination. If you ask, why is "khalq" indefinite? I say: it is like your saying "the first man who came to me was Zayd," meaning "the first of the men," but you made it singular and indefinite to intend their detail, man by man. Likewise, the meaning of "awwal khalq" is "the first of creation" in the sense of "the first of creatures," because "khalq" is a verbal noun that is not pluralized.

The third issue: They differed about the manner of the repetition. Some said: Allah, exalted is He, separates the parts of bodies without annihilating them, then He restores their composition, and that is the repetition. Others said: He, exalted is He, annihilates them completely, then He brings them back into existence in their very same form a second time. This verse is evidence for this view, because He, glory be to Him, likened repetition to origination. Since origination is not an expression for the composition of scattered parts but for existence after non-existence, the situation in repetition must be the same. Those who hold the first view argue with His words: ﴿And the heavens will be rolled up in His right hand﴾ [al-Zumar: 67], which shows that the heavens, while they are rolled up, exist; and with His words: ﴿On the day the earth will be replaced by another earth﴾ [Ibrahim: 48], which shows that the parts of the earth remain but are made into other than the earth.

As for His words: ﴿a promise binding upon Us﴾, there are two opinions:

The first: that "wa'dan" is an emphatic verbal noun, because His words "nu'iduhu" are a promise of repetition.

The second: that the meaning is "a truth binding upon Us," on account of the information about it and the connection of knowledge to its occurrence, since the occurrence of what Allah knows will occur is necessary. Then, exalted is He, confirmed this with His words: ﴿Indeed, We are ever doing it﴾, meaning: We shall certainly do that, and this is an emphasis of the promise He mentioned.

As for His words: ﴿And We had already written in the Zabur, after the Dhikr﴾ there are issues:

The first issue: Hamza read "al-Zubur" with a damma on the zay, and the rest read it with a fatha. The word "al-Zabur" is like "al-halub" and "al-rakub." It is said: "zabartu al-kitab," meaning "I wrote the book." "Al-Zubur" with a damma on the zay is the plural of "zibr," like "qishr" and "qushur." The meaning of the two readings is one, because al-Zabur is the book.

The second issue: Regarding al-Zabur and al-Dhikr there are several views:

First: This is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Kalbi, Muqatil and Ibn Zayd: al-Zabur is the revealed books, and al-Dhikr is the Book which is the Mother of the Book in heaven, because in it is the writing of everything that will occur, as a lesson for the angels, and the books of the prophets, peace be upon them, are copied from that Book.

Second: al-Zabur is the Qur'an, and al-Dhikr is the Torah. This is the view of Qatadah and al-Sha'bi.

Third: al-Zabur is the Zabur of Dawud, peace be upon him, and al-Dhikr is what is narrated from him, peace be upon him, who said: "Allah existed and there was nothing with Him; then He created the Dhikr."

In my view there is a fourth opinion: that the intended meaning of al-Dhikr is knowledge, i.e., "We wrote that in the Zabur after We had knowledge that is not subject to inattention or forgetfulness." For whoever writes something and commits to it, but inattention is possible for him, is not relied upon; but whoever is not subject to inattention or failure, when he commits to something, that thing is necessarily going to occur.

As for His words: ﴿that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants﴾ there are several views:

First: The earth is the earth of Paradise, and the righteous servants are the believers who act in obedience to Allah, exalted is He. The meaning is that Allah, exalted is He, wrote in the books of the prophets, peace be upon them, and in the Preserved Tablet, that He would make those of His servants who are righteous inherit Paradise. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrimah, al-Suddi and Abu al-'Aliyah. These scholars supported this view with several points:

Firstly: His words: ﴿And He has caused us to inherit the earth; we settle in Paradise wherever we will. And excellent is the reward of the workers﴾ [al-Zumar: 74].

Secondly: Because it is the earth which is specific to the righteous, since it was created for them; others who are in Paradise with them are there by way of following. As for the earth of this world, it is for both the righteous and the non-righteous.

Thirdly: Because this earth is mentioned right after the repetition and after the repetition; the earth described in this way can only be Paradise.

Fourthly: It has been reported in a report that it is the earth of Paradise, for it is white and pure.

Second: The intended earth is the earth of this world, for He, glory be to Him, will make the believers inherit it in this world. This is the view of al-Kalbi and Ibn 'Abbas in some narrations. The evidence for this view is His words, glory be to Him: ﴿Allah has promised those who believe﴾ [al-Nur: 55] up to His words: ﴿He will surely make them successors in the earth﴾ [al-Nur: 55], and His words, exalted is He: ﴿Musa said to his people: "Seek help in Allah and be patient. Indeed, the earth belongs to Allah; He causes whom He wills of His servants to inherit it"﴾ [al-A'raf: 128].

Third: It is the Holy Land, which the righteous will inherit. Its evidence is His words: ﴿And We caused the people who had been oppressed to inherit the eastern and western parts of the land which We had blessed﴾ [al-A'raf: 137]. Then, in the end, it will be inherited by the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ) at the descent of 'Isa son of Maryam, peace be upon him.

As for His words: ﴿Indeed, in this is a message for a people who worship﴾, His words "this" refer to what is mentioned in this surah of reports, promises, warnings and effective admonitions. "Al-balagh" means sufficiency and that by which the desired aim is reached. It has been said about "al-'abidin" that they are the scholars; it has been said: rather, they are those who act. The better view is that they are those who combine both matters, because knowledge is like a tree and action is like fruit; a tree without fruit is of no benefit, and fruit without a tree does not exist.

As for His words: ﴿And We have not sent you, [O Muhammad], except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ there are several issues:

The first issue: He, peace be upon him, was a mercy in religion and in this world. As for religion, he, peace be upon him, was sent when people were in ignorance and error, and the People of the Two Books were in confusion about their religion because of the long passage of time, the breaking of continuous transmission, and the occurrence of disagreement in their books. So Allah, exalted is He, sent Muhammad (ﷺ) when there was no path for the seeker of truth to attain success and reward. He called them to the truth, showed them the way to reward, legislated rulings for them, and distinguished the lawful from the unlawful. Then, only the one whose aspiration is to seek the truth benefits from this mercy, so he does not rely on blind imitation or on obstinacy and arrogance; and success accompanies him. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: "It is, for those who believe, guidance and healing"﴾ [Fussilat: 44] up to His words: ﴿And it is blindness for them﴾ [Fussilat: 44].

As for this world, they were freed through him from much humiliation, fighting and wars, and they were given victory through the blessing of his religion. If it is said: How was he a mercy when he came with the sword and the seizing of wealth? We reply: the answer has several aspects:

First: He came with the sword only against the one who was arrogant and obstinate and did not reflect or contemplate; and among the attributes of Allah are "the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate," and then He is an avenger against the disobedient. And He said: ﴿And We sent down from the sky blessed water﴾ [Qaf: 9], and then it may be a cause of corruption.

Second: Every prophet before our Prophet, when his people denied him, Allah destroyed the deniers by sinking, transformation or drowning; and Allah, exalted is He, delayed the punishment of those who denied our Messenger until death or until the Resurrection. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾ [al-Anfal: 33]. It may be objected: did He not say: ﴿Fight them; Allah will punish them by your hands﴾ [al-Tawbah: 14], and: ﴿That Allah may punish the hypocrite men and hypocrite women﴾ [al-Ahzab: 73]? We reply: specification of the general does not undermine it.

Third: He, peace be upon him, was at the peak of good character. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed, you are of a great moral character﴾ [al-Qalam: 4]. Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "It was said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'Invoke curse upon the polytheists.' He said: 'I was sent only as a mercy, and I was not sent as a punishment.'" And in a narration from Hudhayfah he said: "I am only a human; I become angry as humans become angry. So whichever man I insult or curse, O Allah, make that a blessing for him on the Day of Resurrection."

Fourth: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: ﴿except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ means specifically the believers. The Imam Abu al-Qasim al-Ansari said: the two views return to one meaning, because we have shown that he was a mercy to all if they had reflected upon the signs of Allah and the signs of His Messenger; as for the one who turned away and was arrogant, he fell into trial from his own side, as He said: ﴿And it is blindness for them﴾ [Fussilat: 44].

**Second issue:** The Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazilites, a theological school that emphasized divine justice and human free will) said: If God willed disbelief from the disbelievers, and did not will from them the acceptance of the Messenger, but willed from them nothing except that they reject him, and created that in them, and created them only in that state, as the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah, the majority Sunni theological position) say, then his sending would necessarily be a vengeance and a punishment upon them, not a mercy. That would contradict this text. It cannot be said that his mission, peace be upon him, is a mercy to the disbelievers in that he did not hasten their punishment in this world, as he hastened the punishment of the other nations. For we say: his being a mercy is of one degree for all, and what you have mentioned for the disbelievers is also obtained by the believers. So it must be that it is a mercy to the disbelievers from the same aspect in which it became a mercy to the believers. Furthermore, the worldly blessings that they mentioned were already obtained by the disbelievers before his mission (ﷺ), just as they were after it. Rather, their worldly blessings before his mission were greater, because after his mission, grief and fear of him came upon them, and then he was commanded to wage jihad (struggle, including armed struggle), in which most of them perished. Therefore, it is not permissible that this be what is meant.

**The answer:** We say: When God, glory be to Him and exalted, knew that Abu Lahab would never believe, and informed about him that he would not believe, then commanding him to believe would be a command that turns His knowledge into ignorance and His true report into a lie, and that is impossible. So He would have commanded him to do the impossible. And if the mission, together with this statement, is a mercy, then why is it not permissible to say: the mission is a mercy even though He created disbelief in the disbeliever? Also, if the disbeliever's capacity is suitable only for disbelief, then the question remains binding upon them. And if his capacity is suitable for both opposites, it requires a determining factor (murajjih) from God, the Exalted, to decide between them, in order to avoid an infinite regress (tasalsul). In that case the objection returns. Then we say: Why is it not permissible that it be a mercy to the disbeliever in the sense of delaying the punishment of annihilation (isti'sal) from him?

As for his statement: "First, since it is a mercy to all in one degree, it must be a mercy to the disbelievers from the aspect in which it was a mercy to the believers," we say: There is nothing in the verse indicating that he, peace be upon him, is a mercy to all in one respect or in two different respects. Your claim that the aspect is one is therefore an arbitrary assertion (tahakkum).

As for his statement: "The blessings of this world were already obtained by the disbelievers before," we say: Yes. But when he, peace be upon him, was sent as a mercy to the believers, fear of the descent of punishment arose among the disbelievers. When that fear was removed from them through his presence, that became a mercy in regard to the disbelievers.

**Third issue:** They (the Mu'tazilah, or the scholars who hold this view) used this verse to argue that he (ﷺ) is superior to the angels. They said: The angels are among the "worlds" (al-'alamin), so by the ruling of this verse he, peace be upon him, must be a mercy to the angels, and therefore he must be superior to them. The answer: This is countered by God's statement regarding the angels: ﴿And they seek forgiveness for those who believe﴾ [Ghafir: 7], and that is a mercy from them toward the believers, and the Messenger, peace be upon him, is included among the believers. Likewise is His statement: ﴿Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾ [al-Ahzab: 56].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 21, verse 112:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "It is only revealed to me that your God is one God; so will you submit?"﴾ ﴿But if they turn away, say, "I have announced to you on equal terms, and I do not know whether what you are promised is near or far.﴾ ﴿Indeed, He knows what is spoken openly and He knows what you conceal.﴾ ﴿And I do not know; perhaps it is a trial for you and enjoyment for a time.﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, judge with truth. And our Lord is the Most Merciful, the one sought for help against what you describe."﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had presented to the disbelievers the proofs that there is no god besides Him, from the aspects that have already been mentioned, and had explained that He sent His Messenger as a mercy to the worlds, He followed that with what would serve as a warning and a notice in the struggle against them and in confronting them. So He said: ﴿Say, "It is only revealed to me"﴾. And in this there are several issues:

The first issue: The author of the "Kashshaf" said: "Innama (only) restricts a ruling to a thing, or restricts a thing to a ruling, like your saying: Innama Zayd qa'im (Zayd is only standing), or innama yaqumu Zayd (only Zayd stands). Both examples have been combined in this verse, because ﴿It is only revealed to me﴾ together with its agent is in the position of innama yaqumu Zayd, and ﴿that your God is one God﴾ is in the position of innama Zayd qa'im. The benefit of combining them is the indication that the revelation to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is restricted to affirming the oneness of Allah, the Exalted. And in His saying, ﴿so will you submit?﴾, there is [the implication] that revelation that comes in this manner requires that you single out tawhid for Him and that you free yourselves from ascribing rivals to Him. And in it is the indication that tawhid may be established by revelation (sam'). If it is said: if innama indicates restriction, it would follow that nothing was revealed to the Messenger except tawhid, and it is known that this is false. We say: what is intended by it is emphasis (mubalaghah)."

As for His saying, ﴿But if they turn away, say, "I have announced to you on equal terms"﴾, the author of the "Kashshaf" said: "Adhana is derived from adhina, meaning he knew, but its usage became frequent in the sense of warning, and from it is His saying: ﴿then be informed of a war from Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Baqarah: 279]."

Having understood this, we say: The exegetes have mentioned several aspects regarding it:

First: Abu Muslim said: the announcement "on equal terms" is a call to war openly, based on His saying: ﴿then throw back to them on equal terms﴾ [al-Anfal: 58]. The benefit of this is that it was possible for someone to assume about the polytheists of Quraysh that their situation differed from the rest of the disbelievers in the matter of fighting, so He informed them by this that they are like the disbelievers in that.

Second: The meaning is: "I have informed you of what is obligatory upon you, of tawhid and other matters, on equal terms, so I did not differentiate between you in conveying and explaining, because I was sent as a teacher." The purpose of this is to remove any excuse, lest they say: ﴿Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 134].

Third: "on equal terms" means openly and publicly.

Fourth: "on equal terms" means gradually (ala mahal), and the meaning is that I do not hasten with war concerning which I have announced to you, but I give respite and delay, hoping for your Islam.

As for His saying, ﴿And I do not know whether what you are promised is near or far﴾, there are two aspects. One: ﴿whether what you are promised is near or far﴾ refers to the Day of Resurrection and to the punishment of this world. It was then said: this was abrogated by His saying: ﴿and the true promise has drawn near﴾ [al-Anbiya': 97], meaning of both of them, for such a report is not permissible to abrogate.

The second: the meaning is that concerning what He announced to them of war, he does not know whether it is near

or far, lest it be assumed that it will be delayed. It is as if He, exalted is He, commanded him to warn them of the jihad which would be revealed to him to come later, and did not inform him of the time; therefore He commanded him to say that he does not know whether its nearness or its distance. Through this it becomes clear that the surah is Meccan, and that the command to fight came after the Hijrah.

Third: "what you are promised" of the victory of the Muslims over them is certain to occur, and humiliation and abasement will necessarily befall them, although I do not know when it will be, because Allah, exalted is He, has not informed me of it.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, He knows what is spoken openly and He knows what you conceal﴾, the purpose of it is the command to sincerity and the abandonment of hypocrisy, because when He, exalted is He, knows the hidden thoughts, it is obligatory upon the rational person to be thorough in sincerity.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And I do not know; perhaps it is a trial for you and enjoyment for a time﴾, there are several aspects:

First: "perhaps" means the delay of the punishment from you.

Second: "perhaps" the ambiguity of the time at which the punishment will descend upon you is a trial for you, meaning an affliction and a test for you, to see your conduct, and whether you will produce repentance and return from your disbelief or not.

Third: al-Hasan said: "perhaps what you are in of this world is an affliction for you," and fitnah means trial and testing.

Fourth: "perhaps the delay of the jihad is a trial for you, if you remain upon your disbelief, because what leads to great harm is a trial." He said "I do not know" to allow the possibility that they would believe, so their being left would not be a trial, but would turn out to be a blessing and mercy.

Fifth: the meaning may be: "And I do not know; perhaps what I have explained, informed and warned of is a trial for you, because it is an increase in your punishment if you do not believe, since the one who turns away from faith despite clear explanation, state after state, will have a greater punishment, and when Allah, exalted is He, provides for him in this world, that will be like a proof against him."

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿He said, "My Lord, judge with truth"﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: It was read: "Qul Rabbi uhkum bil-haqq" (say, "My Lord, judge with truth") with the kasrah being sufficient; "Rabbu uhkum" with the damma; "Rabbi ahkamu" as the superlative form (af'al al-tafdil); and "Rabbiya ahkama" from ihkam.

The second issue: ﴿My Lord, judge with truth﴾ has several aspects:

First: that is, "My Lord, decide between me and my people with truth," meaning with punishment; as if he said: decide between me and those who denied me with punishment. Qatadah said: Allah, exalted is He, commanded him to follow the prophets in this supplication, and they used to say: ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people with truth﴾ [al-A'raf: 89]. So Allah, exalted is He, indeed judged against them with killing on the day of Badr.

Second: "Separate between me and them by what makes the truth manifest to all, which is that You support me against them."

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And our Lord is the Most Merciful, the one sought for help against what you describe﴾, there are two aspects:

One: that is, of shirk and disbelief, and of the falsehoods and denials by which you oppose my call. It is as if He, glorified is He, said: say, calling upon Me: ﴿My Lord, judge with truth﴾, and say, warning the disbelievers: ﴿And our Lord is the Most Merciful, the one sought for help against what you describe﴾. Ibn 'Amir read it with a yā' with a dot below (i.e., "yasifu," "they describe"), meaning: say to your companions, the believers, "And our Lord is the Most Merciful, the one sought for help against what the disbelievers describe of falsehoods," that is, of help in repelling their falsehoods.

Second: They used to hope that they would have power and dominance, so Allah belied their assumptions, frustrated their hopes, granted victory to His Messenger ﷺ and the believers, and humiliated them. The judge (al-Qadi) said: Allah concluded this surah with His saying: ﴿He said, "My Lord, judge with truth"﴾ because he, peace be upon him, had reached the utmost limit in clarity for them, and they had reached the extreme in harming and denying him. So the most that could be said concerning this, exalted is He, is consolation for him and an indication that the aim is their benefit. When they refuse except to persist in their disbelief, then you must turn to your Lord so that He may judge between you and them with truth, either by hastening punishment through jihad or otherwise, or by delaying that, for their matter, though delayed, is what is coming and near. What is reported, that he, peace be upon him, used to say that in his wars, is like an indication that He commanded him to say this statement

as urging the command to fight them. And success is from Allah. May His blessings be upon the best of His creation, Muhammad the Prophet, and his family and companions, and may He grant them abundant peace. Amen.

The twenty-second part is complete, and it is followed by the twenty-third part, whose beginning is Surat al-Hajj.
